examTip.trick: **q = k H (N_f/N_d) = 3×10⁻⁴ × 5 × (12/20) = 9.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s per metre.** The shape factor 0.6 is pure geometry.
examTip.trap: **N_f and N_d count the SPACES, not the LINES** — 13 flow lines give 12 channels, 21 equipotentials give 20 drops. If a question gives LINES, subtract one from each.
examTip.mnemonic: **The fields must be SQUARE so that the side b cancels in the derivation** — that is what makes each channel carry equal flow and each drop equal head. And squares CROWD where the gradient is dangerous, so a flow net shows you the piping risk before you compute it.

questions.stem: A saturated clay is subjected to an unconfined compression test and fails at an axial stress of 120 kN/m². Its undrained cohesion is:
questions.solution:
**60 kN/m².**

**The relation:**

> **c_u = q_u / 2**, where q_u is the unconfined compressive strength.

> **c_u = 120/2 = 60 kN/m²** ✓

**Why the factor of two — the Mohr circle argument:**

> **In an unconfined compression test the CONFINING pressure is ZERO:**

> **σ₃ = 0 and σ₁ = q_u = 120 kN/m²**

> **So the Mohr circle has:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Diameter (σ₁ − σ₃)** | **120 kN/m²** |
| **RADIUS (σ₁ − σ₃)/2** | **60 kN/m²** |
| **Centre** | **at 60 kN/m² on the normal stress axis** |

> **For a SATURATED clay tested undrained, φ_u = 0, so the failure envelope is a HORIZONTAL LINE.**

> **A horizontal envelope tangent to the circle touches it at its TOP — at a height equal to the RADIUS.**

> **And the height of the envelope above the axis IS the cohesion.**

> **Hence c_u = radius = (σ₁ − σ₃)/2 = q_u/2 = 60 kN/m²** ✓

> **So the factor of two is the difference between a DIAMETER and a RADIUS, which is the whole content of the relation.**

> **Note that option (a) 120 kN/m² is the diameter — the deviator stress itself — offered to catch precisely that confusion.**

**Why φ_u = 0 for a saturated clay — the reason worth understanding:**

> **In an UNDRAINED test on a SATURATED specimen, no water can leave and the specimen cannot change volume.**

> **So when the confining pressure is raised, the additional pressure is carried ENTIRELY BY THE WATER: the pore pressure rises by exactly the same amount.**

> **The EFFECTIVE stress σ' = σ − u is therefore UNCHANGED.**

> **And since strength depends on effective stress, the strength is unchanged too.**

> **Hence every undrained test on the same saturated clay, at any cell pressure, gives the SAME deviator stress at failure — Mohr circles of EQUAL DIAMETER at different positions — and the common tangent is HORIZONTAL: φ_u = 0.**

> **That is a complete and satisfying explanation, and it means the result need not be memorised as a fact.**

> **It also carries a corollary: the undrained strength of a saturated clay is a SINGLE NUMBER, independent of depth or confining pressure, for a given state of consolidation.** Which is why c_u is quoted as one value and used directly in short-term stability calculations.

**The consistency classification, since c_u is what defines it:**

| c_u (kN/m²) | Consistency | Field identification |
|---|---|---|
| **< 12.5** | **Very soft** | **Extrudes between the fingers when squeezed** |
| **12.5 - 25** | **Soft** | Easily moulded with the fingers |
| **25 - 50** | **Medium (firm)** | **Moulded by strong finger pressure** |
| **50 - 100** | **Stiff** | **Indented by the thumb; cannot be moulded** ← c_u = 60 |
| **100 - 200** | **Very stiff** | Indented by the thumbnail |
| **> 200** | **Hard** | Difficult to indent at all |

> **So this clay is STIFF — a competent foundation soil.**

> **The FIELD IDENTIFICATION column is genuinely useful: an experienced engineer can classify a clay by hand to within one category, and the ability to do so is the difference between reading a borehole log and understanding it.**

> **And note that q_u — the unconfined strength — is twice c_u, so the same classification in terms of q_u runs 25, 50, 100, 200, 400 kN/m². Both scales are in use, and confusing them shifts every classification by one category.**

**The unconfined compression test's place among the shear tests:**

| | **Unconfined compression** | **Triaxial UU** |
|---|---|---|
| **Cell pressure** | **ZERO** | Applied |
| **Result** | **c_u = q_u/2** | c_u from the Mohr circles |
| **Speed and cost** | **Very quick and cheap** ← | Slower |
| **Suits** | **Saturated intact clay** | Any clay |
| **Fails on** | **Fissured clay — it falls apart; sandy or silty clay — it will not stand unsupported** |

> **Its limitation is precisely its virtue: needing no cell, it needs the specimen to stand up by itself.**

> **A FISSURED clay will part along a fissure at a stress far below its intact strength, and the test then measures the fissures rather than the clay.**

> **And a silty or sandy clay may simply crumble on the platen.**

> **So the unconfined test is a rapid classification and control test for intact saturated clay, and the triaxial test is the reference** — which is the usual relationship between a quick index test and a definitive one.

**Why the UNDRAINED strength is the right parameter for some problems and not others:**

| Problem | Use |
|---|---|
| **Bearing capacity of a footing on clay, immediately after construction** | **c_u — the UNDRAINED case, φ = 0 analysis** ← |
| **Stability of a cut slope in clay, immediately after excavation** | **c_u — the short-term case, which is the CRITICAL one for a CUT** |
| **Stability of an EMBANKMENT on clay, long term** | **c', φ' — the DRAINED case, which is critical for a FILL** |
| **Settlement** | **Never c_u — settlement needs the compressibility, m_v and c_v** |

> **The contrast in the middle two rows is worth fixing, because it is counter-intuitive and it matters:**

> **A CUT slope is most critical in the SHORT term. Excavation REDUCES the total stress, so the pore pressure falls below equilibrium and then rises with time, weakening the soil — so the factor of safety DECREASES with time and the long-term drained case governs. (The short-term case is checked, but the cut gets worse, not better.)**

> **An EMBANKMENT on soft clay is most critical in the SHORT term for the reverse reason: loading raises the pore pressure, which then dissipates and strengthens the foundation — so the factor of safety INCREASES with time.**

> **That is precisely why embankments on soft ground are built in STAGES, with waiting periods: each stage consolidates the clay, raising its strength enough to carry the next.** A single-stage fill of the full height would fail, while the same fill placed in three stages over two years stands — the same material, the same geometry, and a different outcome entirely from the sequencing.
tags: short term versus long term stability

examTip.trick: **c_u = q_u/2 = 120/2 = 60 kN/m².** With σ₃ = 0, the Mohr circle's diameter is q_u and the horizontal φ_u = 0 envelope touches it at its top — so c_u is the RADIUS.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 120 is the DIAMETER, the deviator stress itself.** The factor of two is nothing more than diameter versus radius.
examTip.mnemonic: **φ_u = 0 because raising the cell pressure on a sealed saturated specimen raises u equally, leaving σ' unchanged** — so every undrained circle has the same diameter and the envelope is horizontal. And CUT slopes are critical long-term; EMBANKMENTS on clay short-term, which is why fills are staged.

questions.stem: In the method of slices for slope stability analysis, the FELLENIUS (ordinary) method is known to give a factor of safety that is:
options: Higher than the more rigorous methods, and therefore unsafe
Conservative — lower than the more rigorous methods
questions.solution:
**CONSERVATIVE — lower than the more rigorous methods, typically by 5 to 20 per cent.**

**Why the Fellenius method under-predicts:**

> **The FELLENIUS (Swedish, ordinary method of slices) method makes one drastic simplification: it NEGLECTS THE INTERSLICE FORCES ENTIRELY.**

> **That is, the forces each slice exerts on its neighbours are assumed to cancel, so each slice is analysed in isolation with only its weight, the normal reaction and the shear resistance on its base.**

> **The consequence is that the computed NORMAL force on each slice's base is too small.**

> **And since the frictional component of strength is (N tan φ), a normal force that is too small gives a shear resistance that is too small — hence a FACTOR OF SAFETY that is too low.**

> **So the error is on the SAFE side, and the method is conservative.**

**The magnitude of the error, since "conservative" is not enough:**

| Condition | Fellenius error against Bishop |
|---|---|
| **φ = 0 (undrained clay)** | **Small — a few per cent; the frictional term vanishes** |
| **Moderate φ, no pore pressure** | **5 to 10 per cent low** |
| **High φ with HIGH PORE PRESSURE** | **Up to 50 per cent low — seriously in error** ← |
| Deep circles, steep slopes | Larger errors |

> **The last row is the important qualification: the Fellenius method's error is NOT uniformly modest.**

> **With high pore pressures the computed normal stress can even come out NEGATIVE for slices near the toe, which is physically impossible and shows the method has broken down.**

> **So "conservative" should not be read as "safe to use": a method that may be 50 per cent wrong is uneconomic where it is right and untrustworthy where it fails.**

> **Its place today is as a HAND-CALCULATION check and a teaching method, not as a design tool** — and being honest about that is more useful than defending it.

**The methods compared, in order of rigour:**

| Method | Interslice forces | Equilibrium satisfied | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FELLENIUS (ordinary)** | **NEGLECTED** | **Moment only** | **Simplest; conservative; non-iterative** ← |
| **BISHOP'S SIMPLIFIED** | **NORMAL forces included; shear neglected** | **Moment, and vertical for each slice** | **ITERATIVE; the practical standard** |
| **JANBU'S simplified** | Normal included | **FORCE equilibrium** | Suits non-circular surfaces |
| **SPENCER** | **Both, with a CONSTANT inclination** | **Both force and moment** | Rigorous |
| **MORGENSTERN-PRICE** | **Both, with an assumed VARIABLE function** | **Both force and moment** | **The most general; the reference method** |

> **BISHOP'S SIMPLIFIED method is the one to know, because it is what practice actually uses:**

> **It includes the interslice NORMAL forces and neglects only the interslice SHEAR, which turns out to be a small approximation — Bishop's results are typically within 1 to 2 per cent of the fully rigorous methods.**

> **Its cost is that the factor of safety appears on BOTH sides of the equation, so it must be solved ITERATIVELY: guess F, compute F, repeat until it converges.**

> **Convergence is normally rapid — three or four cycles — which is why the method was practical even before computers.**

**Why option (d) is wrong, and instructively:**

> **The method of slices works for ANY soil, and it is in fact most reliable for φ = 0 undrained clay, where the interslice force error nearly vanishes.**

> **For a purely COHESIONLESS soil the method of slices is unnecessary: a dry sand slope's stability is given by the infinite slope result:**

> **F = tan φ / tan β**

> **— independent of the slope's height, which is a remarkable and useful result.**

> **The slope stands if β < φ and fails if β > φ, whatever its size.** So the stable angle of a dry sand slope is simply its angle of internal friction, which is also its ANGLE OF REPOSE.

> **That is why a sand pile always forms the same cone angle regardless of how much sand is poured** — and why the method of slices, with all its machinery, is reserved for soils with cohesion, layering or pore pressure.

**The infinite slope with SEEPAGE, since it is the case that catches people:**

> **For a cohesionless slope with seepage PARALLEL to the surface:**

> **F = (γ' / γ_sat) × (tan φ / tan β)**

> **And γ'/γ_sat ≈ 10/20 = 0.5, so the factor of safety is HALVED.**

> **Which means the stable angle of a saturated sand slope with seepage is roughly tan⁻¹(0.5 tan φ) — about 20° for φ = 35°, against 35° when dry.**

> **That single factor of two explains why slopes fail during and after heavy rain rather than in dry weather**, and why drainage is the most cost-effective slope stabilisation measure available.

> **It is worth stating plainly: for most slope failures, WATER is the cause. Not the soil, not the angle, not the loading — the water.** And the corollary is that a drainage measure that costs a fraction of a retaining structure will often do more good.

**The critical circle, since the analysis must be repeated:**

> **Every method of slices analyses ONE assumed failure surface.**

> **The factor of safety of the SLOPE is the MINIMUM over all possible surfaces, so many trial circles must be analysed to find the critical one.**

> **That search is what makes slope stability a computer problem in practice, and it is also where a hand calculation most often goes wrong: analysing one plausible circle and reporting its factor of safety as the slope's.**

> **Taylor's stability charts exist precisely to shortcut the search for simple homogeneous cases**, giving the critical stability number directly for a given slope angle and depth factor — which remains a useful check on any computer output.

examTip.trick: **Fellenius NEGLECTS the interslice forces**, so the computed normal force on each base is too small, the frictional term N tan φ is too small, and **F comes out LOW — conservative.**
examTip.trap: **"Conservative" is not the same as "safe to use": with high pore pressure the error reaches 50 per cent**, and the normal stress can come out negative near the toe, which means the method has broken down. It is a check method, not a design tool.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bishop's simplified keeps the interslice NORMAL forces and drops only the SHEAR** — within 1-2 % of rigorous, at the cost of iteration. And for a cohesionless infinite slope F = tanφ/tanβ, HALVED by seepage: which is why water, not geometry, causes most slope failures.

questions.stem: A smooth vertical retaining wall 6 m high retains a cohesionless backfill of unit weight 18 kN/m³ and angle of internal friction 30°. The total ACTIVE thrust per metre run is:
questions.solution:
**108 kN per metre run.**

**Step 1 — Rankine's coefficient of active earth pressure:**

> **K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45° − φ/2)**

> **For φ = 30°:  K_a = (1 − 0.5)/(1 + 0.5) = 0.5/1.5 = 1/3**

> **The value 1/3 for φ = 30° is worth knowing by heart — it is the commonest case in examinations.**

**Step 2 — the total thrust:**

> **P_a = ½ K_a γ H²**

> **= ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 6²**

> **= ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 36**

> **= ½ × 216 = 108 kN per metre** ✓

**Step 3 — its point of application:**

> **The pressure distribution is TRIANGULAR — zero at the top, maximum at the base — so the resultant acts at the CENTROID of that triangle:**

> **At H/3 = 6/3 = 2 m ABOVE THE BASE.**

> **The maximum pressure at the base is K_a γ H = (1/3)(18)(6) = 36 kN/m², and ½ × 36 × 6 = 108 kN** ✓ — confirming the thrust.

**Why the distractors are what they are:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **324 kN** | **½ γ H² with K_a omitted: ½ × 18 × 36 = 324** |
| **216 kN** | **K_a γ H² without the ½ — the pressure treated as uniform** |
| **108 kN** | ✓ |
| **972 kN** | **½ K_p γ H² with K_p = 3 — the PASSIVE thrust** ← |

> **Option (d) is the most instructive: 972 kN is the PASSIVE thrust for the same wall, which is NINE TIMES the active.**

> **The factor is exactly nine because K_p = 1/K_a for a smooth vertical wall with a level backfill: K_p = 3 against K_a = 1/3.**

> **That ratio K_p/K_a = 9 for φ = 30° is worth carrying, because it makes the physical asymmetry vivid.**

**Why ACTIVE and PASSIVE differ so enormously — the physical explanation:**

| | **ACTIVE** | **PASSIVE** |
|---|---|---|
| **The wall** | **MOVES AWAY from the soil** | **PUSHES INTO the soil** |
| **The soil** | **EXPANDS laterally; its own strength helps hold it up** | **is COMPRESSED laterally; its strength must be OVERCOME** |
| **Coefficient (φ=30°)** | **1/3** | **3** |
| **Magnitude** | **MINIMUM possible lateral pressure** | **MAXIMUM possible lateral resistance** |
| **Wall movement needed** | **SMALL — about 0.1-0.5 % of H** | **LARGE — 2-5 % of H, sometimes more** ← |

> **The last row is the practically decisive one and it is frequently overlooked.**

> **ACTIVE pressure develops after a very small wall movement — a few millimetres on a 6 m wall — which is why it can be relied upon: any real wall moves that much.**

> **PASSIVE resistance requires a LARGE movement to develop fully — perhaps 150 mm on a 6 m wall.**

> **So a design that counts on full passive resistance is counting on a displacement that may be unacceptable for the structure it supports.**

> **That is why codes require passive resistance to be reduced by a substantial factor — often taking only half or a third of the theoretical value — while active pressure is used at full value.**

> **The asymmetry in the safety treatment mirrors the asymmetry in the required movement, which is a satisfying instance of a code rule that encodes real behaviour.**

**The AT-REST condition, which lies between them:**

> **K₀ ≈ 1 − sin φ** for a normally consolidated soil.

> **For φ = 30°: K₀ = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5, giving a thrust of ½ × 0.5 × 18 × 36 = 162 kN.**

| State | K (φ=30°) | Thrust | Applies to |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **0.333** | **108 kN** | **A wall free to move — a cantilever retaining wall** ← |
| **AT REST** | **0.50** | **162 kN** | **A wall PREVENTED from moving — a basement wall, a braced excavation, a wall keyed into rock** |
| **PASSIVE** | **3.00** | **972 kN** | The resisting side of a sheet pile or a footing |

> **Choosing between active and at-rest is a real design decision and not a formality: a basement wall restrained by the floor slabs cannot move, so it must be designed for K₀ — a 50 per cent greater thrust than active.**

> **Designing a restrained wall for active pressure is a genuine and not-uncommon error**, and it under-designs the wall by half.

**The assumptions built into Rankine's theory, since they are what limit it:**

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **The wall is SMOOTH — no friction between wall and soil** | **CONSERVATIVE for active pressure: real wall friction reduces the active thrust** ← |
| **The soil is homogeneous, isotropic, cohesionless (in this form)** | Extended forms handle cohesion and layers |
| **The backfill surface is level** | Sloping-backfill forms exist |
| **The failure surface is a PLANE** | True for active; less so for passive |
| **Plastic equilibrium throughout the mass** | The theoretical basis |

> **The smooth-wall assumption is worth flagging as CONSERVATIVE for the active case: real wall friction has a downward component on the soil, which helps support it and REDUCES the active thrust.**

> **COULOMB'S theory includes wall friction and gives a smaller active thrust than Rankine's — so using Rankine for a rough wall is safe, if slightly uneconomic.**

> **For the PASSIVE case the situation reverses: Rankine's smooth-wall assumption gives a value that is too LOW, and Coulomb's rough-wall passive coefficient can be very much larger — which sounds attractive and is treated with caution, because the plane failure surface assumption becomes poor for passive conditions.**

> **So the honest summary is that Rankine active is conservative and reliable, and passive resistance from any theory should be discounted heavily.**

examTip.trick: **K_a = (1−sin30)/(1+sin30) = 1/3; P_a = ½ K_a γ H² = ½ × ⅓ × 18 × 36 = 108 kN**, acting at H/3 = 2 m above the base.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 972 kN is the PASSIVE thrust — NINE times the active**, because K_p = 1/K_a = 3. Options (a) and (b) drop K_a and the ½ respectively.
examTip.mnemonic: **Active needs only 0.1-0.5 % of H in wall movement; passive needs 2-5 %** — which is why active is used at full value and passive is heavily discounted. And a RESTRAINED wall (basement, braced) must be designed for K₀ ≈ 1 − sinφ = 0.5, half again as much as active.

questions.stem: The depth of a foundation below which the increase in vertical stress caused by the structure is generally taken as negligible, and to which soil exploration is therefore normally carried, is:
options: Equal to the width of the loaded area
Twice the width of the loaded area
One and a half times the width of the loaded area
Between 1.5 and 2 times the width, where the stress increase falls to about 10 per cent
questions.solution:
**Between 1.5 and 2 times the width, where the stress increase has fallen to about 10 per cent of the applied pressure.**

**The rule and its basis:**

> **The SIGNIFICANT DEPTH of exploration is taken as the depth at which the stress increase Δσ from the foundation has fallen to about 10 PER CENT of the applied bearing pressure — or to 10 per cent of the existing OVERBURDEN pressure, whichever is shallower.**

> **For a square or circular footing of width B, that depth is roughly 1.5 B to 2 B below the founding level.**

> **The 10 per cent criterion is the substance of the answer: it is a stress criterion, and the depth in terms of B is its consequence.**

**Where the depth comes from — Boussinesq stress distribution:**

| Depth below a square footing | Δσ as a fraction of the applied pressure |
|---|---|
| **0 (at the base)** | **1.00** |
| **0.5 B** | **~0.70** |
| **1.0 B** | **~0.34** |
| **1.5 B** | **~0.18** |
| **2.0 B** | **~0.11** ← the 10 per cent level |
| **3.0 B** | **~0.06** |
| **4.0 B** | ~0.04 |

> **So the stress decays rapidly with depth, and beyond about 2 B the foundation's influence is small compared with the natural variability of the soil.**

> **The pressure BULB — the region enclosed by the contour of 10 or 20 per cent stress increase — is the useful picture: the soil inside it matters and the soil outside it does not.**

> **Note the decay is NOT linear: the stress halves in the first half-width and then takes a further 1.5 widths to halve again.**

**Why the WIDTH is the length scale, and the consequence — which is the real lesson here:**

> **The depth of influence scales with the SIZE of the loaded area, not with the load.**

> **So a 2 m wide footing influences the soil to about 4 m depth, while a 20 m wide raft carrying the SAME PRESSURE influences it to about 40 m.**

| Foundation | Width | Depth of influence |
|---|---|---|
| **Isolated column footing** | **2 m** | **~4 m** |
| **Strip footing** | **1.5 m** | ~3 m |
| **Large RAFT** | **20 m** | **~40 m** ← |
| **Pile group** | The GROUP width, not the pile width | **Measured from the pile TOES downward** |

> **The raft case has a serious practical consequence: a soft layer at 15 m depth is IRRELEVANT to a 2 m footing and CRITICAL to a 20 m raft, at the same bearing pressure.**

> **So the depth of a borehole cannot be decided from the pressure alone — it depends on the FOUNDATION SIZE, and therefore on the structural scheme.**

> **Which means soil exploration cannot be fully planned before the foundation type is contemplated, and a borehole programme drilled "to the standard depth" without regard to the structure can miss the very layer that governs.**

> **The PILE GROUP row is the one most often mishandled: the significant depth is measured from the pile TOES, not from the ground surface — so a 20 m pile group 10 m wide needs exploration to roughly 20 + 15 = 35 m.**

**The other rules that govern exploration depth, since the 2B rule is not the only one:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **To 1.5-2 B below the foundation (10 % stress)** | **The general rule** ← |
| **Until a HARD INCOMPRESSIBLE stratum is proved, and a little into it** | **Proving it, not merely reaching it — at least 3 m or 3 B into rock** |
| **Below the depth of any expected EXCAVATION or scour** | Bridge foundations especially |
| **Below the ZONE OF SEASONAL MOISTURE CHANGE in expansive clay** | **Typically 3-4 m; this can govern in black cotton soil** |
| **Below the frost line, where relevant** | Cold climates |
| **To the depth of any planned deep basement, plus the influence depth** | — |

> **The "proving it" point deserves emphasis: a borehole that stops on encountering a hard layer has NOT proved that layer's thickness.**

> **A 1 m thick gravel band over soft clay looks exactly like bedrock at the moment the sampler refuses**, and foundations have been designed on that mistake.

> **Hence the requirement to penetrate a stated distance INTO the bearing stratum — 3 m or three times the foundation width into rock — before accepting it.**

**Number and spacing of boreholes, since the question sits in exploration planning:**

| Situation | Typical spacing |
|---|---|
| **Uniform, well-known ground; light structure** | **30-100 m** |
| **Ordinary building** | **15-30 m; at least one per 300-500 m² of built area** |
| **Erratic ground, or a heavy structure** | **10-15 m or closer** |
| **Minimum for any building** | **At least THREE, so a plane can be established through the strata** ← |
| Bridge | One at every pier and abutment, without exception |

> **The minimum of three has a clean geometric justification: two boreholes define a line and cannot reveal whether a stratum dips across it.** Three define a plane and give the dip.

> **And the bridge rule is absolute in practice because a single unexpected condition at one pier governs the whole structure** — the cost of a borehole is trivial against the cost of a redesigned pier, let alone a failed one.

**What exploration is FOR, since the depth rule is only a means:**

| Objective | Note |
|---|---|
| **Identify the strata and their thicknesses** | The soil profile |
| **Locate the WATER TABLE and any perched or artesian conditions** | **Often the single most consequential finding** ← |
| **Obtain samples for strength and compressibility** | For bearing capacity and settlement |
| **Perform in-situ tests (SPT, CPT, vane, pressuremeter)** | Where sampling is unreliable |
| **Detect problem soils — expansive, collapsible, organic, sensitive** | Each requires a different response |
| **Assess aggressiveness to concrete and steel (sulphates, chlorides)** | Durability, not strength |

> **Locating the water table is worth singling out: it affects the effective stress and hence the bearing capacity, the buoyancy and hence uplift, the excavation method and dewatering, the durability of buried concrete, and the construction sequence.**

> **It is one observation that changes almost every subsequent decision — and it is also the one most likely to differ between the dry season, when the borehole was drilled, and the monsoon, when the excavation is open.** Which is why a single water-table reading should always be accompanied by an estimate of its seasonal range.

examTip.trick: **Explore to where the stress increase falls to about 10 % of the applied pressure — roughly 1.5 B to 2 B below the founding level.** The criterion is the STRESS; the depth in terms of B is its consequence.
examTip.trap: **The depth scales with the foundation WIDTH, not the load.** A soft layer at 15 m is irrelevant to a 2 m footing and critical to a 20 m raft at the same pressure — so exploration depth cannot be fixed before the foundation type is considered.
examTip.mnemonic: **A borehole that STOPS on hard ground has not PROVED it** — a 1 m gravel band over soft clay feels like rock to the sampler. Penetrate 3 m or 3 B into the bearing stratum. And take at least THREE boreholes: two define a line, three define the dip.

questions.stem: A square footing 2 m × 2 m is founded at 1.5 m depth in a cohesionless soil of unit weight 18 kN/m³ and φ = 30°. Using Terzaghi's equation with N_q = 22.5 and N_γ = 19.7, and NEGLECTING the shape factors, the NET ultimate bearing capacity is:
questions.solution:
**935 kN/m².**

**Terzaghi's equation for a cohesionless soil (c = 0):**

> **q_u = c N_c + γ D_f N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ**

> **With c = 0 the cohesion term vanishes, leaving two terms.**

**Step 1 — the surcharge (depth) term:**

> **γ D_f N_q = 18 × 1.5 × 22.5 = 27 × 22.5 = 607.5 kN/m²**

**Step 2 — the width (self-weight) term:**

> **0.5 γ B N_γ = 0.5 × 18 × 2 × 19.7 = 18 × 19.7 = 354.6 kN/m²**

**Step 3 — the GROSS ultimate bearing capacity:**

> **q_u = 607.5 + 354.6 = 962.1 kN/m²**

**Step 4 — the NET value, which is what was asked:**

> **q_nu = q_u − γ D_f = 962.1 − 27.0 = 935.1 kN/m² ≈ 935 kN/m²** ✓

**Every distractor is a specific, identifiable step:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **962 kN/m²** | **The GROSS ultimate — the net subtraction omitted** ← the intended trap |
| **864 kN/m²** | **The answer WITH the square-footing shape factor 0.4 applied**, which the stem directs be neglected: 607.5 + 0.4(18)(2)(19.7) − 27 = 864.2 |
| **608 kN/m²** | **The SURCHARGE term alone — the width term forgotten** |
| **935 kN/m²** | ✓ |

> **Note that option (b) punishes doing MORE than the question asked.** Applying the shape factor is correct engineering and wrong here, because the stem excluded it — which is why reading such an instruction is part of the task.

**The NET versus GROSS distinction, which is the point of the question:**

| Quantity | Definition | Value here |
|---|---|---|
| **GROSS ultimate, q_u** | **The TOTAL pressure at the base at failure** | **962.1 kN/m²** |
| **NET ultimate, q_nu** | **q_u − γD_f — the INCREASE over what was already there** | **935.1 kN/m²** ← |
| **NET SAFE, q_ns** | **q_nu / F**, with F typically 2.5 to 3 | 312-374 kN/m² |
| **SAFE bearing capacity (gross)** | **q_ns + γD_f** | 339-401 kN/m² |
| **ALLOWABLE bearing pressure** | **The LESSER of the safe bearing capacity and the SETTLEMENT-limited pressure** | **Usually settlement governs** |

> **The reason for the net concept is straightforward: the soil at founding level was ALREADY carrying the overburden γD_f before the footing existed.**

> **Excavating removes that weight and the footing replaces it, so only the EXCESS over γD_f is a new load on the soil.**

> **Applying the factor of safety to the NET value is therefore correct; applying it to the gross value would factor down a pressure the soil demonstrably carried already.**

> **The subtraction is small here — 27 out of 962, under 3 per cent — because the footing is shallow. For a basement raft at 10 m depth it is 180 kN/m², which is not small at all.**

**Why the ALLOWABLE pressure is usually governed by SETTLEMENT, not bearing capacity:**

> **This is the practical point the arithmetic conceals, and it is worth stating firmly.**

> **The net safe bearing capacity here exceeds 300 kN/m². Almost no ordinary building applies that much.**

> **What limits the design instead is the SETTLEMENT the structure can tolerate — typically 25 mm total and 20 mm differential for a framed building.**

| Governs | When |
|---|---|
| **BEARING CAPACITY** | **Soft clay; narrow footings; loose sand — where failure is a real prospect** |
| **SETTLEMENT** | **Most ordinary cases, especially sands and stiff clays** ← |

> **So a bearing capacity calculation of this kind establishes that FAILURE is not the issue, and the design is then completed by a settlement calculation.**

> **And the corollary: DIFFERENTIAL settlement matters more than total.** A building that settles 50 mm uniformly is undamaged; one that settles 25 mm at one column and 5 mm at the next is cracked.

> **Which is why footings on the same building are often proportioned for EQUAL SETTLEMENT rather than equal pressure** — a lightly loaded footing on the same soil gets a smaller area than equal-pressure design would give it, precisely so that it settles as much as its neighbours.

**The bearing capacity factors, and their sensitivity:**

| Factor | Represents |
|---|---|
| **N_c** | **The COHESION contribution** |
| **N_q** | **The SURCHARGE (depth) contribution** |
| **N_γ** | **The soil's own WEIGHT within the failure wedge** |

> **All three depend on φ ALONE:**

| φ | N_c | N_q | N_γ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0°** | **5.7** | **1.0** | **0** |
| **20°** | **17.7** | **7.4** | **5.0** |
| **30°** | **37.2** | **22.5** | **19.7** ← |
| **40°** | **95.7** | **81.3** | **100.4** |

> **Note how violently they grow: from φ = 30° to φ = 40°, N_q rises 3.6-fold and N_γ more than fivefold.**

> **So bearing capacity in sand is EXTREMELY sensitive to φ, and an error of a few degrees in the estimated friction angle shifts the answer by tens of per cent.**

> **Which is a reason for honest caution about precise-looking bearing capacity figures in sand: the arithmetic is exact and the input is not.**

> **And note N_q = 1, N_γ = 0 at φ = 0: a purely cohesive soil gives q_u = 5.7c + γD_f, INDEPENDENT of the footing width.**

> **That is why widening a footing does not help on soft clay** — the bearing capacity per unit area does not improve, so the total capacity rises only in proportion to the area, and rafts or piles are used instead.

**The shape factors, for completeness:**

> **Terzaghi's equation as written above is for a STRIP footing. For other shapes:**

| Shape | Corrected equation |
|---|---|
| **Strip (continuous)** | **c N_c + γD_f N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ** |
| **SQUARE** | **1.3 c N_c + γD_f N_q + 0.4 γ B N_γ** ← |
| **CIRCULAR** | **1.3 c N_c + γD_f N_q + 0.3 γ B N_γ** |

> **The cohesion term is INCREASED (1.3) and the width term REDUCED (0.4 or 0.3) for a compact shape.**

> **The physical reason for the reduction is that a square or circular footing's failure wedge is confined on all sides and the soil can escape more readily than beneath a long strip, so the self-weight term contributes less** — a three-dimensional effect that the two-dimensional theory corrects empirically.

examTip.trick: **With c = 0: q_u = γD_f N_q + 0.5γB N_γ = 607.5 + 354.6 = 962.1 gross; then NET = 962.1 − γD_f = 935 kN/m².**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 962 is the GROSS value — the net subtraction omitted; option (b) 864 is the answer with the shape factor the stem told you to NEGLECT.** One distractor punishes doing less, the other doing more than asked.
examTip.mnemonic: **In practice SETTLEMENT governs, not bearing capacity** — 25 mm total, 20 mm differential — and differential matters more than total. Note too that N_γ = 0 at φ = 0, so widening a footing does not raise the bearing capacity on soft clay.

questions.stem: A normally consolidated clay layer 4 m thick has a void ratio of 0.90 and a compression index of 0.30. If the effective stress at mid-depth increases from 100 to 200 kN/m², the consolidation settlement is:
questions.solution:
**190 mm.**

**The settlement equation for a normally consolidated clay:**

> **Δ = (C_c H)/(1 + e₀) × log₁₀(σ'₁/σ'₀)**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **C_c** | **Compression index** | **0.30** |
| **H** | **Thickness of the compressible layer** | **4 m = 4000 mm** |
| **e₀** | **Initial void ratio** | **0.90** |
| **σ'₀** | **Initial effective stress at mid-depth** | **100 kN/m²** |
| **σ'₁** | **Final effective stress** | **200 kN/m²** |

**The computation:**

> **log₁₀(200/100) = log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010**

> **Δ = (0.30 × 4000)/(1 + 0.90) × 0.3010**

> **= 1200/1.90 × 0.3010**

> **= 631.6 × 0.3010 = 190.1 mm** ✓

> **Note the intermediate 631.6 mm: that is the settlement that would occur for a TENFOLD increase in stress (log = 1).** Recognising it makes the final step a single multiplication.

**Why the distractors are what they are:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **190 mm** | ✓ |
| **95 mm** | **Half the answer — 1 + e₀ misread, or H taken as 2 m** |
| **63 mm** | **Using ln instead of log₁₀ inverted, or the log₁₀ 2 factor misapplied** |
| **380 mm** | **Twice the answer — the (1 + e₀) divisor omitted and something else compensating; or ln 2 = 0.693 used in place of log 2** |

> **The log₁₀ versus ln confusion is the standard error here: using ln 2 = 0.693 instead of log₁₀ 2 = 0.301 would give 631.6 × 0.693 = 438 mm.**

> **The equation is defined with log to base TEN, because the e-log p curve is plotted on a base-10 logarithmic axis** — which is worth remembering as the reason rather than the rule.

**What the compression index MEANS:**

> **C_c is the SLOPE of the virgin compression line on the e-log σ' plot:**

> **C_c = −Δe / Δ(log₁₀ σ')**

> **So C_c is the change in void ratio per TENFOLD increase in effective stress.**

> **For this clay, C_c = 0.30 means the void ratio falls by 0.30 — from 0.90 to 0.60 — for each tenfold stress increase.**

> **Check: doubling the stress reduces e by 0.30 × 0.301 = 0.090, from 0.90 to 0.810.**

> **And the strain is Δe/(1+e₀) = 0.090/1.90 = 0.0475, so the settlement is 0.0475 × 4000 = 190 mm** ✓ — the same answer by the physical route, which is the check worth making.

**Typical compression indices, so the answer can be judged:**

| Soil | C_c |
|---|---|
| **Dense sand** | **0.01 - 0.03** |
| **Stiff clay** | **0.1 - 0.3** |
| **Soft clay** | **0.3 - 1.0** ← |
| **Organic clay / peat** | **1.0 - 4.0 or more** |

> **Skempton's correlation: C_c ≈ 0.009 (LL − 10)**, so a clay with LL = 43 would give C_c ≈ 0.30 — consistent.

> **That correlation is genuinely useful for a preliminary estimate, since the liquid limit is a cheap and quick test while a consolidation test takes a week or more.**

**Why the OVERCONSOLIDATION state changes everything — the caution:**

> **The equation used here applies to a NORMALLY CONSOLIDATED clay: one that has never carried a greater stress than its present one.**

> **For an OVERCONSOLIDATED clay — one that has been loaded and then unloaded, by erosion, by the melting of ice, or by a desiccation — the behaviour is quite different:**

| Loading range | Governed by | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Below the PRECONSOLIDATION pressure σ'_c** | **The RECOMPRESSION index C_r** | **C_r is typically 1/5 to 1/10 of C_c — settlement is SMALL** ← |
| **Above σ'_c** | **C_c** | Settlement becomes large |

> **So the settlement of an overconsolidated clay depends critically on whether the final stress stays BELOW or crosses ABOVE the preconsolidation pressure.**

> **If it stays below, the settlement may be five to ten times smaller than this equation would predict.**

> **If it crosses, the calculation must be done in TWO parts:**

> **Δ = (C_r H)/(1+e₀) log(σ'_c/σ'₀) + (C_c H)/(1+e₀) log(σ'₁/σ'_c)**

> **Which is why establishing the PRECONSOLIDATION PRESSURE — from the Casagrande construction on the e-log p curve — is the single most important output of a consolidation test.**

> **A designer who assumes normal consolidation for an overconsolidated clay will grossly OVERESTIMATE the settlement, and will build a more expensive foundation than the ground requires.** The error is on the safe side and it is still an error, and one that can make a scheme uneconomic.

**The RATE of settlement, which the magnitude does not tell us:**

> **This calculation gives HOW MUCH the clay will settle, and says nothing about HOW LONG it will take.**

> **The time comes from the coefficient of consolidation:**

> **t = T_v d² / c_v**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **T_v** | **Time factor — 0.197 for 50 % consolidation, 0.848 for 90 %** |
| **d** | **The LONGEST DRAINAGE PATH — H/2 for double drainage, H for single** ← |
| **c_v** | Coefficient of consolidation |

> **The d² dependence is the point worth extracting: DOUBLING the drainage path QUADRUPLES the time.**

> **So a 4 m clay layer draining both ways (d = 2 m) consolidates FOUR TIMES faster than the same layer draining only upward (d = 4 m).**

> **Which is exactly why SAND DRAINS and PREFABRICATED VERTICAL (wick) DRAINS are installed in soft clay: they do not reduce the settlement at all, they simply shorten the drainage path so that the settlement happens during construction rather than over the following twenty years.**

> **A wick drain grid at 1.5 m spacing reduces the drainage path from metres to under a metre, cutting the consolidation time by a factor of several hundred** — turning a problem of long-term differential settlement into a problem of scheduling.

> **That distinction between the AMOUNT of settlement and its TIMING is one of the most practically important in geotechnics, and the two calculations answer entirely different questions.**

examTip.trap: **log₁₀, not ln** — using ln 2 = 0.693 gives 438 mm. The equation uses base 10 because the e-log p curve is plotted on a base-10 axis.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check by the physical route: Δe = C_c log(σ'₁/σ'₀) = 0.090, strain = Δe/(1+e₀) = 0.0475, settlement = 0.0475 × 4000 = 190 mm.** And this gives HOW MUCH, never HOW LONG — time goes as d², which is why wick drains shorten the path rather than reduce the settlement.

questions.stem: The BULK MODULUS of a liquid is defined as:
options: The ratio of shear stress to the rate of shear strain
The ratio of surface tension to the radius of curvature
The ratio of dynamic viscosity to mass density
questions.solution:
**The RECIPROCAL of the compressibility.**

**The definition:**

> **K = − dp / (dV/V)** — the increase in pressure divided by the resulting FRACTIONAL decrease in volume.

> **And COMPRESSIBILITY is defined as its reciprocal:**

> **β = 1/K = − (dV/V)/dp**

> **The negative sign makes K positive, since an INCREASE in pressure produces a DECREASE in volume.**

> **Note that dV/V is DIMENSIONLESS, so K has the dimensions of PRESSURE — N/m² or Pa.**

**Typical values, which give the property its meaning:**

| Fluid / material | Bulk modulus |
|---|---|
| **WATER** | **2.05 - 2.20 × 10⁹ N/m² (about 2.1 GPa)** ← |
| Mercury | 26 GPa |
| Oil | ~1.5 GPa |
| **Air (isothermal)** | **~0.1 MPa — twenty thousand times smaller** |
| **STEEL (for comparison)** | **~160 GPa — about 80 times water's** |

> **The comparison with steel is the one worth carrying: water is only about eighty times more compressible than steel, which is far stiffer than intuition suggests.**

> **A quantitative feel: at 2.1 GPa, raising the pressure on water by 1 MPa (10 atmospheres) compresses it by 1/2100 = 0.048 per cent.**

> **Even at the bottom of the deepest ocean trench — about 110 MPa — water is compressed only about 5 per cent.**

> **Which is why water is treated as INCOMPRESSIBLE in virtually all civil engineering hydraulics, and the assumption is excellent rather than merely convenient.**

**Where compressibility CANNOT be neglected — the important exceptions:**

| Situation | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **WATER HAMMER in a pipeline** | **The pressure wave travels at the speed of sound in water, c = √(K/ρ) — which EXISTS only because water is compressible** ← |
| **Surge and transient analysis generally** | Same reason |
| **Hydraulic machinery and high-pressure systems** | Large pressure changes |
| **Acoustic and sonar problems** | Sound is a compression wave |
| **Cavitation and vapour collapse** | Phase change with pressure |

> **WATER HAMMER is the case that matters to a civil engineer, and it is worth working through:**

> **c = √(K/ρ) = √(2.1 × 10⁹ / 1000) = √(2.1 × 10⁶) = 1449 m/s**

> **So a pressure wave travels along a rigid pipe full of water at about 1450 m/s — roughly four times the speed of sound in air.**

> **If water were truly incompressible, K would be infinite, c would be infinite, and closing a valve would stop the entire column instantaneously — implying an infinite pressure rise.**

> **So the very phenomenon of water hammer, and its finite magnitude, depends on the compressibility that hydraulics otherwise ignores.**

> **That is a genuinely instructive point: the assumption of incompressibility is excellent for steady flow and catastrophically wrong for transients.**

> **In a real pipe the wave speed is lower than 1450 m/s, because the PIPE ITSELF also stretches — the effective modulus combines the water's and the pipe wall's flexibility:**

> **c = √[K/ρ] / √[1 + (K D)/(E t)]**

> **Which is why a flexible plastic pipe suffers a much lower water hammer pressure than a rigid steel one, and why surge pressures in PVC systems are far less severe.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each defines a DIFFERENT property:**

| Option | The property it actually defines |
|---|---|
| **(a) Shear stress / rate of shear strain** | **DYNAMIC (absolute) VISCOSITY μ — Newton's law of viscosity** |
| **(c) Surface tension / radius of curvature** | **Not a standard property; the closest relation is Δp = 2σ/r, a PRESSURE** |
| **(d) Dynamic viscosity / mass density** | **KINEMATIC VISCOSITY ν = μ/ρ** |

> **Options (a) and (d) are the two viscosities, and they are worth distinguishing clearly since they are constantly confused:**

| | **DYNAMIC viscosity μ** | **KINEMATIC viscosity ν** |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | **τ / (du/dy)** | **μ / ρ** |
| **SI unit** | **N·s/m² = Pa·s (poise in CGS)** | **m²/s (stokes in CGS)** |
| **Dimensions** | **M L⁻¹ T⁻¹** | **L² T⁻¹ — note: NO mass** ← |
| **Water at 20 °C** | **1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s** | **1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s** |
| **Appears in** | Shear stress calculations | **REYNOLDS NUMBER, Re = VL/ν** |

> **The dimensions of KINEMATIC viscosity contain no mass, which is where the name comes from: it is a purely KINEMATIC quantity, of length² per time — the same dimensions as a diffusivity.**

> **And that is exactly what it is physically: the DIFFUSIVITY OF MOMENTUM.** A high kinematic viscosity means momentum spreads quickly through the fluid, which is why it and not μ governs the Reynolds number.

> **A trap worth noting: AIR has a dynamic viscosity about 55 times SMALLER than water's, and a KINEMATIC viscosity about 15 times LARGER** — because air's density is some 800 times less.

> **So air is "less viscous" by one measure and "more viscous" by the other, and which one matters depends on the problem.** For a Reynolds number it is the kinematic one, which is why flow around a body is turbulent at a much lower velocity in water than in air of the same speed and size.

**The other fluid properties, for completeness, since this family of definitions recurs:**

| Property | Definition | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **Mass density ρ** | **Mass per unit volume** | kg/m³ |
| **Specific weight γ** | **WEIGHT per unit volume = ρg** | N/m³ |
| **Specific gravity** | **ρ / ρ_water — DIMENSIONLESS** | — |
| **Specific volume** | **Volume per unit mass = 1/ρ** | m³/kg |
| **SURFACE TENSION σ** | **Force per unit LENGTH at a free surface** | **N/m** |
| **VAPOUR PRESSURE** | **The pressure at which the liquid boils at that temperature** | **N/m² — governs CAVITATION** |
| **BULK MODULUS K** | **dp / (−dV/V)** | **N/m²** ← |

> **VAPOUR PRESSURE deserves a note because it is the property behind CAVITATION, which is the one fluid property failure a civil engineer is most likely to meet:**

> **Where the local pressure in a flow falls to the vapour pressure, the water BOILS at ambient temperature, forming vapour cavities.**

> **Carried into a region of higher pressure, those cavities COLLAPSE violently, and the implosion pits and erodes metal and concrete.**

> **It is why the suction lift of a pump is limited, why spillway profiles are shaped to avoid negative pressures, and why the draft tube of a turbine is set at a carefully computed elevation.** All three are the same property setting the same limit.

examTip.trick: **K = dp/(−dV/V), and compressibility β = 1/K.** For water K ≈ 2.1 GPa, so 1 MPa compresses water by only 0.05 per cent.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (d) are the two VISCOSITIES** — dynamic μ = τ/(du/dy), kinematic ν = μ/ρ. Note kinematic viscosity has dimensions L²/T with NO mass: it is the DIFFUSIVITY OF MOMENTUM, which is why it governs the Reynolds number.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water hammer exists only BECAUSE water is compressible**: c = √(K/ρ) = 1450 m/s. If K were infinite so would be the pressure rise on valve closure — so incompressibility is an excellent assumption for steady flow and a disastrous one for transients.

questions.stem: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m deep has its top edge at the water surface. The depth of the CENTRE OF PRESSURE below the water surface is:
questions.solution:
**2.0 m below the water surface.**

**The general formula for the centre of pressure:**

> **h_cp = h̄ + I_G / (A h̄)**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **h̄** | **Depth of the CENTROID** | **3/2 = 1.5 m** |
| **I_G** | **Second moment about the centroidal HORIZONTAL axis** | **bd³/12 = 2(3)³/12 = 4.5 m⁴** |
| **A** | **Area** | **2 × 3 = 6 m²** |

**The computation:**

> **h_cp = 1.5 + 4.5/(6 × 1.5) = 1.5 + 4.5/9 = 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 m** ✓

**The shortcut worth knowing:**

> **For a VERTICAL rectangle with its TOP EDGE AT THE SURFACE, the centre of pressure is always at TWO THIRDS of the depth:**

> **h_cp = (2/3) × 3 = 2.0 m** ✓

> **The reason is that the pressure distribution is a TRIANGLE — zero at the surface, maximum at the base — and the centroid of a triangle lies at two thirds of its height from the apex.**

> **So the answer can be written down in a second, without the formula**, and recognising the case is the whole skill.

> **Note that option (a) 1.5 m is the CENTROID depth**, offered to catch the commonest confusion in hydrostatics: the centre of pressure is NOT the centroid.

**Why the centre of pressure is always BELOW the centroid:**

> **Pressure INCREASES linearly with depth, so the lower part of the surface carries more pressure than the upper.**

> **The resultant is therefore biased downward, and the term I_G/(Ah̄) is always POSITIVE.**

> **So h_cp > h̄ always — with one instructive limiting case.**

**How the two converge with depth, which is the useful insight:**

> **The correction term I_G/(Ah̄) has h̄ in its DENOMINATOR, so it SHRINKS as the surface is submerged deeper.**

> **For the same 2 m × 3 m gate at various depths of its top edge:**

| Top edge depth | h̄ | Correction I_G/(Ah̄) | h_cp | h_cp − h̄ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0 (at the surface)** | **1.5 m** | **0.500 m** | **2.00 m** | **0.500 m** ← |
| **3 m** | **4.5 m** | **0.167 m** | **4.667 m** | **0.167 m** |
| **10 m** | **11.5 m** | **0.065 m** | **11.565 m** | **0.065 m** |
| **50 m** | **51.5 m** | **0.015 m** | **51.515 m** | **0.015 m** |

> **So for a DEEPLY SUBMERGED surface the centre of pressure converges on the centroid.**

> **The physical reason is that the pressure variation ACROSS the surface becomes small compared with the average pressure — the distribution approaches uniform, and the resultant of a uniform pressure acts at the centroid.**

> **That has a practical consequence: for a small valve or gate deep in a pipeline or reservoir, treating the pressure as uniform and the resultant as acting at the centroid is a good approximation.** For a large gate near the surface it is a serious error — half a metre out of three here.

**The total force, since the two quantities always go together:**

> **F = γ A h̄ = 9.81 × 6 × 1.5 = 88.3 kN**

> **And it acts at 2.0 m depth, giving a moment about the base of 88.3 × (3 − 2.0) = 88.3 kNm.**

> **Note that the FORCE depends only on the CENTROID depth, while its LOCATION requires the second moment.**

> **So a candidate who confuses the two gets the force right and the moment wrong** — which in a gate design is precisely the error that matters, since the gate's hinge and its structure are designed for the moment.

**The INCLINED surface case, since it is the general form:**

> **For a plane surface inclined at θ to the horizontal, measure distances ALONG THE PLANE from the point where it meets the free surface:**

> **y_cp = ȳ + I_G/(A ȳ)** — the same formula, with y measured along the plane.

> **The vertical depth is then h_cp = y_cp sin θ.**

> **And the total force is STILL F = γ A h̄, with h̄ the VERTICAL depth of the centroid.**

> **The rule that makes this reliable: FORCE uses VERTICAL depth; LOCATION uses distance ALONG THE PLANE.** Mixing the two is the standard error in inclined-surface problems.

**A curved surface, for completeness, since the method changes entirely:**

> **For a CURVED surface the pressure is not unidirectional, so the resultant is found in two components:**

| Component | How to find it |
|---|---|
| **HORIZONTAL, F_H** | **The force on the VERTICAL PROJECTION of the surface — the same plane-surface calculation** |
| **VERTICAL, F_V** | **The WEIGHT of the volume of liquid vertically above the surface, real or imagined** ← |

> **The vertical component's rule — the weight of the liquid above, real or imaginary — is the elegant part.**

> **For a surface with liquid genuinely above it, F_V is the weight of that liquid and acts downward.**

> **For a surface with liquid BELOW it, F_V is the weight of the liquid that WOULD occupy the space above and acts UPWARD.**

> **That single rule handles both cases, and it is why the underside of a curved sluice gate experiences an upward thrust equal to the weight of an imaginary column of water** — a result which surprises people and which is simply the buoyancy argument applied to part of a surface.

examTip.trick: **For a vertical rectangle with its TOP EDGE AT THE SURFACE, h_cp = 2/3 of the depth = 2.0 m** — because the pressure diagram is a triangle and its centroid is at two thirds. No formula needed.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 1.5 m is the CENTROID** — the centre of pressure is never the centroid for a surface reaching the free surface. The FORCE depends on the centroid depth; only its LOCATION needs I_G.
examTip.mnemonic: **The correction I_G/(Ah̄) shrinks with depth**, so a deeply submerged gate has its centre of pressure essentially at the centroid — the pressure across it is nearly uniform. Half a metre of error near the surface, 15 mm at 50 m depth.

questions.stem: Water flows through a 150 mm diameter pipe at 3 m/s and then through a 75 mm diameter section. The velocity in the smaller section is:
questions.solution:
**12 m/s.**

**Continuity for an incompressible fluid:**

> **A₁ V₁ = A₂ V₂**

> **Since A ∝ d², the relation in terms of diameters is:**

> **V₂ = V₁ (d₁/d₂)²**

**The computation:**

> **V₂ = 3 × (150/75)² = 3 × 2² = 3 × 4 = 12 m/s** ✓

> **Note that option (a) 6 m/s is what you get by using the diameter ratio to the FIRST power** — the commonest error, and the one the option set is built to catch.

> **The velocity varies as the INVERSE SQUARE of the diameter, because it is the AREA that must be conserved against, and area goes as d².**

> **So HALVING the diameter QUADRUPLES the velocity.** That single statement answers most continuity questions without any arithmetic.

**A check by computing the discharge both ways:**

> **Q₁ = A₁V₁ = (π/4)(0.150)² × 3 = 0.01767 × 3 = 0.0530 m³/s**

> **Q₂ = A₂V₂ = (π/4)(0.075)² × 12 = 0.004418 × 12 = 0.0530 m³/s** ✓

> **Equal, as continuity requires** — and computing Q is worth doing because it is usually what the next part of the question asks for.

**What CONTINUITY actually expresses:**

> **Continuity is CONSERVATION OF MASS. In its general form:**

> **ρ₁ A₁ V₁ = ρ₂ A₂ V₂**

> **For an INCOMPRESSIBLE fluid ρ₁ = ρ₂, so the densities cancel and the equation reduces to the volumetric form used above.**

> **Which means the familiar A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ is a SPECIAL CASE, valid only for incompressible flow** — and for a gas at high speed the density term must be retained.

**Why the quadratic dependence has such large practical consequences:**

> **The velocity rises as 1/d², and several important quantities depend on the velocity SQUARED — which compounds the effect:**

| Quantity | Dependence on velocity | Effect of HALVING the diameter |
|---|---|---|
| **Velocity** | **V ∝ 1/d²** | **× 4** |
| **Velocity head V²/2g** | **∝ V² ∝ 1/d⁴** | **× 16** ← |
| **Friction loss (Darcy, per unit length)** | **∝ V²/d ∝ 1/d⁵** | **× 32** |
| **Dynamic pressure on an obstruction** | ∝ V² | × 16 |
| **Reynolds number** | ∝ Vd ∝ 1/d | × 2 |

> **The friction-loss row is the striking one: halving a pipe's diameter multiplies its head loss per unit length THIRTY-TWO fold at the same discharge.**

> **h_f = f L V²/(2gd), and substituting V = 4Q/(πd²) gives h_f ∝ Q²/d⁵.**

> **The FIFTH POWER dependence is the single most important economic fact in pipeline design: a modest increase in diameter produces an enormous reduction in pumping cost.**

> **Going from a 150 mm to a 200 mm pipe — a 33 per cent increase in diameter — cuts the friction loss by (150/200)⁵ = 0.24, a factor of more than four.**

> **So pipeline sizing is a balance between the CAPITAL cost of the pipe, which rises roughly as d to d², and the PUMPING cost, which falls as d⁵** — and the optimum is usually a larger pipe than intuition suggests.

**The velocity of 12 m/s, since it deserves comment:**

| Velocity | Assessment for a water pipeline |
|---|---|
| **Below 0.6 m/s** | **Risk of sediment deposition** |
| **0.9 - 2.5 m/s** | **The normal design range** |
| **Up to 3 m/s** | Acceptable for short lengths |
| **12 m/s** | **FAR too high for a water main — severe friction loss, erosion of the pipe, and noise** ← |

> **So the smaller section in this problem is not a pipeline but a NOZZLE, a venturi throat or a measuring section** — somewhere a high velocity is deliberately created over a short length.

> **Recognising that is a legitimate reading of the numbers: a sustained 12 m/s in a water main would erode the lining, generate audible noise and waste an enormous amount of energy in friction (h_f ∝ V², so 144 times the loss at 1 m/s).**

**Continuity for a BRANCHING or JUNCTION, since real networks branch:**

> **At a junction, the flow IN equals the flow OUT:**

> **ΣQ_in = ΣQ_out**

> **That is the network form of continuity, and it is one of the two conditions on which all pipe network analysis rests:**

| Condition | Statement | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTINUITY at each junction** | **ΣQ = 0** | **Kirchhoff's CURRENT law** |
| **ENERGY around each loop** | **Σh_f = 0** | **Kirchhoff's VOLTAGE law** |

> **The electrical analogy is exact in form, and it is why the HARDY CROSS method — the classic hand technique for pipe networks — is essentially a relaxation solution of the same equations an electrical engineer solves for a resistor network.**

> **The one difference is that head loss goes as Q² rather than as Q (Ohm's law is linear), which is why the method must ITERATE rather than solve directly.**

examTip.trick: **V₂ = V₁(d₁/d₂)² = 3 × 2² = 12 m/s.** Velocity varies as the INVERSE SQUARE of the diameter, so halving the diameter QUADRUPLES the velocity.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 6 m/s uses the diameter ratio to the FIRST power** — the commonest error. It is the AREA that continuity conserves against, and area goes as d².
examTip.mnemonic: **Friction loss goes as Q²/d⁵** — the fifth power is the central economic fact of pipeline design. A 33 % larger pipe cuts friction loss by a factor of four, which is why the optimum diameter is usually bigger than it looks.

questions.stem: For laminar flow in a circular pipe, the ratio of the maximum velocity to the mean velocity is:
questions.solution:
**2.0 — the maximum velocity is TWICE the mean.**

**Where the result comes from:**

> **In LAMINAR flow through a circular pipe (Hagen-Poiseuille flow), the velocity profile is a PARABOLOID:**

> **u = u_max [1 − (r/R)²]**

> **Integrating over the cross-section to get the discharge:**

> **Q = ∫₀^R u (2πr dr) = u_max ∫₀^R [1 − r²/R²] 2πr dr = u_max × (πR²/2)**

> **And since Q = V_mean × πR²:**

> **V_mean = u_max/2, hence u_max/V_mean = 2.0** ✓

> **So the mean velocity of a parabolic profile is exactly half its peak, and the result is an exact consequence of the geometry rather than an empirical figure.**

**The contrast with TURBULENT flow, which is the point of the question:**

| | **LAMINAR** | **TURBULENT** |
|---|---|---|
| **Velocity profile** | **PARABOLIC (paraboloid of revolution)** | **LOGARITHMIC — much FLATTER, with a thin steep layer at the wall** |
| **u_max / V_mean** | **2.00** ← | **about 1.15 - 1.25 (commonly taken as 1.22)** |
| **Reynolds number** | **Re < 2000** | **Re > 4000** |
| **Shear stress at the wall** | ∝ V | **∝ V²** |
| **Friction factor** | **f = 64/Re — depends ONLY on Re** | **Depends on Re AND on relative roughness** |
| **Head loss** | **∝ V (linear!)** | **∝ V^1.75 to V²** |

> **Note that option (b) 1.22 is the TURBULENT value**, offered to catch a candidate who does not read which regime is meant.

> **The physical reason turbulent profiles are flatter is worth stating: turbulent eddies MIX momentum across the pipe, transferring fast-moving fluid from the centre outward and slow fluid inward.**

> **That mixing flattens the profile, leaving nearly uniform velocity across most of the section and confining the steep gradient to a very thin layer at the wall.**

> **Laminar flow has no such mixing — momentum crosses the streamlines only by molecular viscosity, which is far less effective — so the profile is fully developed and parabolic.**

**The KINETIC ENERGY correction factor, since it follows from the same profiles:**

> **The kinetic energy of a flow computed from the MEAN velocity understates the true value, because energy goes as V³ and the fast parts of the profile contribute disproportionately.**

> **α = (1/A)∫(u/V)³ dA**

| Regime | **α (kinetic energy)** | **β (momentum)** |
|---|---|---|
| **LAMINAR pipe flow** | **2.0** | **1.33** |
| **TURBULENT pipe flow** | **1.03 - 1.06** | **1.01 - 1.02** |

> **So for laminar flow the true velocity head is TWICE V²/2g — a very large correction — while for turbulent flow the correction is a few per cent and is routinely neglected.**

> **That is why Bernoulli's equation is written with V²/2g and no correction factor: nearly all engineering flows are turbulent, where α ≈ 1.**

> **And it is a caution about laminar problems: applying Bernoulli's equation to laminar pipe flow without α = 2 is a 100 per cent error in the velocity head.**

**Hagen-Poiseuille, since it is the companion result:**

> **h_f = 32 μ V L / (ρ g d²)**

> **Or in terms of discharge:  Q = π Δp d⁴ / (128 μ L)**

> **The FOURTH POWER of diameter in the discharge form is remarkable — even steeper than the turbulent case.**

> **And note that the head loss is proportional to V to the FIRST power, which is unique to laminar flow.**

| Regime | Head loss dependence |
|---|---|
| **LAMINAR** | **h_f ∝ V** ← linear |
| **Turbulent, smooth pipe** | h_f ∝ V^1.75 |
| **Turbulent, fully rough** | **h_f ∝ V²** |

> **The linear dependence has a striking consequence: in laminar flow, DOUBLING the flow doubles the pressure drop, whereas in turbulent flow it roughly quadruples it.**

> **Which is why laminar flow is energetically far more efficient, and why it is exploited wherever it can be arranged — in lubrication films, in capillary viscometers, and in the flow of groundwater through soil, which is laminar and is exactly why DARCY'S LAW is linear in the gradient.**

> **That connection is worth drawing out: Darcy's law v = ki is linear precisely BECAUSE seepage through soil pores is laminar.** At very high gradients in coarse gravel the flow turns turbulent and Darcy's law fails — which is why it does not apply to flow through rockfill.

**The Reynolds number and the transition, since the regime must be identified first:**

> **Re = ρVd/μ = Vd/ν**

| Re (pipe flow) | Regime |
|---|---|
| **< 2000** | **LAMINAR** |
| **2000 - 4000** | **TRANSITIONAL — unpredictable** |
| **> 4000** | **TURBULENT** |

> **For water at 20 °C (ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s) in a 150 mm pipe, Re = 2000 corresponds to V = 2000 × 10⁻⁶/0.15 = 0.013 m/s.**

> **Thirteen millimetres per second — a barely perceptible creep.**

> **So laminar flow in a water pipe of engineering size is essentially never encountered**, and every practical water pipeline is turbulent.

> **Which is why this question is a theory question rather than a design one, and why the turbulent value 1.22 is the number a practising engineer actually uses.**

examTip.trick: **Laminar pipe flow has a PARABOLIC profile, whose mean is exactly HALF its peak: u_max/V_mean = 2.0.**
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 1.22 is the TURBULENT value** — turbulent eddies MIX momentum across the pipe, flattening the profile and confining the steep gradient to a thin wall layer.
examTip.mnemonic: **Laminar: h_f ∝ V (linear), α = 2.0, f = 64/Re. Turbulent: h_f ∝ V^1.75 to V², α ≈ 1.05.** Darcy's law is linear precisely because seepage is laminar — and it fails in rockfill, where it is not.

questions.stem: Water is pumped through a 300 mm pipe 800 m long at 0.09 m³/s. Taking the Darcy friction FACTOR as f = 0.02, the head loss due to friction is:
questions.solution:
**4.41 m.**

**Step 1 — the mean velocity:**

> **A = (π/4)(0.3)² = 0.07069 m²**

> **V = Q/A = 0.09/0.07069 = 1.273 m/s**

**Step 2 — the Darcy-Weisbach equation:**

> **h_f = f L V² / (2 g d)**

> **Numerator: 0.02 × 800 × (1.273)² = 16 × 1.621 = 25.94**

> **Denominator: 2 × 9.81 × 0.3 = 5.886**

> **h_f = 25.94 / 5.886 = 4.41 m** ✓

**The factor-of-four convention trap, which the option set is built on:**

> **Two forms of the same equation are in circulation, and they differ by a factor of four:**

| Form | Equation | Coefficient |
|---|---|---|
| **DARCY-WEISBACH with the friction FACTOR f** | **h_f = f L V²/(2gd)** | **f — the MOODY DIAGRAM value; f = 64/Re in laminar flow** ← used here |
| **The older form with the friction COEFFICIENT f'** | **h_f = 4 f' L V²/(2gd)** | **f' = f/4** |

> **So the SAME physical pipe has f = 0.02 in one convention and f' = 0.005 in the other.**

> **A bare statement of "friction coefficient 0.02" is therefore AMBIGUOUS unless the intended equation is known — and the stem here says FACTOR explicitly, which settles it.**

**Every distractor is one reading of that ambiguity:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **1.10 m** | **The answer divided by four — f treated as f' the wrong way round** |
| **17.63 m** | **Four TIMES the answer — 0.02 read as f', so f = 0.08** |
| **2.19 m** | **Half the answer — the velocity head halved, or 2g mishandled** |
| **4.41 m** | ✓ |

**The MAGNITUDE CHECK that resolves the ambiguity in practice:**

> **For a commercial steel, concrete or PVC pipe in turbulent flow, the DARCY factor f is almost always between 0.015 and 0.04.**

> **A quoted value of 0.005 is therefore in the OLDER convention; a value of 0.08 is either the older convention or a genuinely very rough pipe.**

> **So the number itself usually reveals which convention is meant**, and that check should be applied whenever a friction coefficient arrives without its equation.

> **The stakes justify the care: a factor-of-four error in the friction coefficient is a factor-of-four error in the pumping head, hence in the pump selected and in the energy bill for the life of the installation.**

**Putting the answer in perspective:**

> **h_f = 4.41 m over 800 m is a hydraulic gradient of 4.41/800 = 0.0055, or 1 in 181.**

> **The velocity of 1.27 m/s sits comfortably in the normal design range of 0.9 to 2.5 m/s, so the pipe is sensibly sized.**

> **The power absorbed by friction alone:**

> **P = ρ g Q h_f = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.09 × 4.41 = 3894 W ≈ 3.9 kW**

> **At 70 per cent pump efficiency that is 5.6 kW of electrical input, and over a year of continuous running about 49,000 kWh** — which is why the fifth-power diameter law matters commercially rather than academically.

> **Recall that h_f ∝ Q²/d⁵: increasing this pipe to 350 mm would cut the friction loss to 4.41 × (300/350)⁵ = 2.14 m, halving that energy for a modest increase in pipe cost.**

**The other losses, since friction is only part of the total:**

| Loss | Expression | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **FRICTION (the major loss)** | **f L V²/(2gd)** | **Dominates in a LONG pipe** ← |
| **Sudden ENLARGEMENT** | **(V₁ − V₂)²/2g** | Exact, derived from momentum |
| **Sudden CONTRACTION** | **≈ 0.5 V²/2g** | The loss occurs at the vena contracta |
| **ENTRY** | **0.5 V²/2g sharp-edged; 0.05 for a bellmouth** | Shape matters greatly |
| **EXIT** | **V²/2g — the ENTIRE velocity head** | **Unavoidable; the kinetic energy is simply lost** |
| **Bends, valves, fittings** | **k V²/2g** | Tabulated k values |

> **The LONG pipe / SHORT pipe distinction decides whether the minor losses may be neglected:**

> **The usual rule is that if L/d exceeds about 1000, the minor losses amount to a few per cent of the friction loss and may be ignored.**

> **Here L/d = 800/0.3 = 2667 — comfortably a LONG pipe**, so treating friction as the whole loss is justified.

> **For a SHORT pipe — a pump suction, a culvert, a plumbing run — the minor losses can EXCEED the friction loss, and every fitting must be counted.**

> **That is why a plumbing calculation looks so different from a pipeline calculation despite using identical equations: in one the pipe dominates and in the other the fittings do.**

> **And note the ENTRY loss figures: a sharp-edged entry costs 0.5 velocity heads and a bellmouth only 0.05 — a tenfold reduction for nothing more than a shaped inlet.** It is among the cheapest hydraulic improvements available, which is why intakes, culverts and pump suctions are almost always given a rounded entry.

examTip.trap: **The factor-of-four convention: h_f = fLV²/(2gd) with the DARCY FACTOR, or h_f = 4f'LV²/(2gd) with the older COEFFICIENT f' = f/4.** Every distractor here is one misreading of that — ×4, ÷4, or ÷2.
examTip.mnemonic: **Magnitude check: the DARCY factor for commercial pipe in turbulent flow is 0.015 to 0.04**, so 0.02 must be f and 0.005 would be f'. And with L/d = 2667 this is a LONG pipe, so neglecting minor losses is legitimate.

questions.stem: For a trapezoidal channel, the MOST ECONOMICAL section is one in which:
options: The bed width equals the depth of flow
The hydraulic radius equals half the depth of flow
The top width equals twice the depth of flow
The side slope is 1 vertical to 2 horizontal
questions.solution:
**The HYDRAULIC RADIUS equals HALF THE DEPTH of flow: R = y/2.**

**What "most economical" means:**

> **The most economical (or most efficient) section is the one that carries the MAXIMUM DISCHARGE for a given cross-sectional area — equivalently, the one requiring the MINIMUM AREA for a given discharge.**

> **From Manning's equation Q = (1/n) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}, with A, n and S fixed, Q is maximum when R is maximum.**

> **And R = A/P, so with A fixed, R is maximum when the WETTED PERIMETER P is MINIMUM.**

> **So the condition for the most economical section is simply: MINIMUM WETTED PERIMETER for the given area.**

> **Which is also the condition for minimum LINING COST and minimum excavation — which is why the word "economical" is apt rather than merely conventional.**

**The resulting conditions for a trapezoidal channel:**

| Condition | Statement |
|---|---|
| **R = y/2** | **The hydraulic radius is HALF the depth** ← the general and universal condition |
| **A SEMICIRCLE drawn with its centre at the mid-point of the water surface, radius y, is TANGENT to both sides and the bed** | The geometric statement of the same thing |
| **Top width = 2 × (sloping side length)** | For a trapezoid |
| **For the BEST side slope as well (θ = 60°)** | The section becomes HALF A REGULAR HEXAGON |

> **The condition R = y/2 is worth singling out because it holds for the most economical RECTANGLE and TRAPEZIUM alike, and it is the form most easily applied.**

**Checking it on the most economical RECTANGLE, which is the simplest case:**

> **For a rectangle, the most economical section has b = 2y — the width is twice the depth.**

> **Then A = 2y², P = b + 2y = 2y + 2y = 4y**

> **R = A/P = 2y²/4y = y/2** ✓

> **So the general condition is satisfied, which confirms it.**

> **Note that option (a) "bed width equals depth" is therefore wrong for a rectangle too — the correct rectangular condition is b = 2y.**

**The most economical TRAPEZIUM in full, since it is the case that matters:**

> **For a trapezium of bed width b, depth y and side slope z horizontal to 1 vertical:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Area** | **A = y(b + zy)** |
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = b + 2y√(1+z²)** |
| **Most economical condition (for a GIVEN z)** | **b + 2zy = 2y√(1+z²)**, i.e. **top width = 2 × sloping side** |
| **The BEST side slope** | **z = 1/√3, i.e. 60° to the horizontal** |
| **The resulting shape** | **HALF A REGULAR HEXAGON** ← |

> **The half-hexagon result is elegant and worth understanding: among all trapezoidal shapes, the half-hexagon minimises the wetted perimeter for a given area.**

> **And it is a step toward the general truth: among ALL possible shapes, the SEMICIRCLE has the least perimeter for a given area — it is the most efficient channel section of all.**

> **A half-hexagon is the best that can be done with straight sides, which is why it is the theoretical ideal for a lined trapezoidal canal.**

**Why the theoretical optimum is rarely built — the honest qualification:**

> **The 60° side slope (1 vertical to 0.577 horizontal) is far too steep to stand in most soils.**

| Material | Stable side slope (H : V) |
|---|---|
| **Rock** | **Near vertical to 0.25 : 1** |
| **Stiff clay, lined** | **0.5 : 1 to 1 : 1** |
| **The theoretical optimum** | **0.577 : 1** ← only achievable in firm material |
| **Firm loam** | **1 : 1 to 1.5 : 1** |
| **Sandy soil** | **2 : 1 or flatter** |
| **Very loose sand** | **3 : 1** |

> **So in a sandy soil requiring a 2 : 1 slope, the side slope is fixed by STABILITY and only the b/y ratio remains free to optimise.**

> **That is why the practical condition used is the one for a GIVEN z — top width equals twice the sloping side — rather than the full half-hexagon.**

> **And it is a good instance of a theoretical optimum being constrained by a physical requirement: the shape that minimises the perimeter is not the shape that stands up.**

**Other considerations that displace the economical section in practice:**

| Consideration | Effect |
|---|---|
| **SLOPE STABILITY** | **Fixes the side slope, as above** ← |
| **Non-scouring / non-silting velocity** | **The velocity must lie in a band; the most economical section may fall outside it** |
| **FREEBOARD** | Adds depth above the design water level |
| **Construction practicality** | **A very deep narrow channel is hard to excavate and to maintain** |
| **Land acquisition cost** | May favour a deeper, narrower section than the optimum |
| **Maintenance access** | A channel too deep to enter safely is a liability |

> **The velocity constraint is the one most likely to override the economical section outright: the most efficient section for a given area gives the HIGHEST velocity, which may exceed the scouring limit for an unlined channel.**

> **So for an UNLINED alluvial canal the section is governed by regime theory (Kennedy, Lacey) and the economical section is irrelevant.**

> **The most economical section belongs to LINED channels**, where scour is not a concern and the lining cost is directly proportional to the wetted perimeter — which is exactly the quantity being minimised.

> **That is the clean statement of where this theory applies: minimise the perimeter when you are PAYING for the perimeter.**

examTip.trick: **R = y/2 is the universal condition** — it holds for the most economical rectangle (b = 2y) and trapezium alike. Check on the rectangle: A = 2y², P = 4y, R = y/2 ✓.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the rectangle's condition MISSTATED** — it is b = 2y, not b = y. And the most economical trapezium with the best side slope is HALF A REGULAR HEXAGON, side slope 60°.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Most economical" reduces to MINIMUM WETTED PERIMETER for a given area** — which is also minimum lining cost. So it applies to LINED channels; an unlined alluvial canal is governed by regime theory instead, where the velocity limit overrides efficiency.

questions.stem: In a hydraulic jump, the quantity that is conserved across the jump is:
questions.solution:
**The SPECIFIC FORCE — the momentum function.**

**Why momentum and not energy:**

> **A hydraulic jump is a violently TURBULENT phenomenon: the flow rolls over on itself, entrains air, and dissipates energy as heat and noise.**

> **So ENERGY IS NOT CONSERVED — indeed the whole engineering purpose of a jump is to DESTROY energy.**

> **But MOMENTUM is conserved, because the external forces on the control volume are known and small:**

| Force on the control volume | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **Hydrostatic pressure on the upstream face** | Included |
| **Hydrostatic pressure on the downstream face** | Included |
| **BOUNDARY FRICTION over the short length of the jump** | **NEGLECTED — the jump is short** ← |
| **Component of weight along a nearly horizontal bed** | Neglected |

> **With friction and weight neglected, the momentum equation gives an exact relation between the two depths — and that is why the jump is analysed by MOMENTUM, not by energy.**

> **This is the classic example in open channel hydraulics of choosing the right conservation principle: use ENERGY where losses are negligible, use MOMENTUM where they are not but the forces are known.**

**The specific force (momentum function):**

> **M = A ȳ + Q²/(g A)**

> **For a rectangular channel, per unit width:  M = y²/2 + q²/(g y)**

> **Setting M₁ = M₂ and solving gives the SEQUENT (conjugate) DEPTH relation:**

> **y₂/y₁ = ½ [√(1 + 8 Fr₁²) − 1]**

> **Note the two terms of M: the FIRST is the hydrostatic pressure force, the SECOND the momentum flux. Their sum is conserved, and each alone is not.**

**A worked example, to make the relation concrete:**

> **Take y₁ = 0.5 m with Fr₁ = 3.0:**

> **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8 × 9) − 1] = ½[√73 − 1] = ½[8.544 − 1] = 3.772**

> **So y₂ = 3.772 × 0.5 = 1.886 m**

> **The energy loss:  ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4 y₁ y₂) = (1.386)³/(4 × 0.5 × 1.886) = 2.663/3.772 = 0.706 m**

> **And the upstream specific energy: E₁ = y₁(1 + Fr₁²/2) = 0.5(1 + 4.5) = 2.75 m**

> **So the jump destroys 0.706/2.75 = 26 per cent of the energy** — which is the whole point of building one.

**The classification of jumps, since the efficiency depends on Fr₁:**

| Fr₁ | Type | Energy dissipated |
|---|---|---|
| **1.0 - 1.7** | **UNDULAR — a train of standing waves, no roller** | **Under 5 % — negligible** |
| **1.7 - 2.5** | **WEAK — a smooth surface roller** | **5 - 15 %** |
| **2.5 - 4.5** | **OSCILLATING — an unstable jet, waves travel downstream** | **15 - 45 %; AVOID — the waves damage banks** ← |
| **4.5 - 9.0** | **STEADY — well-balanced, stable position** | **45 - 70 %; the DESIGN RANGE** ← |
| **> 9.0** | **STRONG (choppy) — rough and effective** | **70 - 85 %; large, and erosive** |

> **The OSCILLATING jump (2.5 to 4.5) is the one to design AWAY from, and the reason is practical rather than theoretical:**

> **Its jet oscillates between the bed and the surface irregularly, generating waves that travel far downstream and erode banks and damage structures.**

> **So a stilling basin is deliberately proportioned to give Fr₁ in the STEADY range 4.5 to 9.0 — by setting the basin's floor level so that the incoming supercritical depth produces the desired Froude number.**

> **That is a real design decision, and it shows that the classification table is not descriptive taxonomy but a design tool.**

**Where hydraulic jumps are USED, since they are deliberately created:**

| Application | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **STILLING BASIN below a spillway or weir** | **DESTROY the energy of the falling water before it reaches the river bed** ← |
| **Below a sluice gate** | Same |
| **At the end of a chute or drop structure** | Same |
| **In a MIXING basin (water treatment)** | **The turbulence mixes chemicals rapidly** |
| **To RE-AERATE water** | The air entrainment raises dissolved oxygen |
