| **To raise the water level for a downstream offtake** | The jump lifts the depth from y₁ to y₂ |

> **The stilling basin is the primary case, and the alternative is unacceptable: supercritical flow arriving on an unprotected river bed will scour a hole deep enough to undermine the structure itself.**

> **So the choice is not whether to dissipate the energy but WHERE — in a concrete basin designed for it, or in the river bed, at the foot of the dam.**

**Why the jump's LOCATION matters, and how it is controlled:**

> **A jump forms where the supercritical depth y₁ and the available TAILWATER depth satisfy the sequent depth relation.**

| Tailwater | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Tailwater EQUALS y₂** | **The jump forms exactly at the design point — ideal** |
| **Tailwater LESS than y₂** | **The jump is SWEPT DOWNSTREAM, out of the basin, onto the unprotected bed** ← the dangerous case |
| **Tailwater GREATER than y₂** | **The jump is DROWNED (submerged) — it moves upstream, dissipates less energy, and a high-velocity jet may travel along the surface** |

> **A swept-out jump is the failure mode a stilling basin is designed to prevent, and it is why basins are often built with an END SILL or a depressed floor: both raise the effective tailwater within the basin and hold the jump in place.**

> **BAFFLE BLOCKS and CHUTE BLOCKS serve the same purpose from the other direction, by adding drag that shortens the jump and stabilises it** — which is why a modern stilling basin has a floor covered in concrete blocks rather than being a plain rectangular box.

> **The USBR basin types (I to IV) are precisely a set of block-and-sill arrangements matched to different Froude number ranges**, and knowing that they exist is more useful than memorising their dimensions.

examTip.trick: **Momentum is conserved; ENERGY is not** — a jump exists precisely to destroy energy. So the analysis uses the specific force M = Aȳ + Q²/(gA), giving y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1+8Fr₁²) − 1].
examTip.trap: **Option (a) specific energy is the trap: it is NOT conserved.** The general rule — use ENERGY where losses are negligible, MOMENTUM where they are not but the forces are known.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design for Fr₁ = 4.5 to 9 (STEADY jump, 45-70 % dissipation) and AVOID 2.5 to 4.5 (OSCILLATING)** — whose waves travel downstream and erode banks. And a SWEPT-OUT jump, from insufficient tailwater, is the failure a stilling basin exists to prevent.

questions.stem: A catchment of 120 km² receives 80 mm of rainfall in a storm. If the resulting runoff volume is 3.84 × 10⁶ m³, the runoff coefficient is:
questions.solution:
**0.40.**

**Step 1 — the volume of rainfall over the catchment:**

> **Area = 120 km² = 120 × 10⁶ m²**

> **Depth = 80 mm = 0.080 m**

> **Rainfall volume = 120 × 10⁶ × 0.080 = 9.6 × 10⁶ m³**

**Step 2 — the runoff coefficient:**

> **C = runoff volume / rainfall volume = 3.84 × 10⁶ / 9.6 × 10⁶ = 0.40** ✓

> **Equivalently, as depths: runoff depth = 3.84 × 10⁶/(120 × 10⁶) = 0.032 m = 32 mm, and C = 32/80 = 0.40** ✓

> **Note that option (c) 0.32 is the RUNOFF DEPTH in metres × 10, or the runoff depth read as a coefficient** — a trap for a candidate who computes 32 mm and stops.

**The unit conversion that this class of problem is really testing:**

> **The one step that goes wrong is mixing km² with mm.**

> **A convenient identity worth carrying:**

> **1 mm of rainfall over 1 km² = 1000 m³**

> **Check: 10⁶ m² × 0.001 m = 1000 m³** ✓

> **So 80 mm over 120 km² = 80 × 120 × 1000 = 9.6 × 10⁶ m³** ✓ — the same answer in one line, with no powers of ten to lose.

> **That identity turns most catchment volume problems into simple multiplication, and it is worth memorising in preference to converting units each time.**

**What the runoff coefficient represents:**

> **C is the fraction of rainfall that appears as surface runoff. The remainder is lost to:**

| Loss | Note |
|---|---|
| **INFILTRATION into the soil** | **Usually the largest loss** ← |
| **EVAPORATION and transpiration** | Significant over a long period, less in a single storm |
| **INTERCEPTION by vegetation** | Rain held on leaves and never reaching the ground |
| **DEPRESSION STORAGE** | Puddles, hollows, ponds |
| **Channel and detention storage** | Delays rather than removes |

> **So C = 0.40 means 60 per cent of the rain did not run off, which is entirely typical for a mixed rural catchment in a moderate storm.**

**Typical runoff coefficients, so the answer can be judged:**

| Surface | C |
|---|---|
| **Forest, flat, sandy soil** | **0.05 - 0.15** |
| **Cultivated land, moderate slope** | **0.20 - 0.40** ← |
| **Grassland, clayey soil** | **0.30 - 0.50** |
| **Residential, suburban** | **0.35 - 0.55** |
| **Dense urban, commercial** | **0.70 - 0.90** |
| **ASPHALT or CONCRETE pavement** | **0.85 - 0.95** |
| **Roofs** | **0.75 - 0.95** |

> **The urbanisation contrast is the important one: converting a rural catchment (C ≈ 0.3) to dense urban development (C ≈ 0.85) roughly TRIPLES the peak runoff from the same rainfall.**

> **And it does more than that — it also SHORTENS the time of concentration, because paved surfaces and pipes convey water far faster than fields and natural channels.**

> **A higher peak arriving sooner is the double effect of urbanisation on flooding**, and it is why urban drainage capacity has to be so much greater than the rural drainage it replaces, and why a downstream town can be flooded by development it never saw.

**The RATIONAL METHOD, where C is chiefly used:**

> **Q_peak = C i A / 3.6**, with Q in m³/s, i in mm/h and A in km²

> **Or in consistent units: Q = C i A.**

| Assumption of the rational method | Note |
|---|---|
| **The rainfall intensity is UNIFORM over the whole catchment** | **Reasonable only for a SMALL area** ← |
| **The rainfall duration equals or exceeds the TIME OF CONCENTRATION** | So the whole catchment contributes simultaneously |
| **The runoff coefficient is constant** | In reality C rises during a storm as the soil saturates |
| **The return period of the peak equals that of the rainfall** | An approximation |

> **The method is therefore restricted to SMALL catchments — usually under about 50 km², and preferably under 25 km² — which is why it is the standard tool for URBAN DRAINAGE and CULVERT design and is not used for a river basin.**

> **The 120 km² catchment in this question is too large for the rational method**, and a peak flow for it would be estimated by a unit hydrograph, a regional flood frequency relation, or a rainfall-runoff model.

> **That is worth noting as an honest limitation: the runoff coefficient computed here is a valid VOLUME ratio for the storm, and it should not be fed into the rational method for a catchment of this size.**

**The TIME OF CONCENTRATION, since the method depends on it:**

> **t_c is the time for water to travel from the HYDRAULICALLY MOST REMOTE point of the catchment to the outlet.**

> **The design rainfall intensity is read for a duration EQUAL TO t_c, and the reason is a genuine optimum:**

> **A SHORTER storm does not engage the whole catchment — only part of it contributes at any instant.**

> **A LONGER storm engages all of it but at a LOWER intensity, since intensity-duration curves fall with duration.**

> **So the peak flow occurs for a storm of duration exactly t_c** — which is why that duration, and not the heaviest rainfall ever recorded, is the design condition.

> **Kirpich's formula is the usual estimate: t_c = 0.01947 L^{0.77} S^{−0.385} minutes, with L in metres and S the average slope** — empirical, and adequate for the small catchments where the method applies.

examTip.trap: **Option (c) 0.32 is the runoff DEPTH (32 mm) mistaken for the coefficient.** Divide by the rainfall depth, not by anything else: 32/80 = 0.40.
examTip.mnemonic: **Urbanisation both RAISES the peak (C from 0.3 to 0.85) and SHORTENS the time of concentration** — a bigger flood arriving sooner. And the RATIONAL method is for catchments under ~50 km²; 120 km² needs a unit hydrograph instead.

questions.stem: A 4-hour unit hydrograph has a peak of 30 m³/s. The peak of the direct runoff hydrograph produced by 4 hours of rainfall generating 3.5 cm of effective rain, on a base flow of 5 m³/s, is:
questions.solution:
**110 m³/s.**

**Step 1 — scale the unit hydrograph.**

> **A UNIT hydrograph is the response to ONE UNIT of effective rainfall — in SI practice, 1 CENTIMETRE.**

> **So a 3.5 cm effective rainfall of the same duration produces a hydrograph 3.5 TIMES as large at every ordinate:**

> **Direct runoff peak = 3.5 × 30 = 105 m³/s**

**Step 2 — add the base flow.**

> **The question asks for the peak of the runoff hydrograph on a base flow of 5 m³/s:**

> **Total peak = 105 + 5 = 110 m³/s** ✓

> **Note the distinction the option set is built on:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **105 m³/s** | **The DIRECT RUNOFF peak — base flow omitted** |
| **110 m³/s** | **The TOTAL hydrograph peak** ✓ |
| **35 m³/s** | 30 + 5 — the unit hydrograph peak plus base flow, without scaling |
| **38.5 m³/s** | 35 × 1.1 — a compounded confusion |

> **So reading whether the DIRECT RUNOFF or the TOTAL flow is wanted is the task, and both figures are legitimate answers to different questions.**

> **Here the stem says "on a base flow of 5 m³/s", which asks for the total.**

**The two principles a unit hydrograph rests on:**

| Principle | Statement |
|---|---|
| **LINEARITY (proportionality)** | **Rainfall of n units produces ordinates n times the unit hydrograph's** ← used here |
| **SUPERPOSITION** | **Hydrographs from successive rainfall blocks are ADDED with appropriate time offsets** |
| **TIME INVARIANCE** | **The same rainfall produces the same hydrograph whenever it occurs** |

> **These are strong assumptions, and they are what make the method usable by hand — and also what limit it.**

> **In reality catchment response is NOT linear: a very intense storm produces proportionally MORE runoff than a light one, because the soil saturates and infiltration falls.**

> **So a unit hydrograph derived from moderate storms will UNDER-predict the peak from an extreme one** — which is a real limitation and one worth stating rather than glossing over.

**What the "unit" and the "duration" each mean, since both are in the name:**

> **A "4-hour unit hydrograph" specifies TWO things:**

| Element | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **"UNIT"** | **The DEPTH of effective rainfall: 1 cm** |
| **"4-HOUR"** | **The DURATION over which that 1 cm falls** ← |

> **Both matter, and confusing them is the standard error.**

> **The DEPTH scales the ordinates linearly, as used above.**

> **The DURATION does NOT scale linearly — a 2-hour unit hydrograph is NOT half a 4-hour one.** Changing the duration changes the SHAPE of the response, and requires the S-CURVE method or the method of superposition.

> **So this question is straightforward precisely because the storm duration (4 hours) MATCHES the unit hydrograph duration (4 hours).** Had the storm been 2 or 8 hours long, the unit hydrograph would first have to be converted.

**Converting the duration, since the question would otherwise be different:**

| Target duration | Method |
|---|---|
| **An INTEGER MULTIPLE of the original (4 h → 8 h, 12 h)** | **SUPERPOSITION: lag copies of the UH by the original duration, add, and divide by the number of copies** |
| **ANY other duration (4 h → 3 h, 5 h)** | **The S-CURVE (S-hydrograph) method** ← the general technique |

> **The S-CURVE is the hydrograph that would result from a CONTINUOUS effective rainfall at a constant rate of 1 cm per unit duration, indefinitely.**

> **It is built by summing UHs lagged successively by the unit duration, and it rises to an equilibrium discharge:**

> **Q_equilibrium = 2.778 A/D**, with A in km² and D the duration in hours, giving Q in m³/s

> **Offsetting two S-curves by the DESIRED duration and taking the difference, scaled appropriately, gives the unit hydrograph for that duration.**

> **It is fiddly by hand and it is the standard method, and the equilibrium check is what verifies it: an S-curve that does not level off at 2.778A/D contains an error.**

**BASE FLOW SEPARATION, since it is the step that produced the 5 m³/s:**

> **A unit hydrograph is derived from DIRECT RUNOFF only, so base flow must first be removed from the observed hydrograph.**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **STRAIGHT LINE** | **Join the point where the rise begins to the point where the recession returns to that level — simplest and commonest** ← |
| **Fixed base length** | Extend the pre-storm recession forward N days, N from an empirical relation |
| **Variable slope** | Project the pre-storm and post-storm recessions and join them |
| **Recession curve analysis** | Most defensible; extends the pre-storm recession under the hydrograph |

> **The honest position is that base flow separation is somewhat ARBITRARY: the methods give different answers, and there is no physical boundary in the ground between "base flow" and "direct runoff".**

> **What matters is CONSISTENCY: the same separation method must be used when deriving the unit hydrograph and when applying it.**

> **Any bias introduced in the derivation is then cancelled in the application**, which is a satisfying practical resolution of a theoretically untidy problem — and a reminder that hydrology tolerates approximation provided the approximation is applied uniformly.

examTip.trick: **Scale then add: 3.5 cm × 30 m³/s = 105 m³/s direct runoff, plus 5 m³/s base flow = 110 m³/s total.**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 105 is the DIRECT RUNOFF peak with base flow omitted** — both are correct answers to different questions, so read whether the total flow is wanted. The stem's "on a base flow of 5" asks for the total.
examTip.mnemonic: **"4-hour unit hydrograph" fixes TWO things: 1 cm DEPTH and 4-hour DURATION.** Depth scales linearly; duration does NOT — a 2-hour UH is not half a 4-hour one, and converting needs the S-CURVE method.

questions.stem: A body floating in water is in STABLE equilibrium when:
options: The centre of gravity lies below the centre of buoyancy
The metacentre lies above the centre of gravity
The centre of buoyancy coincides with the centre of gravity
questions.solution:
**When the METACENTRE lies ABOVE the CENTRE OF GRAVITY — that is, when the metacentric height GM is POSITIVE.**

**The three states of equilibrium:**

| Condition | State | Behaviour when tilted |
|---|---|---|
| **M above G (GM > 0)** | **STABLE** | **A RIGHTING couple restores the body** ← |
| **M coincides with G (GM = 0)** | **NEUTRAL** | **It stays in the tilted position** |
| **M below G (GM < 0)** | **UNSTABLE** | **An OVERTURNING couple capsizes it** |

> **So option (d) — zero metacentric height — describes NEUTRAL equilibrium, not stable.**

**What the METACENTRE is, and why it is the right criterion:**

> **When a floating body TILTS through a small angle, the shape of the submerged volume changes, so the CENTRE OF BUOYANCY B MOVES sideways to a new position B'.**

> **The buoyant force acts UPWARD through B', while the weight acts DOWNWARD through G.**

> **The METACENTRE M is the point where the new line of action of the buoyant force cuts the original vertical centreline of the body.**

> **And the couple formed by the two forces is:**

> **Righting moment = W × GM × sin θ**

> **If M is ABOVE G, that couple pushes the body BACK upright — stable.**

> **If M is BELOW G, it pushes it FURTHER over — unstable.**

> **So the whole question of floating stability reduces to the SIGN of GM, and the metacentre is what makes that possible.**

**Why option (a) is TRUE for a SUBMERGED body and NOT the criterion for a FLOATING one — the important distinction:**

| | **FULLY SUBMERGED body (a submarine, a balloon)** | **FLOATING body (a ship, a pontoon)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Does B move when it tilts?** | **NO — the displaced volume is fixed, so B stays put** | **YES — the waterplane shape changes, so B shifts sideways** |
| **Stability criterion** | **G must be BELOW B** ← this is option (a) | **M must be ABOVE G — GM > 0** ✓ |
| **Can G be above B?** | **NO — that is unstable** | **YES, and it usually IS** |

> **That last row is the point most often missed, and it is worth stating plainly: in almost every ship, THE CENTRE OF GRAVITY IS ABOVE THE CENTRE OF BUOYANCY — and the ship is perfectly stable.**

> **It is stable because the metacentre is higher still.**

> **So option (a) is not merely a wrong answer; it states a criterion that virtually no real vessel satisfies, and applying it would condemn every ship afloat.**

> **The reason a submerged body is different is that its displaced volume cannot change shape — so B is fixed, and the only way to get a righting couple is to hang the weight below the buoyancy, like a pendulum.** Which is exactly how a submarine is ballasted.

**Computing the metacentric height:**

> **GM = BM − BG**, where:

> **BM = I / V** — with **I** the second moment of the WATERPLANE AREA about the axis of rotation, and **V** the DISPLACED VOLUME.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **I** | **Second moment of the WATERPLANE — the area of the horizontal section at the water surface** ← |
| **V** | Volume of water displaced |
| **BM** | **The metacentric RADIUS** |
| **BG** | Distance from the centre of buoyancy to the centre of gravity |

> **The appearance of the WATERPLANE second moment is the key insight: stability comes from the SHAPE OF THE BODY AT THE WATERLINE, not from its shape below.**

> **Which explains why a WIDE, SHALLOW vessel is so much more stable than a narrow deep one: I for a rectangular waterplane is LB³/12, so it goes as the CUBE OF THE BREADTH.**

> **DOUBLING the beam multiplies BM — and hence the stability — by EIGHT, for the same displacement.**

> **That is why a raft, a catamaran or a pontoon is extraordinarily stable, and why a narrow racing shell is not.**

**A worked illustration, since the cube law deserves numbers:**

> **A rectangular pontoon 6 m long, 3 m wide, floating at 0.6 m draught, with G at 0.9 m above the base:**

> **V = 6 × 3 × 0.6 = 10.8 m³**

> **I = LB³/12 = 6 × 27/12 = 13.5 m⁴**

> **BM = I/V = 13.5/10.8 = 1.25 m**

> **B is at half the draught = 0.30 m above the base, so BG = 0.90 − 0.30 = 0.60 m**

> **GM = 1.25 − 0.60 = +0.65 m — STABLE** ✓

> **Note that G (0.90 m) is ABOVE B (0.30 m) and the pontoon is stable regardless** — the illustration of the point made above.

> **Now WIDEN it to 4 m: I = 6 × 64/12 = 32 m⁴, V = 14.4 m³, BM = 2.22 m, and GM rises to about 1.6 m.** A 33 per cent increase in beam more than doubles the metacentric height.

**The practical trade-off, since more stability is not simply better:**

> **The period of ROLL is:  T = 2π √(k²/(g × GM))**, with k the radius of gyration.

| GM | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **LARGE GM** | **Very stable, but a SHORT, VIOLENT roll period — uncomfortable, and hard on cargo and structure** ← |
| **SMALL positive GM** | **A slow, easy roll — comfortable, but little reserve of stability** |
| **Zero or negative** | **Unstable** |

> **So a vessel can be TOO stable: the righting moment is so stiff that it snaps back violently, which is unpleasant for passengers and damaging to cargo lashings and to the hull itself.**

> **Naval architects therefore aim for a GM in a band — typically 0.3 to 1.0 m for a merchant ship — rather than maximising it.**

> **And it explains a counter-intuitive practice: adding ballast LOW in a ship increases GM and stability, and can make the roll so stiff that some ships are deliberately ballasted HIGHER to soften it.** Stability is a design target, not a quantity to be maximised.

examTip.trick: **Stable when M is ABOVE G, i.e. GM > 0.** GM = 0 is NEUTRAL (option d), GM < 0 unstable. Righting moment = W × GM × sinθ.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the criterion for a FULLY SUBMERGED body, not a floating one.** In almost every ship G is ABOVE B and the ship is stable — because M is higher still. A submarine is different because its displaced volume cannot change shape, so B never moves.
examTip.mnemonic: **BM = I/V, with I the WATERPLANE second moment** — so stability comes from the shape at the WATERLINE. I ∝ B³, so doubling the beam multiplies stability by EIGHT. But a large GM gives a violent roll, so it is a target band (0.3-1.0 m), not a maximum.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m over its whole length. The maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**90 kNm, at mid-span.**

**The standard result:**

> **M_max = w L² / 8**

> **= 20 × 6² / 8 = 20 × 36/8 = 720/8 = 90 kNm** ✓

**Deriving it, so the formula need not be trusted blindly:**

> **Total load = wL = 20 × 6 = 120 kN, shared equally: R_A = R_B = 60 kN**

> **At mid-span, taking moments of everything to the left:**

> **M = R_A × (L/2) − (w × L/2) × (L/4)**

> **= 60 × 3 − (20 × 3) × 1.5 = 180 − 90 = 90 kNm** ✓

> **The two terms are worth noticing: the reaction contributes 180 and the load on the left half takes back 90, leaving half the reaction's moment.** That structure — the answer being wL²/4 minus wL²/8 — is why the coefficient is 1/8 and not 1/4.

**Why the maximum is at MID-SPAN — the general rule:**

> **The bending moment is maximum where the SHEAR FORCE IS ZERO (or changes sign).**

> **Because dM/dx = V: the shear force is the SLOPE of the bending moment diagram, so M is stationary where V = 0.**

> **For this beam, V = 60 − 20x, which is zero at x = 3 m — the mid-span.** ✓

> **That relation is the single most useful tool for locating a maximum moment, and it works for any loading:**

| Relation | Statement |
|---|---|
| **dV/dx = −w** | **The LOAD is the slope of the shear diagram (negative)** |
| **dM/dx = V** | **The SHEAR is the slope of the moment diagram** ← |
| **Area under the load diagram** | = the CHANGE in shear |
| **Area under the shear diagram** | **= the CHANGE in moment** |

> **The last row is a fast way to build a moment diagram: the moment at any point equals the accumulated AREA of the shear diagram up to that point.**

> **Check here: the shear diagram is a triangle from 60 down to 0 over 3 m, whose area is ½ × 3 × 60 = 90 kNm** ✓ — the mid-span moment, obtained without any formula.

**The shapes of the two diagrams, since the degrees follow a pattern:**

| Loading | Shear diagram | Moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load** | **Rectangular (constant, with a jump)** | **Linear (triangular)** |
| **UDL** | **LINEAR** | **PARABOLIC** ← this case |
| **Triangular (linearly varying) load** | **Parabolic** | **CUBIC** |
| **No load** | Constant | Linear |

> **Each integration raises the degree by one, which is the pattern: load → shear → moment climbs from degree n to n+1 to n+2.**

> **So a UDL gives a linear shear and a parabolic moment, and if a candidate has drawn a parabolic shear diagram under a UDL, something is wrong.**

**The comparable standard cases, for contrast — and the distractors come from here:**

| Beam and load | Maximum moment |
|---|---|
| **Simply supported, UDL w** | **wL²/8** ← 90 kNm |
| **Simply supported, central point load W** | **WL/4** |
| **Cantilever, UDL w** | **wL²/2** (at the fixed end) |
| **Cantilever, point load W at the tip** | **WL** |
| **FIXED both ends, UDL w** | **wL²/12 at the supports, wL²/24 at mid-span** ← 60 kNm and 30 kNm |
| **Propped cantilever, UDL w** | **wL²/8 at the fixed end** |

> **Option (b) 60 kNm is wL²/12 — the SUPPORT moment of a FIXED beam** carrying the same load.

> **Option (d) 120 kNm is wL²/4 — twice the answer, from forgetting that the load on the left half takes back half the reaction's moment.**

> **Option (c) 45 kNm is wL²/16.**

> **So the option set is drawn from the standard-case table, and reading the SUPPORT CONDITIONS is what discriminates.**

**Why FIXING the ends helps so much — worth extracting from that table:**

> **Fixing both ends reduces the maximum moment from wL²/8 to wL²/12 — a reduction of one third.**

> **The reason is that the fixed ends develop NEGATIVE (hogging) moments, and a hogging moment at the support subtracts from the sagging moment at mid-span.**

> **So the total moment demand is shared between the supports and the span rather than concentrated at mid-span.**

> **And the deflection improves even more dramatically: from 5wL⁴/384EI simply supported to wL⁴/384EI fixed — a factor of FIVE.**

> **That is why continuity is so valuable in reinforced concrete construction, where it is nearly free: casting a floor monolithically makes every span continuous, and the same slab thickness spans considerably further than a series of simply supported slabs would.**

> **The price is that the support moments require TOP reinforcement over the supports, and getting that steel in the right place is where continuous construction most often goes wrong on site** — top bars pushed down by foot traffic before the concrete is placed lose most of their effective depth exactly where the moment is largest.

examTip.trick: **M_max = wL²/8 = 20 × 36/8 = 90 kNm** at mid-span.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 60 kNm is wL²/12 — the SUPPORT moment of a FIXED beam** with the same load, and (d) 120 is wL²/4. The option set is drawn from the standard-case table, so read the SUPPORT CONDITIONS.
examTip.mnemonic: **M is maximum where V = 0, because dM/dx = V** — and the moment at any point equals the AREA of the shear diagram up to it. Here the shear triangle ½ × 3 × 60 = 90 kNm gives the answer with no formula at all.

questions.stem: A cantilever beam 4 m long carries a uniformly distributed load of 12 kN/m over its entire length. The maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**96 kNm, at the fixed end.**

**The standard result:**

> **M_max = w L² / 2**

> **= 12 × 4²/2 = 12 × 16/2 = 192/2 = 96 kNm** ✓

**Deriving it — the simplest derivation in structural mechanics:**

> **Treat the whole load as a single resultant:**

> **Total load W = wL = 12 × 4 = 48 kN**

> **Acting at the CENTROID of the load, which for a UDL is at mid-length, L/2 = 2 m from the fixed end.**

> **M = W × (L/2) = 48 × 2 = 96 kNm** ✓

> **So the cantilever case needs no equilibrium equations at all: the moment at the fixed end is simply the total load times the distance to its centroid.**

> **That is why cantilever problems are the easiest of all — there are no reactions to find first, because everything can be computed from the free end.**

**Why a cantilever is so much more heavily stressed than a simply supported beam:**

| Beam | Maximum moment (same w and L) | Ratio |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported, UDL** | **wL²/8** | **1** |
| **Propped cantilever, UDL** | **wL²/8** | 1 |
| **Fixed both ends, UDL** | **wL²/12** | **0.67** |
| **CANTILEVER, UDL** | **wL²/2** | **4** ← |

> **A cantilever carries FOUR TIMES the moment of a simply supported beam of the same span and load.**

> **And its deflection is worse still: wL⁴/8EI against 5wL⁴/384EI, a ratio of 9.6.**

> **The reason is that a cantilever has only ONE support, so the entire load must be carried back to it, and the whole moment accumulates at that one point.**

> **A simply supported beam splits the load between two supports and the moment peaks at mid-span at a value the two reactions have already halved.**

> **Which is why cantilevers are kept SHORT: the moment goes as L² and the deflection as L⁴, so a cantilever twice as long is four times as heavily stressed and sixteen times as flexible.**

> **A rule of thumb in building design is to keep a cantilever to about one third of the adjacent span**, both for the moment and because the cantilever's uplift on the backspan must be resisted.

**The distractors, each a specific misstep:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **24 kNm** | **wL²/8 — the SIMPLY SUPPORTED coefficient applied to a cantilever** |
| **48 kNm** | **wL²/4, or equivalently the total load W = 48 kN read as a moment** |
| **192 kNm** | **wL² — the load times the FULL length, forgetting the centroid is at L/2** ← |
| **96 kNm** | ✓ |

> **Option (c) 192 kNm is the most instructive error: it treats the UDL as if it acted at the FREE END.**

> **A distributed load's resultant acts at its CENTROID, and forgetting that doubles the answer for a UDL.**

> **The check is a physical one: a UDL cannot possibly produce as much moment as the same total load concentrated at the tip, because most of it is nearer the support.** Exactly half as much, as it turns out.

**The shape of the diagrams, and where the maximum sits:**

| Position from the free end | Shear | Moment |
|---|---|---|
| **0 (free end)** | **0** | **0** |
| **x** | **wx** | **wx²/2 — PARABOLIC** |
| **4 m (fixed end)** | **48 kN** | **96 kNm** ← maximum |

> **Both are maximum AT THE FIXED END and zero at the free end — which is the signature of a cantilever and the opposite of a simply supported beam, where the moment is zero at both supports and maximum in the middle.**

> **That difference dictates where the reinforcement goes, and it is the most consequential practical fact about cantilevers:**

> **A cantilever HOGS — it bends with its top surface in TENSION.**

> **So the main reinforcement of a cantilever slab or beam goes at the TOP, near the support.**

> **A simply supported beam SAGS, with tension at the BOTTOM, and its steel goes at the bottom near mid-span.**

> **Placing a cantilever's main steel at the bottom is among the most serious and most common errors in small-scale construction — a balcony reinforced as though it were a simply supported slab has essentially no flexural capacity where it needs it, and the failure is sudden and total.**

> **The steel must also be ANCHORED PROPERLY INTO THE BACKSPAN**, not merely stopped at the support face: the tension at the top of a cantilever continues into the supporting member and must be developed there, which is why cantilever top bars extend a substantial distance into the adjacent span.

> **Those two details — top steel, anchored back — account for most cantilever failures between them, and neither is a matter of calculation.**

examTip.trick: **M = total load × distance to its CENTROID = (12 × 4) × 2 = 96 kNm.** No reactions needed — a cantilever can be worked entirely from the free end.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 192 kNm treats the UDL as acting at the FREE END.** A distributed load acts at its CENTROID, at L/2 — so wL²/2, exactly half of wL².
examTip.mnemonic: **A cantilever HOGS: tension at the TOP, so the main steel goes at the TOP and must be ANCHORED INTO THE BACKSPAN.** A balcony reinforced like a simply supported slab has almost no capacity, and it fails suddenly.

questions.stem: A steel bar 25 mm in diameter and 200 mm long is subjected to an axial pull of 60 kN. Taking E = 200 GPa, the elongation is:
questions.solution:
**0.122 mm.**

**The formula:**

> **δ = P L / (A E)**

**Step 1 — the area:**

> **A = (π/4)(25)² = 0.7854 × 625 = 490.9 mm²**

**Step 2 — the elongation:**

> **δ = (60,000 × 200) / (490.9 × 200,000)**

> **= 12,000,000 / 98,175,000**

> **= 0.1222 mm** ✓

**A useful two-step route, which is less error-prone:**

> **First the STRESS:  σ = P/A = 60,000/490.9 = 122.2 N/mm² = 122.2 MPa**

> **Then the STRAIN:  ε = σ/E = 122.2/200,000 = 6.11 × 10⁻⁴**

> **Then the elongation:  δ = ε L = 6.11 × 10⁻⁴ × 200 = 0.1222 mm** ✓

> **Working through the stress is worth the extra line, because the stress is a number that can be JUDGED — 122 MPa against a yield of 250 MPa for mild steel is comfortably elastic, so Hooke's law applies and the calculation is legitimate.**

> **A candidate who computes δ directly never sees whether the bar has yielded, in which case δ = PL/AE would be meaningless.**

> **That check matters: had the load been 150 kN, the stress would be 306 MPa, above yield, and the elastic formula would not apply at all.**

**Keeping the units straight, since that is where this calculation fails:**

| Quantity | Consistent set |
|---|---|
| **Force** | **N** |
| **Length** | **mm** |
| **Area** | **mm²** |
| **E** | **N/mm² — and 200 GPa = 200,000 N/mm²** ← |
| **Result** | **mm** |

> **The single conversion to get right is E: 200 GPa = 200 × 10⁹ Pa = 200 × 10³ N/mm² = 200,000 N/mm².**

> **Note that 1 GPa = 1000 N/mm² exactly, which is worth memorising because it removes the whole class of error.**

> **And observe that option (d) 1.22 mm is the answer with E taken as 20,000 rather than 200,000 — a factor-of-ten slip in exactly that conversion.**

**The distractors:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **0.061 mm** | **Half the answer — the area computed as πd²/2, or E doubled** |
| **0.244 mm** | **Twice the answer — area as πr² with r = d, or πd²/8** |
| **0.122 mm** | ✓ |
| **1.22 mm** | **E taken as 20 GPa — a factor of ten in the unit conversion** |

**The elastic constants, since E is one of four related quantities:**

| Constant | Symbol | Definition | Steel |
|---|---|---|---|
| **YOUNG'S modulus** | **E** | **Direct stress / direct strain** | **200 GPa** |
| **Modulus of RIGIDITY (shear modulus)** | **G** | **Shear stress / shear strain** | **~80 GPa** |
| **BULK modulus** | **K** | **Volumetric stress / volumetric strain** | **~160 GPa** |
| **POISSON'S ratio** | **ν** | **Lateral strain / longitudinal strain** | **0.3** |

> **Only TWO of the four are independent — the other two follow from these relations:**

> **E = 2G(1 + ν)**

> **E = 3K(1 − 2ν)**

> **And combining them:  E = 9KG/(3K + G)**

> **Check for steel: E = 2 × 80 × 1.3 = 208 GPa** ✓ ≈ 200

> **And E = 3 × 160 × (1 − 0.6) = 3 × 160 × 0.4 = 192 GPa** ✓ ≈ 200

> **So a value of any two constants determines the others**, and the relations are worth carrying because examinations frequently give G and ν and ask for E, or the reverse.

**What POISSON'S RATIO's limits tell us — a point of genuine interest:**

> **From E = 3K(1 − 2ν): if ν were 0.5, then K would be INFINITE — the material would be perfectly INCOMPRESSIBLE.**

> **So ν = 0.5 is the theoretical UPPER LIMIT, and rubber approaches it (ν ≈ 0.4997).**

> **And from E = 2G(1 + ν): a negative ν below −1 would give a negative G, which is impossible.**

> **So the theoretical range is −1 < ν < 0.5.**

| Material | ν |
|---|---|
| **Cork** | **~0.0 — it barely bulges when compressed** |
| **Concrete** | **0.1 - 0.2** |
| **Steel** | **0.27 - 0.30** |
| **Aluminium** | 0.33 |
| **RUBBER** | **~0.4997 — nearly incompressible** ← |

> **CORK's near-zero Poisson's ratio is why it is used for bottle stoppers: pushed into a neck it does not bulge sideways and jam, and pulled out it does not thin and leak.** A material with steel's ν would be far less convenient.

> **And rubber's near-0.5 value is why a rubber bearing pad works: it deforms in shear readily and resists compression almost incompressibly, which is exactly what a bridge bearing needs — free horizontal movement with firm vertical support.**

examTip.trap: **1 GPa = 1000 N/mm² exactly**, so E = 200,000 N/mm². Option (d) 1.22 mm is a factor-of-ten slip in that one conversion.
examTip.mnemonic: **Work through the STRESS so you can judge it** — 122 MPa against a 250 MPa yield confirms Hooke's law applies. And only TWO elastic constants are independent: E = 2G(1+ν) = 3K(1−2ν), which is why ν = 0.5 means incompressible.

questions.stem: A bar is subjected to uniaxial tension producing a longitudinal strain of 0.001. If Poisson's ratio is 0.3, the volumetric strain is:
questions.solution:
**0.0004.**

**The relation for UNIAXIAL stress:**

> **e_v = ε (1 − 2ν)**

> **= 0.001 × (1 − 2 × 0.3) = 0.001 × (1 − 0.6) = 0.001 × 0.4 = 0.0004** ✓

**Where it comes from — the three strains added:**

> **Under a tensile stress along the x-axis:**

| Direction | Strain |
|---|---|
| **Longitudinal (x)** | **+ε = +0.001 — the bar LENGTHENS** |
| **Lateral (y)** | **−νε = −0.0003 — it CONTRACTS** |
| **Lateral (z)** | **−νε = −0.0003 — it CONTRACTS** |

> **Volumetric strain is the SUM of the three principal strains (for small strains):**

> **e_v = ε_x + ε_y + ε_z = ε − νε − νε = ε(1 − 2ν)** ✓

> **= 0.001 − 0.0003 − 0.0003 = 0.0004** ✓

> **So the bar gets longer by 0.1 per cent and thinner in both lateral directions, and the NET volume change is only 0.04 per cent — the lateral contractions cancel most of the longitudinal extension.**

**Why e_v = ε₁ + ε₂ + ε₃ — worth seeing once:**

> **A block of dimensions x, y, z has volume V = xyz. After straining:**

> **V' = x(1+ε₁) × y(1+ε₂) × z(1+ε₃)**

> **Expanding and DISCARDING products of small strains:**

> **V' ≈ xyz (1 + ε₁ + ε₂ + ε₃)**

> **So ΔV/V = ε₁ + ε₂ + ε₃** ✓

> **The discarded terms are of order ε², which for ε = 0.001 is 10⁻⁶ — a millionth, entirely negligible.** Which is why the simple sum is used, and also why it is valid only for SMALL strains.

**The distractors, each identifiable:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **0.0004** | ✓ |
| **0.0010** | **The LONGITUDINAL strain itself — the lateral contractions ignored, i.e. ν treated as 0** |
| **0.0016** | **ε(1 + 2ν) — the SIGN of the lateral strains reversed** ← |
| **0.0002** | **ε(1 − ν)(something) — a partial deduction; or ε × 0.2** |

> **Option (c) 0.0016 is the instructive error: it ADDS the lateral strains instead of subtracting them.**

> **The physical check catches it at once: a bar in TENSION gets THINNER, so its lateral strains must be NEGATIVE, and the volume change must be LESS than the longitudinal strain alone.**

> **So any answer exceeding 0.001 is wrong on sight** — which eliminates option (c) without any arithmetic.

**The important limiting case, which gives the relation its meaning:**

> **If ν = 0.5, then e_v = ε(1 − 1) = ZERO.**

> **A material with ν = 0.5 undergoes NO VOLUME CHANGE whatever — it is perfectly INCOMPRESSIBLE.**

> **That is the theoretical upper limit for Poisson's ratio, and it explains the relation E = 3K(1 − 2ν): as ν → 0.5, K → ∞.**

| ν | e_v for ε = 0.001 | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | **0.0010** | **No lateral contraction at all (cork)** |
| **0.2** | **0.0006** | Concrete |
| **0.3** | **0.0004** | **Steel** ← |
| **0.4** | **0.0002** | |
| **0.5** | **0** | **Incompressible (rubber, and saturated soil under undrained loading)** |

> **The SOIL case in the last row is worth drawing out, because it links this relation to geotechnics:**

> **A SATURATED soil loaded UNDRAINED cannot change volume — water cannot escape and both water and solids are effectively incompressible.**

> **So an undrained saturated soil behaves as though ν = 0.5**, and that is the value used in undrained elastic settlement calculations.

> **Under DRAINED conditions, water can leave and the volume does change, so ν falls to about 0.2 to 0.35.**

> **The same soil therefore has two quite different Poisson's ratios depending on the drainage condition** — which is not a contradiction but a direct statement of what the parameter measures.

**The general three-dimensional form, since uniaxial is a special case:**

> **e_v = (1 − 2ν)/E × (σ_x + σ_y + σ_z)**

> **Note that the volumetric strain depends only on the SUM of the three normal stresses — the first stress invariant, three times the MEAN or hydrostatic stress.**

> **Which is a satisfying result: volume change is caused by the HYDROSTATIC part of the stress alone, and the DEVIATORIC part (which causes shear and distortion) produces no volume change at all in an elastic material.**

> **That separation — hydrostatic stress changes volume, deviatoric stress changes shape — underlies plasticity theory, the von Mises yield criterion, and the critical state soil mechanics framework.**

> **It is also why yielding in metals is independent of hydrostatic pressure: yielding is a shearing process, and hydrostatic stress produces no shear.** A steel specimen at the bottom of the ocean yields at the same deviatoric stress as one at the surface.

examTip.trick: **e_v = ε(1 − 2ν) = 0.001 × 0.4 = 0.0004.** It is the SUM of the three principal strains: +ε, −νε, −νε.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 0.0016 adds the lateral strains instead of subtracting them.** A bar in tension gets THINNER, so e_v must be LESS than ε — any answer above 0.001 is wrong on sight.
examTip.mnemonic: **ν = 0.5 gives ZERO volume change — perfect incompressibility**, which is why K → ∞ there. A saturated soil loaded UNDRAINED behaves at ν = 0.5 and DRAINED at 0.2-0.35: the same soil, two values, because the parameter measures whether water can leave.

questions.stem: A rectangular beam section is 200 mm wide and 300 mm deep. Its section modulus about the axis of bending is:
questions.solution:
**3.0 × 10⁶ mm³.**

**The section modulus:**

> **Z = I / y_max**

> **For a rectangle bent about the axis perpendicular to its depth:**

> **I = b d³/12 = 200 × 300³/12 = 200 × 27 × 10⁶/12 = 5400 × 10⁶/12 = 450 × 10⁶ mm⁴**

> **y_max = d/2 = 150 mm**

> **Z = 450 × 10⁶/150 = 3.0 × 10⁶ mm³** ✓

**The direct formula, worth using:**

> **Z = b d²/6 = 200 × 300²/6 = 200 × 90,000/6 = 18,000,000/6 = 3.0 × 10⁶ mm³** ✓

> **The bd²/6 form is faster and less error-prone than computing I and then dividing.**

> **And note the DEPTH is SQUARED while the width appears to the first power** — which is the single most important fact about beam sections.

**Why the depth matters so much more than the width:**

| Change | Effect on Z (strength) | Effect on I (stiffness) |
|---|---|---|
| **DOUBLE the WIDTH** | **× 2** | **× 2** |
| **DOUBLE the DEPTH** | **× 4** | **× 8** ← |

> **So for the same quantity of material, a beam is FAR stronger and stiffer laid on edge than laid flat.**

> **Check with this section: bent about the OTHER axis, Z = d b²/6 = 300 × 200²/6 = 2.0 × 10⁶ mm³ — which is option (a).**

> **So turning this section on its side reduces its strength by a third (3.0 to 2.0) and its stiffness by more than half (450 × 10⁶ to 200 × 10⁶ mm⁴).**

> **Option (a) is therefore the answer for bending about the WEAK axis, and identifying which axis is meant is part of the task.**

> **For a section with a larger aspect ratio the difference is dramatic: a 50 × 300 plank has Z = 2.25 × 10⁶ on edge and only 0.375 × 10⁶ flat — a factor of SIX.** Which is why floor joists are always installed on edge, and why a plank laid flat as a beam is a recognisable sign of untrained work.

**What the section modulus is FOR:**

> **The flexure formula:  σ = M y / I = M / Z**

> **So Z directly converts a bending moment into the maximum bending stress:**

> **σ_max = M / Z**

> **Which means Z is the section's BENDING STRENGTH INDEX: for a permissible stress σ_perm, the moment capacity is simply M = σ_perm × Z.**

> **For this section in timber with σ_perm = 10 N/mm²: M = 10 × 3.0 × 10⁶ = 30 × 10⁶ Nmm = 30 kNm.**

> **In steel at 165 N/mm²: M = 165 × 3.0 × 10⁶ = 495 kNm** — though a solid steel rectangle of that size would be an absurdly wasteful section, for the reason below.

**Why an I-SECTION beats a rectangle, since the comparison is the point of section design:**

> **Bending stress varies LINEARLY from zero at the neutral axis to a maximum at the extreme fibres.**

> **So material near the neutral axis carries very little stress and is nearly idle.**

> **An I-SECTION removes that idle material from the web and concentrates it in FLANGES at the extreme fibres, where the stress is greatest.**

| Section | Area | Z | **Z per unit area — the efficiency** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle 200 × 300** | **60,000 mm²** | **3.0 × 10⁶ mm³** | **50 mm** |
| **An I-section of the same 300 mm depth and similar Z** | **~7,000 mm²** | **~3.0 × 10⁶ mm³** | **~430 mm** ← |

> **An I-section achieves the same bending strength with something like a TENTH of the material.**

> **Which is why every rolled steel beam is an I or an H, and why a solid rectangular steel beam is never used.**

> **The same reasoning explains the reinforced concrete T-BEAM: the slab acts as a wide compression flange, so the concrete is where the compression is and the steel is where the tension is, and the web merely connects them and carries the shear.**

> **It is the identical principle to the hollow shaft in torsion and the hollow column in buckling: PUT THE MATERIAL WHERE THE STRESS IS.** Three different problems, one answer.

**The price of efficiency, since it is not free:**

| Consequence of an efficient thin-walled section | Note |
|---|---|
| **LOCAL BUCKLING of the thin flange or web** | **A slender flange buckles before the material yields — hence the classification of sections into plastic, compact, semi-compact and slender** ← |
| **LATERAL-TORSIONAL buckling** | **A deep narrow beam can buckle sideways and twist — hence the need for lateral restraint** |
| **WEB crippling and buckling at supports and point loads** | Stiffeners required |
| **Reduced torsional stiffness** | An open section is very poor in torsion |

> **LATERAL-TORSIONAL buckling deserves the note: the very slenderness that makes an I-section efficient in bending makes it weak about its minor axis, so a long unrestrained beam fails by buckling sideways at a moment well below its section capacity.**

> **That is why steel beams are laterally restrained by the floor they support, and why a beam during ERECTION — before the floor is on — is at its most vulnerable.**

> **A beam safely designed for service can buckle under its own weight plus a worker during construction, and temporary bracing is therefore not an optional precaution.**

examTip.trick: **Z = bd²/6 = 200 × 90,000/6 = 3.0 × 10⁶ mm³** — faster and safer than computing I then dividing by d/2.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 2.0 × 10⁶ is Z about the WEAK axis (db²/6)** — the same section turned on its side. Identify which axis is bending.
examTip.mnemonic: **DEPTH is squared in Z and cubed in I; width is linear.** So doubling the depth quadruples strength and multiplies stiffness by eight — which is why joists go on edge and why an I-section gives the same Z for a tenth of the material.

questions.stem: A steel column 3 m long, FIXED AT BOTH ENDS, has I = 4 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and E = 200 GPa. Its Euler crippling load is:
questions.solution:
**3509 kN.**

**Step 1 — the effective length for FIXED-FIXED ends:**

> **L_e = L/2 = 3000/2 = 1500 mm**

**Step 2 — Euler's formula:**

> **P_cr = π² E I / L_e²**

> **Numerator: π² × 200,000 × 4 × 10⁶ = 9.8696 × 200,000 × 4 × 10⁶ = 7.8957 × 10¹² N·mm²**

> **Denominator: (1500)² = 2.25 × 10⁶ mm²**

> **P_cr = 7.8957 × 10¹² / 2.25 × 10⁶ = 3.509 × 10⁶ N = 3509 kN** ✓

**Every distractor is a DIFFERENT END CONDITION — which is the design of the question:**

| End conditions | L_e | P_cr | Option |
|---|---|---|---|
| **One fixed, one FREE (cantilever)** | **2L = 6000 mm** | **219 kN** | (c) |
| **Both HINGED (pinned)** | **L = 3000 mm** | **877 kN** | (a) |
| **One fixed, one hinged** | **L/√2 ≈ 0.7L = 2121 mm** | **1790 kN** | (b) |
| **Both FIXED** | **L/2 = 1500 mm** | **3509 kN** | **(d)** ✓ |

> **So the four options span the four standard cases, and the ONLY thing that distinguishes them is the end restraint.**

> **Note the RANGE: from 219 kN to 3509 kN — a factor of SIXTEEN — for the same column, the same length and the same material.**

> **That factor of sixteen is the effective length ratio squared: (2L)/(L/2) = 4, and 4² = 16.**

> **Which makes end restraint the most powerful variable available to a column designer — more powerful than the section, the material or anything else.**

**Why the effective length concept works:**

> **Euler's basic derivation applies to a PIN-ENDED column, where the buckled shape is a half sine wave over the full length L.**

> **For other end conditions the buckled shape contains a half sine wave of a DIFFERENT length, and the EFFECTIVE LENGTH is the length of that half wave.**

| Case | Buckled shape | Effective length |
|---|---|---|
| **Pinned-pinned** | **A single half sine wave over L** | **L** |
| **Fixed-fixed** | **Points of contraflexure at L/4 from each end, so the central HALF of the column contains the half wave** | **L/2** ← |
| **Fixed-free** | **A quarter wave; mirrored, it is a half wave of length 2L** | **2L** |
| **Fixed-pinned** | One point of contraflexure | **0.7 L** |

> **So the effective length is a GEOMETRIC statement about the buckled shape, and the fixed-fixed case has the shortest half wave and hence the greatest capacity.**

> **The physical reading of L/2 for a fixed-fixed column is worth having: the moments at the two fixed ends hold the ends straight, so the column can only bow in its central portion, behaving like a pin-ended column of half the length.**

**The critical warning about Euler's formula — its range of validity:**

> **Euler's formula predicts a critical STRESS of:**

> **σ_cr = P_cr/A = π² E / λ²**, where λ = L_e/k is the slenderness ratio.

> **As λ decreases, σ_cr rises WITHOUT LIMIT — which is physically impossible, because no column can carry more than its material's crushing strength.**

| Slenderness λ | Failure mode | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **λ > ~80 (mild steel)** | **ELASTIC BUCKLING** | **Euler applies** ← |
| **λ ≈ 30 - 80** | **INELASTIC buckling — partial yielding then buckling** | **Empirical: Rankine-Gordon, or the code's buckling curves** |
| **λ < ~30** | **CRUSHING (squashing)** | **σ = f_y** |

> **The critical slenderness for mild steel: setting σ_cr = f_y = 250 N/mm² gives λ = π√(E/f_y) = π√(200,000/250) = π × 28.3 = 89.**

> **So Euler's formula is valid only above about λ = 89 for mild steel** — and applying it to a stocky column gives an absurdly high answer, which is the signal that it has been used out of range.

> **This column's slenderness cannot be computed from the data given (the area is not stated), which is itself a hint that the question is testing the effective-length concept rather than a real design.**

**Why REAL columns never reach the Euler load — the honest position:**

| Real effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **INITIAL CROOKEDNESS** | **A column is never perfectly straight, so bending begins at first load** ← |
| **ACCIDENTAL ECCENTRICITY of the load** | Same effect |
| **RESIDUAL STRESSES from rolling or welding** | Parts of the section yield early, reducing the effective stiffness |
| **Material non-linearity near yield** | Reduces E in the yielded fibres |
| **Imperfect end restraint** | **A "fixed" end is never fully fixed in practice** |

> **The last row is the practically important one, and it should temper the answer above: a genuinely fixed column end requires a connection stiff enough to develop the full moment, and few real details achieve it.**

> **Codes therefore give effective length factors that are more conservative than the theoretical values — for instance 0.65L rather than 0.5L for a nominally fixed-fixed column** — precisely to allow for the restraint being imperfect.

> **So the theoretical L/2 is an upper bound on the benefit of fixity, and a design that claims it must justify the connection that delivers it.** A column bolted to a base plate on four holding-down bolts is not fixed, whatever the drawing calls it.

examTip.trick: **Fixed-fixed: L_e = L/2 = 1500 mm. P_cr = π²EI/L_e² = 7.896 × 10¹²/2.25 × 10⁶ = 3509 kN.**
examTip.trap: **All four options are the SAME column with different END CONDITIONS** — 219 kN (fixed-free, 2L), 877 kN (pinned, L), 1790 kN (fixed-pinned, 0.7L), 3509 kN (fixed-fixed, L/2). A factor of SIXTEEN across the range.
examTip.mnemonic: **Euler applies only above about λ = 89 for mild steel** (λ = π√(E/f_y)); below that, crushing or inelastic buckling governs, and an absurdly high answer is the signal it was used out of range. Codes also use 0.65L rather than 0.5L, because no real end is truly fixed.

questions.stem: A three-hinged parabolic arch of span 20 m and central rise 4 m carries a point load of 100 kN at the crown. The horizontal thrust at each support is:
questions.solution:
**125 kN.**

**Step 1 — the vertical reactions, by symmetry:**

> **The load is at the crown, so V_A = V_B = 100/2 = 50 kN**

**Step 2 — use the CROWN HINGE.**

> **The defining property of a three-hinged arch is that the CROWN HINGE CANNOT CARRY MOMENT.**

> **So taking moments about the crown hinge C, considering only the LEFT half of the arch:**

| Force on the left half | Moment about C |
|---|---|
| **V_A = 50 kN at 10 m** | **+50 × 10 = 500 kNm** |
| **H at the rise 4 m below C** | **−H × 4** |
| **The 100 kN load** | **Applied AT C — zero moment** |

> **ΣM_C = 0:  50 × 10 − H × 4 = 0**

> **H = 500/4 = 125 kN** ✓

**The general formula for this case:**

> **H = W L / (4 r)** for a central point load on a three-hinged arch.

> **= 100 × 20/(4 × 4) = 2000/16 = 125 kN** ✓

> **And for a UDL of intensity w over the whole span:  H = w L²/(8 r).**

> **Note the parallel with beam moments: the horizontal thrust equals the SIMPLY SUPPORTED BENDING MOMENT at mid-span, DIVIDED BY THE RISE.**

> **Check: a simply supported beam with a central load W has M = WL/4 = 500 kNm, and 500/4 = 125 kN** ✓

> **That relation — H = M_beam/r — is the most useful single fact about three-hinged arches, because it lets any arch thrust be obtained from the corresponding beam moment.**

**Why the RISE governs the thrust — the practical consequence:**

> **H is INVERSELY proportional to the rise r:**

| Rise (span 20 m, 100 kN at crown) | Rise / span | H |
|---|---|---|
| **2 m** | **1:10** | **250 kN** ← option (d) |
| **4 m** | **1:5** | **125 kN** ✓ |
| **5 m** | **1:4** | **100 kN** — option (b) |
| **8 m** | **1:2.5** | **62.5 kN** — option (a) |

> **So every distractor is the SAME arch with a different rise — which is a well-made option set and makes the inverse relation vivid.**

> **A FLAT arch (small rise) develops an ENORMOUS horizontal thrust; a STEEP arch develops little.**

> **In the limit of zero rise the arch becomes a straight beam and the thrust becomes infinite — which is the mathematical statement of the physical truth that an arch works by its curvature.**

> **That is why flat arches over openings need such massive abutments, and why the great masonry bridges are semicircular or nearly so: a semicircular arch (rise = half span) develops the least thrust of any arch form.**

> **And it is why an arch's ABUTMENTS are the critical element: they must resist the horizontal thrust permanently, and an arch whose abutments spread will collapse regardless of how sound the arch ring is.**

> **Most historic arch bridge failures are abutment or foundation failures, not arch failures.**

**Why the arch is so much more efficient than a beam — the point of using one:**

> **In an arch, the horizontal thrust generates a HOGGING moment that OPPOSES the sagging moment from the load.**

> **At any section:  M_arch = M_beam − H y**, where y is the height of the arch axis above the springing.

> **For a PARABOLIC arch under a UDL, those two terms CANCEL EXACTLY at every section, and the bending moment is ZERO throughout.**

> **The arch then carries the load entirely in AXIAL COMPRESSION — which is what masonry and concrete do best.**

> **That is the whole reason for the arch form: it converts bending into compression.**

> **And it explains why a parabola is the ideal shape for a UDL, and a CATENARY for the arch's own self-weight** — each shape is the funicular curve of its own loading.

> **The line along which the thrust actually travels is the LINE OF THRUST, and the design objective is to keep it within the arch ring — for masonry, within the MIDDLE THIRD, so that no tension develops.**

**Why a THREE-hinged arch, since two-hinged and fixed arches also exist:**

| Arch | Unknown reactions | Degree of indeterminacy | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **THREE-hinged** | **4 (2 per pin), plus the crown hinge condition** | **ZERO — DETERMINATE** ← |
| **TWO-hinged** | **4** | **1** |
| **FIXED (hingeless)** | **6** | **3** |

> **The crown hinge supplies the fourth equation (ΣM = 0 at the crown), making the three-hinged arch STATICALLY DETERMINATE — which is why it can be solved as above with nothing but statics.**

> **Its great practical advantage follows from that determinacy: it is INSENSITIVE to support settlement, to temperature change and to shrinkage.**

> **A determinate structure can accommodate those movements by changing shape slightly, developing NO stresses at all.**

> **A fixed arch, being three times indeterminate, develops large stresses from a small settlement or a temperature change — which for a long-span concrete arch can be a governing load case.**

> **So the three-hinged arch is chosen where the foundations are uncertain or where temperature movement is large**, and the fixed arch where the foundations are sound rock and the greater stiffness and smaller deflections are wanted.

> **The trade is the usual one between determinate and indeterminate structures: determinacy buys tolerance of movement, indeterminacy buys stiffness and redundancy.**

examTip.trick: **Take moments about the CROWN HINGE for one half: 50 × 10 − H × 4 = 0, so H = 125 kN.** Or use H = M_beam/r = (WL/4)/r = 500/4.
examTip.trap: **Every distractor is the same arch with a different RISE** — 2 m gives 250 kN, 5 m gives 100 kN, 8 m gives 62.5 kN. H is INVERSELY proportional to the rise, so a flat arch thrusts enormously.
examTip.mnemonic: **H = (simply supported beam moment) ÷ rise** — the most useful fact about three-hinged arches. And a PARABOLIC arch under UDL has ZERO bending moment everywhere: the arch form converts bending into pure compression.

questions.stem: A cantilever beam of length 2 m with EI = 5000 kNm² carries a point load of 10 kN at its free end. The deflection at the free end is:
questions.solution:
**5.33 mm.**

**The standard result:**

> **δ = P L³ / (3 E I)**

> **= 10 × 2³ / (3 × 5000) = 80/15,000 = 5.333 × 10⁻³ m = 5.33 mm** ✓

> **Note the units: with P in kN, L in m and EI in kNm², the deflection comes out in METRES — so multiply by 1000 for millimetres.**

> **Keeping EI in kNm² is the convenient practice, and it avoids the large powers of ten that arise when E is in N/mm² and I in mm⁴.**

**The standard deflection formulae, since the distractors come from them:**

| Beam and load | Maximum deflection | Value here |
|---|---|---|
| **CANTILEVER, point load at the tip** | **PL³/3EI** | **5.33 mm** ✓ |
| **CANTILEVER, UDL over the whole length** | **wL⁴/8EI** | — |
| **Cantilever, point load at MID-LENGTH** | **PL³/24EI** (measured at the tip: 5PL³/48EI) | — |
| **Simply supported, central point load** | **PL³/48EI** | **0.33 mm** |
| **Simply supported, UDL** | **5wL⁴/384EI** | — |
| **FIXED both ends, central point load** | **PL³/192EI** | 0.083 mm |

> **Option (b) 1.33 mm is PL³/12EI and option (c) 2.67 mm is PL³/6EI** — coefficient errors on the same case.

> **Option (d) 16.0 mm is PL³/EI — the coefficient dropped entirely.**

> **So the whole option set tests whether the coefficient 1/3 is known, which is the point.**

**How to remember the coefficients, since there are many:**

> **The pattern for a CANTILEVER: the denominators are 3 (point load at tip) and 8 (UDL).**

> **For a SIMPLY SUPPORTED beam: 48 (central point load) and 384/5 = 76.8 (UDL).**

> **The ratio between the cantilever and the simply supported case is the striking part:**

| Load | Cantilever | Simply supported | **Ratio** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Point load** | **PL³/3EI** | **PL³/48EI** | **16** ← |
| **UDL** | **wL⁴/8EI** | **5wL⁴/384EI** | **9.6** |

> **A cantilever deflects SIXTEEN times as much as a simply supported beam of the same span under the same point load.**

> **Which, together with its four-times-greater moment, is why cantilevers are kept short — and why the deflection, not the strength, usually limits them.**

**Deriving it, so the coefficient can be recovered if forgotten:**

> **The double-integration method: EI d²y/dx² = M.**

> **Measuring x from the FREE end, the moment at distance x is M = −P x.**

> **EI y'' = −Px**

> **EI y' = −Px²/2 + C₁**

> **EI y = −Px³/6 + C₁x + C₂**

> **Boundary conditions at the FIXED end (x = L): y = 0 and y' = 0.**

> **From y' = 0:  C₁ = PL²/2**

> **From y = 0:  C₂ = PL³/6 − PL³/2 = −PL³/3**

> **At the free end (x = 0):  EI y = C₂ = −PL³/3, so δ = PL³/(3EI)** ✓

> **The derivation takes six lines and is worth doing once, because it makes the coefficient a result rather than a memory.**

**The alternative methods, since each suits a different problem:**

| Method | Best for |
|---|---|
| **DOUBLE INTEGRATION** | **Simple loadings; gives the deflection everywhere** |
| **MACAULAY'S method** | **Several point loads or partial UDLs — one equation covers the whole beam** ← |
| **MOMENT-AREA method** | **Deflection at ONE point; excellent for cantilevers and varying EI** |
| **CONJUGATE BEAM method** | Same as moment-area, recast as a beam problem |
| **STRAIN ENERGY / Castigliano** | **Trusses, curved members, and where a single deflection is wanted** |
| **Unit load method** | **The general workhorse for indeterminate structures** |

> **MACAULAY'S method deserves the note: it uses the bracket convention ⟨x − a⟩, in which a term is taken as ZERO whenever the bracket is negative.**

> **That single device lets one moment equation describe a beam with any number of discrete loads, instead of writing a separate equation for each segment** — which is why it is the practical method for a real beam.

> **And the MOMENT-AREA theorems are the fastest route for this particular problem: the tip deflection of a cantilever equals the AREA of the M/EI diagram times the distance from its centroid to the tip.**

> **Here the M/EI diagram is a triangle of height PL/EI and base L, so area = PL²/2EI, and its centroid is at 2L/3 from the tip:**

> **δ = (PL²/2EI) × (2L/3) = PL³/3EI** ✓

> **Two lines, and no integration at all** — which is why the moment-area method is worth having for cantilevers.

**Why DEFLECTION so often governs rather than strength:**

> **Deflection goes as L⁴ for a distributed load and L³ for a point load, while the moment goes only as L² or L.**

> **So as spans increase, deflection grows FASTER than the moment does, and at some span it becomes the binding constraint.**

| Code deflection limit | Applies to |
|---|---|
| **span/250** | **General limit for total deflection (IS 456)** |
| **span/350 or 20 mm, whichever is less** | **After partitions and finishes are in place** ← |
| **span/325 to span/360** | Timber floors |
| **span/500** | Where brittle finishes or machinery are supported |

> **The second row is the one that catches designers: the limit applies to the deflection occurring AFTER the finishes are built, because that is the deflection which cracks a partition or jams a door.**

> **A beam may deflect 30 mm in total and satisfy the code comfortably, provided 20 mm of that occurred before the plaster went on.**

> **Which is why the CONSTRUCTION SEQUENCE affects whether a deflection is acceptable** — a fact that no formula contains and which decides a good many disputes on site.

examTip.trick: **δ = PL³/3EI = 10 × 8/(3 × 5000) = 5.33 × 10⁻³ m = 5.33 mm.** With kN, m and kNm², the answer is in metres.
examTip.trap: **Every distractor is a wrong COEFFICIENT on the right formula** — PL³/12EI, PL³/6EI, PL³/EI. The cantilever tip coefficient is 1/3; the UDL one is 1/8.
examTip.mnemonic: **Moment-area gives it in two lines: area of the M/EI triangle (PL²/2EI) × distance to its centroid (2L/3) = PL³/3EI.** And note a cantilever deflects SIXTEEN times a simply supported beam of the same span — deflection, not strength, usually limits it.

questions.stem: A propped cantilever of span 8 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 12 kN/m over its whole length. The reaction at the PROP (the simple support) is:
questions.solution:
**36 kN.**

**The standard result:**

> **Reaction at the prop:  R_prop = 3wL/8**

> **= 3 × 12 × 8/8 = 3 × 12 = 36 kN** ✓

**And the fixed end takes the rest:**

> **Total load = wL = 12 × 8 = 96 kN**

> **R_fixed = 96 − 36 = 60 kN = 5wL/8** ✓ — which is option (b).

> **So the two reactions are 3wL/8 and 5wL/8, splitting the load 3:5 rather than equally.**

> **Option (a) 48 kN is wL/2 — the EQUAL split of a simply supported beam**, offered to catch a candidate who does not recognise the propped cantilever.

**Why the split is 3:5 and not 1:1 — the physical reason:**

> **The FIXED end is STIFFER than the prop: it resists both rotation and translation, while the prop resists only translation.**

> **Load always finds its way to the STIFFER support, so the fixed end takes MORE — five eighths against three eighths.**

> **That principle is general and worth carrying: in any indeterminate structure, the distribution of forces is governed by the RELATIVE STIFFNESSES of the load paths.**

> **A determinate structure's forces depend only on geometry; an indeterminate structure's depend on stiffness as well** — which is the fundamental difference between the two and the reason indeterminate analysis needs EI while determinate analysis does not.

**Deriving the result by the compatibility method, which is the standard technique:**

> **Treat the PROP REACTION R as the redundant force and remove the prop, leaving a plain cantilever.**

| Step | Deflection at the prop position |
|---|---|
| **Under the UDL alone (prop removed)** | **δ₁ = wL⁴/(8EI) DOWNWARD** |
| **Under the prop reaction R alone** | **δ₂ = RL³/(3EI) UPWARD** |
| **COMPATIBILITY: the prop prevents deflection there** | **δ₁ = δ₂** |

> **wL⁴/(8EI) = RL³/(3EI)**

> **R = 3wL/8** ✓

> **Note that EI CANCELS — so the reaction is independent of the beam's stiffness.**

> **That is true whenever a structure is made of a SINGLE material with UNIFORM section: only the RATIOS of stiffness matter, and a uniform beam's ratios are fixed by geometry alone.**

> **But if the beam had a varying section, or two different materials, EI would NOT cancel and the reaction would depend on it** — which is exactly why haunched beams and composite members must be analysed with their real stiffness distribution.

**The complete set of results for this beam, since the reaction is only the start:**

| Quantity | Formula | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction at the PROP** | **3wL/8** | **36 kN** ✓ |
| **Reaction at the FIXED end** | **5wL/8** | **60 kN** |
| **MOMENT at the fixed end (hogging)** | **wL²/8** | **96 kNm** |
| **Maximum SAGGING moment** | **9wL²/128** | **54 kNm** |
| **Position of maximum sagging moment** | **3L/8 from the prop** | **3 m** |
| **Point of CONTRAFLEXURE** | **L/4 from the fixed end** | **2 m** |
| **Maximum deflection** | **wL⁴/(185 EI)** | at 0.4215L from the prop |

> **The hogging moment at the fixed end (96 kNm) EXCEEDS the maximum sagging moment (54 kNm) — by a factor of nearly two.**

> **Which has a direct consequence for reinforced concrete design: the TOP steel at the fixed end is the critical reinforcement, heavier than the bottom steel in the span.**

> **And note the POINT OF CONTRAFLEXURE at L/4 from the fixed end: that is where the bending moment changes sign, so the top steel must extend at least that far into the span before it can be curtailed — plus a development length beyond.**

> **Curtailing top steel at the support face, or just short of the contraflexure point, is a classic detailing error and produces a crack exactly there.**

**Comparing the three support conditions for the same UDL, since the pattern is instructive:**

| Beam | Max moment | Max deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **SIMPLY SUPPORTED** | **wL²/8 = 96 kNm (sagging, mid-span)** | **5wL⁴/384EI** |
| **PROPPED CANTILEVER** | **wL²/8 = 96 kNm (hogging, fixed end)** | **wL⁴/185EI** ← |
| **FIXED BOTH ENDS** | **wL²/12 = 64 kNm (hogging, supports)** | **wL⁴/384EI** |

> **A curious coincidence in the first two rows: the propped cantilever and the simply supported beam have the SAME maximum moment magnitude, wL²/8.**

> **But the propped cantilever's deflection is 5/384 ÷ 1/185 = 2.4 times SMALLER.**

> **So propping a cantilever — or equivalently fixing one end of a simply supported beam — buys a large gain in STIFFNESS for no change in peak moment at all.**

> **The moment merely MOVES: from mid-span sagging to the fixed end hogging.**

> **That is a genuinely useful design insight: partial fixity improves deflection much more than it improves strength**, which matters because deflection so often governs.

> **And it is why continuity in a concrete frame is worth having even when the moments are not reduced: the floor is stiffer, it deflects less, and the finishes survive.**

examTip.trick: **R_prop = 3wL/8 = 36 kN; the fixed end takes 5wL/8 = 60 kN.** The load splits 3:5, not equally.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 48 kN is wL/2 — the equal split of a SIMPLY SUPPORTED beam**, and (b) 60 kN is the FIXED end's reaction. Load goes to the STIFFER support, so the fixed end takes more.
examTip.mnemonic: **Derive it by compatibility: wL⁴/8EI (cantilever under UDL) = RL³/3EI (cantilever under R), so R = 3wL/8 — and EI CANCELS.** Note the fixed-end hogging moment wL²/8 = 96 kNm EXCEEDS the span sagging moment 9wL²/128 = 54 kNm, so TOP steel governs.

questions.stem: A beam of span 6 m, fixed at both ends, carries a central point load of 40 kN. The bending moment at each support is:
questions.solution:
**30 kNm.**

**The standard result:**

> **For a fixed beam with a central point load W:**

> **M_support = M_centre = W L / 8**

> **= 40 × 6/8 = 240/8 = 30 kNm** ✓

**The remarkable feature of this particular case:**

> **The support moment and the mid-span moment are EQUAL IN MAGNITUDE — both WL/8 — and OPPOSITE IN SIGN.**

| Location | Moment | Sense |
|---|---|---|
| **Each support** | **WL/8 = 30 kNm** | **HOGGING (negative)** |
| **Mid-span** | **WL/8 = 30 kNm** | **SAGGING (positive)** |
| **Points of contraflexure** | **0** | at L/4 from each support |

> **That is a coincidence of the central point load case only — for a UDL the support moment (wL²/12) is TWICE the mid-span moment (wL²/24).**

> **The equality here means the beam is EQUALLY STRESSED at three sections, which is the most efficient possible distribution for a fixed beam and the reason the case is quoted so often.**

**Comparing with the simply supported beam, which is where option (a) comes from:**

| Beam (central point load W) | Maximum moment | Maximum deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **SIMPLY SUPPORTED** | **WL/4 = 60 kNm** | **WL³/48EI** |
| **FIXED BOTH ENDS** | **WL/8 = 30 kNm** | **WL³/192EI** ← |

> **Option (a) 60 kNm is WL/4 — the SIMPLY SUPPORTED moment**, exactly twice the answer.

> **So fixing both ends HALVES the maximum moment and reduces the deflection by a factor of FOUR.**

> **That is the value of fixity, and it is why continuity is exploited wherever it is available.**

> **The mechanism is worth stating: the fixed ends develop hogging moments that oppose the sagging moment in the span, so the total moment demand is SHARED between three sections instead of being concentrated at one.**

**Deriving it by MOMENT DISTRIBUTION, since that is the standard method for fixed and continuous beams:**

> **The FIXED END MOMENT for a central point load is a standard value:**

> **FEM = WL/8**

> **And because both ends are fully fixed, there is NO rotation and hence NO distribution to carry out — the fixed end moments ARE the final moments.**

> **So this beam is solved by looking up one standard FEM, which is why it appears as a foundation case.**

**The fixed end moments worth having, since every moment distribution problem starts there:**

| Loading on a member of span L | FEM at each end |
|---|---|
| **UDL w over the whole span** | **wL²/12** |
| **Central point load W** | **WL/8** ← |
| **Point load W at distance a from the left, b from the right** | **Wab²/L² (left), Wa²b/L² (right)** |
| **Triangular load, maximum w at one end** | **wL²/30 and wL²/20** |
| **UDL over the LEFT HALF only** | **11wL²/192 and 5wL²/192** |
| **Moment M applied at mid-span** | M/4 at each end |

> **The UDL's wL²/12 and the central load's WL/8 are the two that must be automatic.**

> **Note their ratio to the corresponding simply supported moments: wL²/12 against wL²/8 is 2/3, and WL/8 against WL/4 is 1/2** — so fixity helps a point load more than a UDL.

**Why the ASYMMETRIC point load case (Wab²/L²) matters:**

> **The unequal FEMs at the two ends are what make moment distribution necessary in the first place.**

> **Where the loading or the spans are unsymmetrical, the joints are OUT OF BALANCE and must be relaxed: the out-of-balance moment is distributed to the members meeting at the joint in proportion to their STIFFNESSES, and half of what each member receives is CARRIED OVER to its far end.**

| Moment distribution concept | Value |
|---|---|
| **Distribution factor for a member at a joint** | **Its stiffness ÷ the total stiffness at that joint** |
| **Stiffness of a member fixed at the far end** | **4EI/L** |
| **Stiffness of a member PINNED at the far end** | **3EI/L** ← |
| **CARRY-OVER factor (far end fixed)** | **½** |
| **Carry-over factor (far end pinned)** | **ZERO** |

> **The 3EI/L for a far-end-pinned member is the modification that saves the most work: using it means the pinned end need never be balanced, because no moment is carried over to it.**

> **So the end span of a continuous beam simply supported at its outer end is handled with a stiffness of 3EI/L, and the iteration is confined to the interior joints** — which can cut the work of a hand analysis in half.

**The honest caution about fixed-end moments in real structures:**

> **The whole calculation above assumes the ends are FULLY FIXED — zero rotation.**

> **A real support is never fully fixed:**

| Situation | Reality |
|---|---|
| **A beam framing into a slender column** | **The column ROTATES, so the beam end is only partly fixed** ← |
| **A beam built into a masonry wall** | Very little rotational restraint |
| **A beam cast monolithically with a deep stiff column** | Close to fixed |
| **A beam bolted to a plate with four bolts** | Nominally fixed, practically closer to pinned |

> **The consequence is that the real support moment lies BETWEEN WL/8 (fully fixed) and ZERO (pinned), and the real span moment between WL/8 and WL/4.**

> **Which is why reinforced concrete detailing provides BOTH: top steel at the support for the hogging moment that may develop, and bottom steel in the span sized for a moment larger than the fully-fixed analysis predicts.**

> **A design that provides only the fully-fixed span moment, on a support that turns out to be flexible, is under-reinforced in the span** — and the crack appears at mid-span, which is why codes specify minimum span reinforcement irrespective of the analysis.

examTip.trick: **Fixed beam, central point load: M_support = M_centre = WL/8 = 40 × 6/8 = 30 kNm** — equal in magnitude, opposite in sign.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 60 kNm is WL/4, the SIMPLY SUPPORTED value.** Fixing both ends HALVES the moment and cuts the deflection to a QUARTER (WL³/192EI against WL³/48EI).
examTip.mnemonic: **Two FEMs must be automatic: wL²/12 for a UDL and WL/8 for a central point load.** And member stiffness is 4EI/L when the far end is fixed but 3EI/L when it is PINNED — with zero carry-over, which halves the work of a hand analysis.

questions.stem: A building of seismic weight 10,000 kN stands in seismic zone V (Z = 0.36). Taking the importance factor I = 1.0, the response reduction factor R = 5.0 and Sa/g = 2.5, the design seismic base shear as per IS 1893 is:
questions.solution:
**900 kN.**

**The design horizontal seismic coefficient:**

> **A_h = (Z/2) × (I/R) × (Sa/g)**

| Term | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Z/2** | **0.36/2 = 0.18** | **Zone factor halved — see below** |
| **I/R** | **1.0/5.0 = 0.20** | Importance ÷ response reduction |
| **Sa/g** | **2.5** | **Average response acceleration coefficient** |

> **A_h = 0.18 × 0.20 × 2.5 = 0.09**

**The base shear:**

> **V_B = A_h × W = 0.09 × 10,000 = 900 kN** ✓

> **So the design lateral force is 9 per cent of the seismic weight — which is a typical figure for a moderately ductile building in the highest Indian and Nepali seismic zone.**

**Why the ZONE FACTOR IS HALVED — the point most often missed:**

> **Z is the peak ground acceleration for the MAXIMUM CONSIDERED EARTHQUAKE (MCE) — the most severe shaking reasonably expected at the site.**

> **Design is carried out for the DESIGN BASIS EARTHQUAKE (DBE), which is taken as HALF the MCE.**

> **Hence the factor Z/2.**

> **The reasoning behind it is a deliberate two-level design philosophy:**

| Earthquake level | Performance required |
|---|---|
| **DBE (half the MCE) — the design level** | **The structure remains essentially UNDAMAGED and serviceable** |
| **MCE — the full zone factor** | **The structure may be DAMAGED but must NOT COLLAPSE — life is preserved** ← |

> **So the building is designed elastically for half the shaking, and relies on DUCTILITY to survive the full shaking without collapse.**

> **Option (a) 1800 kN is exactly twice the answer — the Z/2 halving omitted**, which is the standard error.

**What the RESPONSE REDUCTION FACTOR R really represents — and it is the most important idea here:**

> **R = 5.0 divides the seismic force by five. It is NOT a safety factor and it is NOT an arbitrary reduction.**

> **R credits the structure's capacity to DISSIPATE ENERGY by yielding — its DUCTILITY and its REDUNDANCY.**

> **A ductile structure absorbs earthquake energy in inelastic deformation, so it needs far less elastic strength to survive the same shaking.**

| Structural system | R |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary moment-resisting RC frame (OMRF)** | **3.0** |
| **SPECIAL moment-resisting RC frame (SMRF)** | **5.0** ← this building |
| **Ordinary RC shear walls** | 3.0 |
| **Ductile shear walls** | 4.0 |
| **Ductile shear walls with SMRF** | **5.0** |
| **Unreinforced masonry** | **1.5 — almost no ductility credit** |
| **Steel frame with ductile detailing** | 5.0 |

> **The critical corollary, and it is a matter of life and safety: taking R = 5.0 OBLIGES the designer to provide the DUCTILE DETAILING of IS 13920.**

> **Those provisions — closely spaced confining stirrups in the plastic hinge zones, 135° hooks, restrictions on lap positions, strong-column/weak-beam capacity design, continuous longitudinal steel through joints — ARE the ductility that R assumes.**

> **A building designed with R = 5.0 and detailed as an ordinary frame has only about one third of the strength it needs, and none of the ductility it was credited with.**

> **That combination — a low design force justified by ductility that was never detailed — is among the commonest causes of collapse in earthquakes in the region, and it is a design office failure rather than a construction one.**

**Why the SEISMIC WEIGHT is not the full gravity load:**

> **W is the seismic weight, and IS 1893 reduces the live load contribution:**

| Component | Fraction included in W |
|---|---|
| **DEAD load** | **100 per cent** |
| **Live load up to 3 kN/m²** | **25 per cent** |
| **Live load above 3 kN/m²** | **50 per cent** |
| **ROOF live load** | **ZERO** |

> **The justification is physical: earthquake force is mass × acceleration, and only mass that MOVES WITH the structure contributes.**

> **Furniture, stored goods and occupants are not rigidly attached and are only partly coupled to the building's motion; and the full design live load is rarely present on every floor at once.**

> **Dead load, by contrast, is rigidly part of the structure and moves with it exactly.**

**How the base shear is DISTRIBUTED up the building, since V_B is only the total:**

> **Q_i = V_B × (W_i h_i²) / Σ(W_j h_j²)**

> **The force at each floor is proportional to its WEIGHT times the SQUARE OF ITS HEIGHT above the base.**
