> **A FREE residual chlorine of at least 0.2 mg/L must be present at the CONSUMER'S TAP, after at least 30 minutes of contact time.**

> **Note the two elements of the requirement — the CONCENTRATION and the CONTACT TIME — and both matter.**

> **Option (a) 1.0 mg/L is the PERMISSIBLE MAXIMUM residual under IS 10500, and option (b) 0.5 mg/L is the residual recommended during an EPIDEMIC or after a main repair** — both real figures in different roles.

**Why a RESIDUAL is required at all — the essential idea:**

> **The residual is not there to disinfect the water that has already been treated. Its purpose is quite different, and understanding it is the point of the question.**

| Function of the residual | Note |
|---|---|
| **A CONTINUING BARRIER against contamination entering the DISTRIBUTION system** | **A leaking joint, a back-siphonage, a repair, an illegal connection** ← the primary purpose |
| **An INDICATOR of the system's integrity** | **A residual that has disappeared means something has consumed it — a warning** |
| **Suppresses regrowth of bacteria and biofilm in the mains** | Pipes are not sterile environments |

> **The SECOND function is the one most worth appreciating: residual chlorine is a continuous, cheap, distributed MONITORING system.**

> **A single field test costing almost nothing tells an operator whether the water at that point has been in contact with anything that consumes chlorine — which is to say, with organic contamination.**

> **So a routine residual measurement is a proxy for a bacteriological test that would take 24 hours in a laboratory, and it can be done at a hundred points a day.**

> **That is why utilities monitor residual chlorine obsessively: it is the only real-time indicator of distribution system integrity available to them.**

**FREE versus COMBINED residual — the distinction the word "free" carries:**

| Form | Chemistry | Disinfecting power |
|---|---|---|
| **FREE chlorine — HOCl and OCl⁻** | **Chlorine not combined with ammonia** | **STRONG and fast** ← |
| **COMBINED chlorine — chloramines** | **Chlorine bound to ammonia (mono-, di- and trichloramine)** | **Weak — perhaps 1/25th as effective — but PERSISTENT** |

> **The trade-off is worth understanding, because both are used deliberately:**

> **FREE chlorine acts fast and dissipates fast, so it suits the treatment plant.**

> **CHLORAMINES act slowly and persist for days, so they suit a large distribution system with long residence times.**

> **That is why some large utilities practise CHLORAMINATION — deliberately adding ammonia — for the distribution residual, while disinfecting with free chlorine at the plant.**

> **Chloramines also produce far fewer trihalomethanes and less taste and odour, which is a further reason for the practice.**

**HOCl against OCl⁻, and why pH governs disinfection:**

> **Chlorine in water hydrolyses:  Cl₂ + H₂O → HOCl + HCl**

> **And HOCl dissociates:  HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻**

> **HYPOCHLOROUS ACID (HOCl) is about 80 TIMES more effective as a disinfectant than the HYPOCHLORITE ION (OCl⁻).**

> **The reason is that HOCl is uncharged and small, so it penetrates the negatively charged cell wall readily, while OCl⁻ is repelled.**

> **And the balance between them depends entirely on pH:**

| pH | Proportion as HOCl |
|---|---|
| **5** | **~100 %** |
| **6** | **~97 %** |
| **7** | **~78 %** |
| **7.5** | **~50 %** ← the pK_a |
| **8** | **~24 %** |
| **9** | **~3 %** |

> **So chlorination is DRAMATICALLY more effective at low pH — and at pH 9 it is almost ineffective.**

> **That has a direct practical consequence: chlorine must be dosed BEFORE lime softening or any pH-raising step, not after, and a water naturally at pH 8.5 needs several times the dose that the same water at pH 7 would require.**

> **It is also why the residual test alone is not sufficient without knowing the pH: 0.2 mg/L at pH 7 is protective, and the same 0.2 mg/L at pH 9 is much less so.**

**BREAKPOINT chlorination, since it explains how the dose is set:**

> **As the chlorine dose to a water containing ammonia and organic matter is increased, the residual behaves in four stages:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Chlorine is destroyed entirely by reducing agents (Fe²⁺, Mn²⁺, H₂S, nitrite) — NO residual** |
| **2** | **Chloramines form — the COMBINED residual rises** |
| **3** | **Chloramines are OXIDISED and destroyed — the residual FALLS to a minimum: the BREAKPOINT** ← |
| **4** | **Beyond the breakpoint, further chlorine appears as FREE residual** |

> **So a FREE residual can only be obtained by dosing BEYOND the breakpoint, and that is what "free residual chlorination" means as a practice.**

> **The breakpoint dose is roughly 10 times the ammonia nitrogen concentration** — which is why a water with significant ammonia is expensive to chlorinate to a free residual, and why ammonia removal may be worth doing first.

> **SUPER-CHLORINATION followed by DECHLORINATION (with sulphur dioxide or activated carbon) is the technique used where a very high dose is needed for a heavily contaminated water: dose far past the breakpoint for a reliable kill, then remove the excess before supply.**

> **And it is worth noting the reason 30 MINUTES of contact is specified: disinfection is a rate process following roughly Chick's law, and the product of concentration and time (the CT value) determines the kill.** A high concentration for a short time and a low one for a long time can be equivalent — which is the principle on which every disinfection standard is written.

examTip.trick: **0.2 mg/L free residual at the consumer's tap, after at least 30 minutes of contact.**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 1.0 mg/L is the permissible MAXIMUM residual; (b) 0.5 mg/L is the epidemic/post-repair figure.** All are real numbers in different roles.
examTip.mnemonic: **The residual is a continuing BARRIER and a real-time INDICATOR of distribution integrity** — a nearly free test that reveals contamination a laboratory would take 24 hours to confirm. And HOCl is ~80× stronger than OCl⁻, so chlorination is far less effective as pH rises.

questions.stem: The minimum SELF-CLEANSING velocity generally adopted in the design of sanitary sewers is:
questions.solution:
**0.6 m/s.**

**The velocity limits for a sanitary sewer:**

| Limit | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **MINIMUM (self-cleansing)** | **0.6 m/s** (0.8 m/s preferred, at least at peak flow) | **Below this, solids SETTLE and the sewer silts up** ← |
| **MAXIMUM (non-scouring)** | **3.0 m/s** | **Above this, the sewer INVERT is ERODED by grit** ← option (d) |
| Typical design velocity | 0.8 - 1.5 m/s | The comfortable band |

> **So a sewer must be designed to run within a BAND, and both ends of it matter.**

> **Option (a) 0.3 m/s is roughly the self-cleansing velocity for a STORM DRAIN carrying only grit and silt, and option (c) 1.5 m/s is a typical design velocity rather than a minimum.**

**Why the minimum exists — the physical argument:**

> **Sewage carries GRIT (sand, ash, eggshells, road detritus) as well as organic solids.**

> **If the velocity falls below the self-cleansing value, that material DEPOSITS on the invert.**

> **The consequences compound in a way worth spelling out:**

| Consequence of deposition | Note |
|---|---|
| **The effective cross-section is REDUCED** | Capacity falls |
| **The reduced section increases the velocity slightly** | A partial self-correction — but not enough |
| **Organic deposits DECOMPOSE ANAEROBICALLY** | **Producing hydrogen sulphide** ← the serious consequence |
| **H₂S is oxidised on the crown to SULPHURIC ACID** | **CROWN CORROSION — the sewer is eaten away from inside, at the top** |
| **H₂S is toxic and explosive** | **A lethal hazard to maintenance workers in manholes** |
| **Blockage and surcharge** | Sewage backs up into properties |

> **The CROWN CORROSION mechanism deserves the emphasis, because it is the reason self-cleansing velocity is a structural requirement and not merely an operational preference:**

> **Anaerobic decomposition of settled organic solids produces hydrogen sulphide, which escapes into the air space above the flowing sewage.**

> **On the moist crown of the pipe, aerobic Thiobacillus bacteria oxidise the H₂S to SULPHURIC ACID.**

> **That acid attacks the cement in a concrete sewer, converting it to gypsum and progressively destroying the pipe FROM THE CROWN DOWNWARD.**

> **So a concrete sewer that silts up is destroyed by its own contents at the top, where no one looks and where the structural loss is most dangerous — the pipe collapses from above.**

> **It is also why acid-resistant linings, PVC and HDPE, or a vitrified clay invert are specified for sewers where H₂S generation is expected**, and why sewer ventilation is provided.

**Why the MAXIMUM exists:**

> **Grit in suspension at high velocity acts as an abrasive, wearing away the invert of the sewer.**

> **The wear is concentrated on the invert because that is where the grit travels, so a scoured sewer develops a groove along its bottom, thinning the pipe exactly where the flow is.**

> **Above about 3 m/s that abrasion becomes significant over a design life, and above about 4.5 m/s it is rapid.**

> **Where a steep gradient makes high velocity unavoidable — as it very often does in a hill town — the answer is a DROP MANHOLE: the sewer is laid at a moderate gradient in reaches, with the level taken down in vertical steps inside manholes.**

> **That converts a continuous steep gradient into a series of gentle ones plus discrete drops, keeping the velocity in the band.** In Nepali hill towns it is a routine and essential detail rather than an occasional one.

**The design difficulty that makes this harder than it looks — and it is the real substance of sewer design:**

> **A sanitary sewer's flow varies ENORMOUSLY: the ratio of peak to minimum flow may be 4:1 or more within a day, and far more in the early years of a scheme designed for future population.**

> **So the SAME PIPE must:**

> **Not exceed 3.0 m/s at PEAK flow, and**

> **Not fall below 0.6 m/s at MINIMUM flow.**

> **That is a demanding pair of conditions, and it is why sewers are designed to run only PARTLY FULL.**

| Design practice | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Design for FULL-BORE capacity at the ultimate peak flow, but check the velocity at MINIMUM flow** | Both limits must hold |
| **Sanitary sewers designed to run at HALF to THREE-QUARTERS depth at peak** | Room for surcharge and ventilation |
| **Storm drains may be designed to run FULL** | Their flow is intermittent by nature |

> **The elegant fact that makes partial flow work in the designer's favour: a circular sewer's VELOCITY at partial depth is not much lower than at full bore, and at about 80 per cent depth it is actually GREATER than when full.**

> **The reason is that the hydraulic radius A/P reaches a maximum near that depth: as the sewer fills the last fifth, the wetted perimeter grows faster than the area does.**

> **So a circular section is a fortunate shape for a sewer — it maintains velocity over a wide range of flows**, which is exactly what a channel with a 4:1 flow variation requires.

> **Where the variation is even greater, an EGG-SHAPED section was traditionally used: narrow at the bottom, so that a small flow is deep and fast, and wide above for the peak.**

> **They are rarely built now, being difficult to manufacture and to lay, but the principle is sound and explains why the shape existed at all.**

examTip.trick: **Sewers must run within a BAND: minimum 0.6 m/s (self-cleansing) and maximum 3.0 m/s (non-scouring).**
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 3.0 m/s is the MAXIMUM, not the minimum** — and (c) 1.5 m/s is a typical design velocity. Read which limit is asked.
examTip.mnemonic: **Silting leads to CROWN CORROSION**: settled organics → H₂S → oxidised to sulphuric acid on the moist crown → the pipe is destroyed from the TOP down. So self-cleansing velocity is a structural requirement, not an operational preference.

questions.stem: A 300 mm diameter circular sewer running FULL is laid at a gradient of 1 in 200. Taking Manning's n = 0.013, the velocity of flow is approximately:
questions.solution:
**0.97 m/s.**

**Step 1 — the hydraulic radius of a FULL circular pipe:**

> **R = A/P = (πD²/4)/(πD) = D/4 = 0.300/4 = 0.075 m**

> **The result R = D/4 for a full circular pipe is worth knowing directly** — it saves computing the area and perimeter separately.

**Step 2 — Manning's equation:**

> **V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**

> **R^{2/3} = (0.075)^{2/3} = 0.1779**

> **S^{1/2} = (1/200)^{1/2} = (0.005)^{1/2} = 0.0707**

> **1/n = 1/0.013 = 76.92**

> **V = 76.92 × 0.1779 × 0.0707 = 76.92 × 0.01258 = 0.968 m/s ≈ 0.97 m/s** ✓

**Step 3 — the discharge, which the next part of such a question usually asks:**

> **Q = A V = (π/4)(0.3)² × 0.968 = 0.07069 × 0.968 = 0.0684 m³/s = 68.4 litres/s**

**Checking against the design limits — the point of doing the calculation:**

| Limit | Value | This sewer |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimum self-cleansing** | **0.6 m/s** | **0.97 > 0.6** ✓ |
| **Maximum non-scouring** | **3.0 m/s** | **0.97 < 3.0** ✓ |

> **So the sewer is satisfactory at full bore — comfortably within the band.**

> **But the design is not complete: the velocity at MINIMUM flow must also be checked, and at a small fraction of full bore it will be lower.** That check is what usually governs the gradient of a sewer in the early years of a scheme.

**The distractors, each a specific slip:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **0.48 m/s** | **Half the answer — R taken as D/8, or S as 1/800** |
| **1.94 m/s** | **Twice the answer — R taken as D/2** |
| **0.97 m/s** | ✓ |
| **0.68 m/s** | **R taken as D/2 with other compensating errors; also close to the DISCHARGE figure 0.0684 misread** ← |

> **The commonest error in this calculation is the hydraulic radius: R = D/4, not D/2.**

> **D/2 is the RADIUS of the pipe, and the HYDRAULIC radius is a different quantity entirely** — an area divided by a perimeter, which for a full circle happens to be half the geometric radius.

> **That coincidence of names is a genuine source of confusion, and the check is dimensional reasoning: R must be A/P, so compute it that way once and the factor is fixed.**

**The Manning n values for sewers:**

| Material | n |
|---|---|
| **Vitrified clay (salt-glazed stoneware)** | **0.012 - 0.014** ← |
| **Concrete, well finished** | **0.013** |
| **Concrete, rough or old** | **0.015 - 0.017** |
| **PVC, HDPE** | **0.009 - 0.011** |
| **Cast iron** | **0.013** |
| **Brick sewer** | **0.015 - 0.017** |

> **n = 0.013 in the stem is consistent with concrete or vitrified clay — the usual sewer materials.**

> **Note that PVC and HDPE are appreciably SMOOTHER, and the consequence is direct: a plastic sewer of the same diameter and gradient carries about 25 per cent more flow, or the same flow at a flatter gradient.**

> **Which matters in flat terrain, where every millimetre of fall is expensive in excavation depth** — a plastic sewer can be laid flatter and therefore shallower, and over a kilometre of main that is a large saving in trench.

**PARTIAL FLOW, since sewers rarely run full — and the result is counter-intuitive:**

> **The velocity and discharge at partial depth, as ratios of the full-bore values:**

| Depth ratio d/D | **V/V_full** | **Q/Q_full** |
|---|---|---|
| **0.2** | **0.62** | **0.09** |
| **0.3** | **0.78** | **0.20** |
| **0.5** | **1.00** | **0.50** |
| **0.8** | **1.14** | **0.98** |
| **0.94** | **1.14 (maximum V)** | **1.08 (maximum Q)** ← |
| **1.0 (full)** | **1.00** | **1.00** |

> **Two results in that table are genuinely surprising and both are practically important:**

> **FIRST — the velocity at HALF depth EQUALS the full-bore velocity.**

> **Because at half depth both the area and the wetted perimeter are exactly halved, so the hydraulic radius R = A/P is unchanged — and Manning's velocity depends only on R and S.**

> **SECOND — the maximum DISCHARGE occurs at about 94 per cent depth, and EXCEEDS the full-bore discharge by 8 per cent.**

> **The reason is that filling the last 6 per cent adds very little area while adding a disproportionate amount of wetted perimeter (the crown), so R falls and with it the velocity.**

> **The practical consequence is real: a sewer running just below the crown carries MORE than it does running full, and the condition is UNSTABLE — the flow alternates between the two states, which is why sewers are never designed to run exactly full.**

> **And the first result is the reassuring one for design: a circular sewer maintains its full-bore velocity all the way down to half depth, so a sewer sized for a future population still runs self-cleansing at half that flow.**

> **Below about 0.3 depth the velocity falls away sharply, and that is where the minimum-flow check bites.** A sewer designed for a 20-year population may run at a tenth of capacity in year one — velocity ratio about 0.5, hence 0.48 m/s here, BELOW self-cleansing.

> **Which is why flushing arrangements are provided at the heads of sewers in new schemes, and why sewer design for a growing town is genuinely difficult: the same pipe must work at both ends of a tenfold flow range.**

examTip.trap: **R = D/4, NOT D/2** — D/2 is the geometric radius; the HYDRAULIC radius is A/P, which for a full circle works out at half of that. Compute A/P once and the factor is fixed.
examTip.mnemonic: **At HALF depth the velocity EQUALS full bore** (A and P both halve, so R is unchanged) — and maximum discharge occurs at 94 % depth, 8 % ABOVE full bore. Which is why sewers are never designed to run exactly full.

questions.stem: Raw sewage with a BOD₅ of 250 mg/L passes through a treatment plant achieving 90 per cent BOD removal. The effluent BOD is:
questions.solution:
**25 mg/L.**

**The computation:**

> **BOD removed = 0.90 × 250 = 225 mg/L**

> **BOD remaining = 250 − 225 = 25 mg/L** ✓

> **Or directly: 250 × (1 − 0.90) = 250 × 0.10 = 25 mg/L** ✓

> **Note that option (c) 225 mg/L is the amount REMOVED, not the amount remaining** — the classic trap in percentage-removal questions.

> **A one-second check: 90 per cent removal must leave one TENTH, so the answer is 250/10 = 25.**

**What BOD is, and why it is measured the way it is:**

> **BOD — BIOCHEMICAL OXYGEN DEMAND — is the mass of dissolved oxygen consumed by micro-organisms in oxidising the biodegradable organic matter in a sample, under standard conditions.**

| Parameter of the standard test | Value |
|---|---|
| **Incubation period** | **5 days** |
| **Temperature** | **20 °C** |
| **What is measured** | **The DROP in dissolved oxygen over that period** |
| **Notation** | **BOD₅ at 20 °C** |

> **The 5-day, 20 °C convention is arbitrary but universal, and the reason for choosing 5 days is worth knowing: it is roughly the travel time of the rivers of England, where the test was devised, from source to sea.**

> **Five days at 20 °C captures about 68 per cent of the ULTIMATE BOD — the full demand, which takes 20 days or more.**

> **So BOD₅ = 0.68 × BOD_ultimate, approximately, and the two must not be confused.**

**Why BOD is an INDIRECT measure, and what that implies:**

> **BOD does not measure organic matter directly. It measures the OXYGEN that organisms consume in eating it.**

> **That is exactly the quantity that matters for a receiving water, which is why the parameter survives despite its inconveniences:**

| Limitation of the BOD test | Note |
|---|---|
| **Takes FIVE DAYS** | **Useless for operational control — the answer arrives after the event** ← |
| **Requires a healthy SEED of micro-organisms** | An industrial effluent may need acclimatised seed |
| **Toxic substances SUPPRESS the result** | A toxic waste can show a deceptively low BOD |
| **Nitrification interferes** | Suppressed with an inhibitor in the modern test |
| **Poor reproducibility** | ±10-20 per cent between laboratories is normal |

> **The five-day delay is the decisive practical objection, and it is why COD is used alongside it:**

| | **BOD** | **COD** |
|---|---|---|
| **What it measures** | **BIODEGRADABLE organic matter, via oxygen consumed by organisms** | **TOTAL oxidisable matter, via chemical oxidation (dichromate)** |
| **Time** | **5 days** | **3 hours (or 15 minutes for the rapid method)** ← |
| **Value** | **Lower** | **HIGHER — it oxidises non-biodegradable matter too** |
| **Typical ratio for domestic sewage** | **BOD/COD ≈ 0.5 - 0.65** | |

> **The BOD/COD RATIO is a genuinely useful diagnostic:**

> **A ratio above about 0.5 means the waste is largely BIODEGRADABLE, so BIOLOGICAL treatment will work.**

> **A ratio below about 0.3 means most of the oxidisable matter is NOT biodegradable, and biological treatment will fail — physico-chemical or advanced oxidation is needed instead.**

> **So a single pair of tests decides the fundamental question of what kind of treatment plant to build**, which is why an industrial effluent characterisation always reports both.

> **And once the ratio for a particular waste is established, COD alone can be used for daily control, with BOD measured occasionally to confirm the relation holds.** That is how the five-day delay is managed in practice.

**Typical BOD values, so the numbers can be judged:**

| Water | BOD₅ (mg/L) |
|---|---|
| **Clean river water** | **under 2** |
| **Treated effluent (Nepali/Indian standard for discharge to inland water)** | **30** ← |
| **This plant's effluent** | **25** ✓ — compliant |
| **Weak domestic sewage** | **100 - 200** |
| **Medium domestic sewage** | **200 - 300** ← the stem's raw sewage |
| **Strong domestic sewage** | **300 - 500** |
| **Dairy waste** | **1,000 - 2,000** |
| **Distillery spent wash** | **40,000 - 100,000** |

> **So the effluent at 25 mg/L meets the usual 30 mg/L discharge standard, and the plant's 90 per cent removal is a typical secondary treatment performance.**

> **Note the scale of some industrial wastes: a distillery effluent at 50,000 mg/L has the BOD load of the sewage of a very large town in a comparatively tiny volume** — which is why a single such industry discharging untreated can destroy a river that receives a whole city's treated sewage without difficulty.

**Where the removal happens in the plant, since 90 per cent is a whole-plant figure:**

| Stage | Typical BOD removal |
|---|---|
| **Screening and grit removal** | **Negligible (0-5 %)** |
| **PRIMARY sedimentation** | **30 - 35 %** |
| **SECONDARY biological (activated sludge or trickling filter)** | **80 - 90 % of what reaches it** ← |
| **Combined primary + secondary** | **85 - 95 %** ✓ |
| **Tertiary (filtration, polishing)** | A further 50-70 % of the remainder |

> **Note that primary sedimentation removes a third of the BOD simply by SETTLING the organic solids — a large return for a purely physical process with no energy input beyond the sludge scrapers.**

> **The remaining BOD is DISSOLVED and COLLOIDAL, which no settling tank can remove, and that is precisely what the biological stage exists for: micro-organisms convert dissolved organics into cell mass, which is then settleable.**

> **So the whole secondary process is a device for turning dissolved pollution into a solid that can be removed by gravity** — which is a clarifying way to see the activated sludge process and explains why the secondary clarifier is as essential to it as the aeration tank.

examTip.trick: **90 per cent removal leaves one TENTH: 250/10 = 25 mg/L.**
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 225 mg/L is the amount REMOVED, not the amount remaining** — the standard trap in percentage-removal questions.
examTip.mnemonic: **BOD/COD ratio decides the treatment**: above 0.5 the waste is biodegradable and biological treatment works; below 0.3 it is not and physico-chemical treatment is needed. That single pair of tests settles what plant to build.

questions.stem: In the activated sludge process, settled sludge is RETURNED from the secondary clarifier to the aeration tank in order to:
options: Dilute the incoming sewage and equalise its strength
Increase the hydraulic retention time of the aeration tank
Maintain the required concentration of micro-organisms (MLSS) in the aeration tank
Reduce the oxygen demand of the mixed liquor
questions.solution:
**To maintain the required concentration of micro-organisms — the MLSS — in the aeration tank.**

**Why the return is essential:**

> **The activated sludge process works by maintaining a large population of micro-organisms in contact with the sewage, so that they consume its organic matter rapidly.**

> **The measure of that population is the MLSS — MIXED LIQUOR SUSPENDED SOLIDS — typically 2000 to 4000 mg/L.**

> **But the sewage flows THROUGH the aeration tank in only 4 to 8 hours, and the organisms would be washed out with it in the same time.**

> **Micro-organisms need DAYS, not hours, to grow and to complete the oxidation.**

> **So the organisms are SETTLED OUT in the secondary clarifier and PUMPED BACK — which decouples the time the ORGANISMS spend in the system from the time the WATER does.**

> **That decoupling is the central idea of the process, and it is expressed in two separate retention times:**

| Time | Symbol | Typical value | What it governs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HYDRAULIC retention time** | **HRT** | **4 - 8 hours** | **How long the WATER stays** |
| **SOLIDS retention time (sludge age)** | **SRT** | **5 - 15 days** | **How long the ORGANISMS stay** ← |

> **The recycle is what makes SRT ≫ HRT, and without it the two would be equal and the process would not work at all.**

> **That is the complete answer to the question, and it also disposes of option (b): the recycle does NOT increase the hydraulic retention time — it increases the SOLIDS retention time, which is a different quantity.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **(a) Dilute the incoming sewage** | **Returned sludge is CONCENTRATED (8,000-12,000 mg/L) — it makes the mixed liquor STRONGER in solids, not weaker. Equalisation is done by a separate equalisation tank if needed** |
| **(b) Increase the HRT** | **The recycle increases the SOLIDS retention time, not the hydraulic one. Adding recycle flow actually REDUCES the HRT slightly if the tank volume is fixed** ← |
| **(c) Maintain the MLSS** | ✓ |
| **(d) Reduce the oxygen demand** | **The OPPOSITE — more organisms means MORE oxygen is required. Aeration is the largest energy cost of the plant** |

> **Option (d) is worth dwelling on because it inverts a real relationship: the returned organisms RESPIRE, and their endogenous respiration is a substantial part of the plant's oxygen demand.**

> **A higher MLSS therefore means a higher air requirement, and aeration typically consumes 50 to 60 per cent of a sewage works' total energy.**

**The F/M RATIO — the parameter that ties it together:**

> **F/M = FOOD to MICRO-ORGANISM ratio = (Q × BOD)/(V × MLSS)**

> **It is the daily mass of BOD applied per unit mass of organisms held, and it is the master control parameter of the process:**

| Process variant | F/M (kg BOD/kg MLSS/day) | SRT (days) | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EXTENDED aeration** | **0.05 - 0.15** | **20 - 30** | **Starved organisms; very stable; little sludge produced; large tank** ← |
| **CONVENTIONAL** | **0.2 - 0.4** | **5 - 15** | **The standard** |
| **HIGH RATE** | **0.4 - 1.5** | **1 - 3** | **Small tank; poorer effluent; more sludge** |

> **The trade-off across that table is instructive and consistent:**

> **A LOW F/M starves the organisms, so they oxidise their own cell material (endogenous respiration) as well as the sewage.**

> **The result is LESS SLUDGE to dispose of and a very stable, well-settling biomass that tolerates shock loads — at the cost of a much larger aeration tank and more air.**

> **A HIGH F/M feeds them abundantly, so they multiply rapidly: a small tank, but a great deal of surplus sludge and a biomass that settles poorly.**

> **Since SLUDGE DISPOSAL is often the most expensive and troublesome part of running a sewage works, the low-F/M option is frequently chosen despite its larger footprint** — which is why extended aeration and oxidation ditches are so common for small and medium works.

**SLUDGE BULKING, since it is the process's characteristic failure:**

> **The whole scheme depends on the sludge SETTLING in the secondary clarifier. If it does not, the organisms escape with the effluent and the process collapses.**

> **BULKING is the condition in which the sludge settles poorly, and it is measured by the SLUDGE VOLUME INDEX:**

> **SVI = (settled volume in mL/L after 30 min) × 1000 / MLSS (mg/L)**

| SVI | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **Below 100** | **Good settling** |
| **100 - 150** | **Acceptable** |
| **Above 150** | **BULKING — poor settling** ← |

> **The commonest cause is the proliferation of FILAMENTOUS bacteria, which form long threads that bridge between floc particles and prevent them compacting.**

> **Their growth is favoured by low dissolved oxygen, low F/M in some conditions, nutrient deficiency (nitrogen or phosphorus), and low pH.**

> **So the remedy is diagnostic rather than mechanical: identify which condition is favouring the filaments and correct it — raise the DO, adjust the F/M, add nutrients, or chlorinate the return sludge selectively.**

> **The nutrient point is worth noting because it catches industrial applications: the organisms need nitrogen and phosphorus in roughly the ratio BOD : N : P = 100 : 5 : 1.**

> **Domestic sewage supplies both amply. An industrial effluent — a sugar or paper waste, say — may be rich in carbon and almost devoid of nitrogen, and biological treatment of it FAILS until nutrients are DELIBERATELY ADDED.**

> **Which is a striking inversion of the usual picture: for such a waste, one must FERTILISE the effluent in order to clean it.**

examTip.trick: **The recycle DECOUPLES the SOLIDS retention time (5-15 days) from the HYDRAULIC retention time (4-8 hours)** — organisms need days, water passes in hours. That is the whole idea of the process.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) confuses the two retention times** — recycle raises the SRT, not the HRT. And (d) inverts the truth: more organisms means MORE oxygen demand, and aeration is 50-60 % of the works' energy.
examTip.mnemonic: **F/M is the master control**: LOW F/M (extended aeration) starves the organisms — less sludge, very stable, big tank; HIGH F/M — small tank, much sludge, poor settling. Since sludge disposal is the expensive part, low F/M often wins despite the footprint.

questions.stem: Under Nepal's environmental legislation, the less detailed of the two principal environmental assessment studies, required for projects of moderate scale and impact, is the:
questions.solution:
**The INITIAL ENVIRONMENTAL EXAMINATION (IEE).**

**The two-tier system:**

| Study | Applies to | Approving authority | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **IEE — Initial Environmental Examination** | **Projects of MODERATE scale and impact** | **The CONCERNED MINISTRY** | **Shorter, simpler, faster** ← |
| **EIA — Environmental Impact Assessment** | **Projects of LARGE scale or with significant/irreversible impacts** | **The Ministry responsible for the ENVIRONMENT** | **Detailed, includes public hearing, longer** |

> **A newer BRIEF ENVIRONMENTAL STUDY (BES) tier has been introduced for small projects below the IEE threshold, making the system effectively three-tiered.**

> **The principle behind the tiering is PROPORTIONALITY: the depth of assessment should match the likely severity of the impact.**

> **Requiring a full EIA for a small project wastes the proponent's money and the regulator's time, and requiring only an IEE for a large one fails to identify serious impacts.** So the screening step — deciding which tier applies — is the first and in some ways the most consequential decision in the process.

**How the tier is decided:**

> **Nepal's Environment Protection Rules SCHEDULE the project types and thresholds explicitly, so the tier is generally determined by a table rather than by judgement.**

| Example (indicative) | Tier |
|---|---|
| **A small hydropower scheme (below a stated capacity)** | **IEE** |
| **A large hydropower scheme** | **EIA** |
| **A road upgrading within the existing alignment** | **IEE** |
| **A new road in a forest area, or of a stated length** | **EIA** |
| **Any project inside a NATIONAL PARK, conservation area or protected forest** | **EIA regardless of size** ← |
| **A project requiring resettlement above a stated number of families** | **EIA** |

> **The rule that LOCATION can override SIZE is worth noting: a small project in a sensitive area requires a full EIA, because the impact depends on where it is as much as on how big it is.**

> **That is the same principle a designer meets elsewhere — a modest structure in a hazardous location warrants more analysis than a large one in a benign location.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each is a real instrument with a different purpose:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **EIA** | **The MORE detailed tier — the stem asks for the less detailed** |
| **SEA — Strategic Environmental Assessment** | **Applied to POLICIES, PLANS and PROGRAMMES rather than to individual projects** ← |
| **Environmental AUDIT** | **A POST-implementation check, conducted after the project is operating, to verify that mitigation was carried out and is working** |
| **IEE** | ✓ |

> **The SEA distinction is conceptually the most interesting and is genuinely important:**

> **A project-level EIA can only ask whether THIS project's impacts are acceptable and how to mitigate them. It cannot ask whether the project should exist, or whether a different approach would serve better.**

> **By the time a hydropower project reaches EIA, the decision to generate power by damming that river has already been taken.**

> **SEA is applied EARLIER — to the energy policy, the river basin plan, the road network master plan — where the genuine alternatives are still open.**

> **So SEA addresses the structural limitation of project EIA: that it arrives too late to influence the questions that matter most.**

> **And the ENVIRONMENTAL AUDIT addresses the other end of the same problem: an EIA is a PREDICTION, and without a subsequent audit no one ever discovers whether the predictions were right or the mitigation was implemented.**

> **The honest observation is that auditing is the weakest link in most systems, Nepal's included: reports are prepared and approved, and compliance is checked far less than it should be.** An EIA whose mitigation measures are never implemented has consumed resources and protected nothing.

**The contents of the reports, since examinations ask for them:**

| Section | IEE | EIA |
|---|---|---|
| **Project description** | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Baseline environmental condition** | **Brief** | **Detailed, with primary data** |
| **Impact identification and prediction** | ✓ | ✓ |
| **ALTERNATIVES analysis** | Limited | **Required, including the NO-PROJECT alternative** ← |
| **Mitigation measures** | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Environmental Management Plan** | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Monitoring plan** | ✓ | ✓ |
| **PUBLIC CONSULTATION** | **Notice and comment** | **PUBLIC HEARING required** ← |
| **Scoping document and Terms of Reference approval** | Not required | **REQUIRED before the study begins** |

> **The two rows marked are the substantive differences, and both are worth understanding.**

> **The ALTERNATIVES analysis, including the NO-PROJECT alternative, is what makes an EIA a decision-making tool rather than a justification exercise.**

> **Without it, an EIA can only describe and mitigate; with it, the assessment can conclude that a different site, technology, scale or alignment is preferable — or that the project should not proceed.**

> **The PUBLIC HEARING is the other substantive element, and its value is largely INFORMATIONAL: affected people know things about local hydrology, land use, seasonal flooding, grazing rights and cultural sites that no consultant's survey will discover.**

> **So a public hearing is not merely a procedural courtesy or a political concession — it is a data-gathering step, and an EIA that skips it is a worse technical document as well as a less legitimate one.**

> **The environmental impacts of a project also carry a matter of professional obligation that belongs with this topic: the engineer's duty of care extends to people who are not the client.** A community downstream of a dam is affected by decisions in which it has no contractual standing, and the assessment process is the mechanism by which that interest is represented.

examTip.trick: **IEE is the LESS detailed tier (moderate projects, approved by the concerned ministry); EIA is the MORE detailed one (large or sensitive projects, public hearing, environment ministry).**
examTip.trap: **SEA applies to POLICIES, PLANS and PROGRAMMES, not projects; an AUDIT is a POST-implementation check.** Each option is a real instrument at a different stage.
examTip.mnemonic: **LOCATION can override SIZE** — any project inside a national park or conservation area needs a full EIA regardless of scale. And the two substantive EIA extras are the ALTERNATIVES analysis (including no-project) and the PUBLIC HEARING.

questions.stem: A canal outlet delivers 120 hectare-centimetres of water to a field, of which 96 hectare-centimetres is stored in the root zone. The water APPLICATION efficiency is:
questions.solution:
**80 per cent.**

**The computation:**

> **η_a = (water stored in the root zone) / (water delivered to the field) × 100**

> **= 96/120 × 100 = 0.80 × 100 = 80 %** ✓

**The family of irrigation efficiencies, which must be distinguished:**

| Efficiency | Definition | Where the loss occurs |
|---|---|---|
| **CONVEYANCE, η_c** | **Water delivered to the field ÷ water diverted at the head** | **SEEPAGE and evaporation in the canals and distributaries** |
| **APPLICATION (farm), η_a** | **Water stored in the ROOT ZONE ÷ water delivered to the field** | **DEEP PERCOLATION below the root zone, and RUNOFF off the field** ← this question |
| **STORAGE, η_s** | **Water stored ÷ water NEEDED in the root zone** | Under-irrigation |
| **DISTRIBUTION (uniformity), η_d** | **A measure of how EVENLY the water is spread over the field** | Uneven application |
| **USE (consumptive use), η_u** | **Water consumed by the crop ÷ water delivered** | Everything |
| **OVERALL (project) efficiency** | **η_c × η_a** | Both |

> **The distinction between CONVEYANCE and APPLICATION is the one this question tests, and it turns on WHERE the water is measured:**

> **CONVEYANCE efficiency is measured from the canal head to the FIELD BOUNDARY.**

> **APPLICATION efficiency is measured from the FIELD BOUNDARY into the ROOT ZONE.**

> **The stem says "delivers to a field" and "stored in the root zone", which places it unambiguously in the second.**

**Typical values, and where the water actually goes:**

| Stage | Typical efficiency |
|---|---|
| **Conveyance — UNLINED canal system** | **60 - 70 %** |
| **Conveyance — LINED canal system** | **80 - 90 %** |
| **Application — BORDER or FURROW irrigation** | **55 - 70 %** |
| **Application — well-managed basin irrigation** | **70 - 85 %** ← 80 % here |
| **Application — SPRINKLER** | **70 - 85 %** |
| **Application — DRIP** | **85 - 95 %** |
| **OVERALL, typical unlined surface scheme** | **35 - 50 %** |
| **Overall, lined system with drip** | **75 - 85 %** |

> **The OVERALL figure is the sobering one: a conventional unlined surface irrigation scheme delivers under half of the water diverted to the crop's root zone.**

> **Since the efficiencies MULTIPLY, improving one alone has limited effect: 0.65 × 0.65 = 0.42, and raising the conveyance efficiency to 0.85 gives only 0.85 × 0.65 = 0.55.**

> **That multiplicative structure is the most important thing to understand about irrigation efficiency, and it has a direct practical consequence: the weakest link limits the whole chain, and improving the strong link is largely wasted.**

> **So a project that lines its canals and leaves the field application at 55 per cent has spent a great deal to reach 47 per cent overall** — which is why modern irrigation improvement addresses conveyance and on-farm application together, or not at all.

**Where the application losses go — and the important qualification:**

| Loss | Note |
|---|---|
| **DEEP PERCOLATION below the root zone** | **Usually the larger part** |
| **Surface RUNOFF from the tail of the field** | Can be recovered and reused |
| **Evaporation from the wetted soil surface** | Genuinely lost |

> **Here is a point of real substance that the efficiency figure conceals: DEEP PERCOLATION IS NOT ENTIRELY LOST.**

> **The water percolating below the root zone recharges the GROUNDWATER, from which it can be pumped and used again.**

> **So in a basin where groundwater is exploited, low application efficiency is partly a TRANSFER of water from surface to subsurface storage rather than a loss.**

> **That is why basin-scale water accounting often shows much higher effective efficiency than the sum of the field-scale figures suggests.**

> **But the qualification has its own qualification, and both matter:**

| Consequence of deep percolation | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **Recharges groundwater for reuse** | **A genuine benefit where the aquifer is exploited** |
| **RAISES THE WATER TABLE** | **The cause of WATERLOGGING and salinity** ← |
| **Leaches nutrients and applied fertiliser downward** | A real agronomic and pollution loss |
| **Carries salts DOWN, away from the root zone** | **A NECESSARY function — the leaching requirement** |
| **Costs pumping energy to recover** | Not free |

> **The LEACHING REQUIREMENT in the fourth row deserves emphasis, because it means a certain amount of "inefficiency" is DELIBERATE AND NECESSARY:**

> **All irrigation water carries dissolved salts. The crop takes up water and leaves the salts behind, so salts accumulate in the root zone.**

> **Unless some water passes THROUGH the root zone and carries those salts downward, the soil salinises and becomes unproductive.**

> **So an irrigation system operating at 100 per cent application efficiency — every drop retained in the root zone — would salinise its own land.**

> **The leaching requirement is typically 5 to 20 per cent of the applied water, depending on the salinity of the water and the crop's tolerance.**

> **Which means the target application efficiency is not 100 per cent but something like 85 to 90 per cent**, and it is a genuine instance of an engineering optimum lying short of the apparent ideal.

> **It also explains a paradox observed in practice: converting a scheme to highly efficient drip irrigation can CAUSE salinisation, because the leaching that the old inefficient flooding provided has been removed.** Drip systems in saline conditions must therefore include periodic leaching irrigations by design.

examTip.trick: **Application efficiency = water stored in the ROOT ZONE ÷ water delivered to the FIELD = 96/120 = 80 %.**
examTip.trap: **Distinguish CONVEYANCE (canal head → field boundary) from APPLICATION (field boundary → root zone).** The stem's wording places it in the second; the two are often confused.
examTip.mnemonic: **Efficiencies MULTIPLY: 0.65 × 0.65 = 42 % overall**, so improving one link alone is largely wasted. And some "inefficiency" is NECESSARY — the LEACHING REQUIREMENT (5-20 %) must pass through the root zone or the soil salinises.

questions.stem: An irrigation project has a culturable command area of 5000 hectares, with an intensity of irrigation of 60 per cent in kharif and 40 per cent in rabi. The total area irrigated annually is:
questions.solution:
**5000 hectares.**

**The computation:**

> **Area irrigated in KHARIF = 0.60 × 5000 = 3000 ha**

> **Area irrigated in RABI = 0.40 × 5000 = 2000 ha**

> **TOTAL annual irrigated area = 3000 + 2000 = 5000 ha** ✓

> **The TOTAL intensity of irrigation is 60 + 40 = 100 per cent** — which means the project irrigates an aggregate area over the year equal to its whole command area.

**The crucial point this question tests:**

> **The total intensity of irrigation CAN EXCEED 100 PER CENT, and frequently does — which surprises candidates who read it as a percentage of land.**

> **It is not a percentage of LAND. It is the sum over the SEASONS, and the same field can be irrigated in more than one season.**

> **So a project with 80 per cent kharif and 70 per cent rabi has a total intensity of 150 per cent — irrigating an aggregate 1.5 times its command area annually, because half of it grows two crops.**

> **In this project the intensity is exactly 100 per cent, which is achieved without any field being irrigated twice — but that is a coincidence of the numbers, not a constraint.**

> **Options (a) 3000 ha and (b) 2000 ha are the two seasonal areas taken alone**, and option (c) 2500 ha is their average — each a plausible misreading of what is asked.

**The area definitions, which form a nested hierarchy and are constantly confused:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS COMMAND AREA (GCA)** | **The TOTAL area lying within the canal's boundary — including villages, roads, ponds, forest and barren land** |
| **CULTURABLE COMMAND AREA (CCA)** | **The part of the GCA that is CULTIVABLE — capable of being cropped** ← the stem's figure |
| **Culturable CULTIVATED area** | The part of the CCA actually under crops |
| **Culturable UNCULTIVATED area** | Cultivable but left fallow |
| **IRRIGABLE command area** | The part of the CCA that the canal can physically command by gravity |
| **NET irrigated area** | The area actually receiving irrigation in a season |

> **The nesting runs GCA ⊃ CCA ⊃ irrigable ⊃ net irrigated, and each step removes something.**

> **Typically the CCA is 70 to 90 per cent of the GCA — the balance being land that cannot be cropped at all.**

> **The distinction matters commercially as well as technically, because water charges, project benefits and cost-benefit ratios are all computed on the CCA or the irrigated area, never on the GCA.**

> **A project appraisal that quotes the GCA as its command is overstating its benefit** — which is a real and not uncommon form of optimism in project documents.

**Why the intensity is limited at all, since a higher intensity is better:**

| Constraint on intensity | Note |
|---|---|
| **AVAILABLE WATER, especially in the dry season** | **Usually the binding constraint** ← |
| **The canal's CAPACITY** | Sized for a design intensity; it cannot deliver more |
| **Cropping pattern and rotation** | Some crops occupy the land for a full year (sugarcane) |
| **Soil condition and the need for fallow** | Continuous cropping exhausts the soil |
| **Labour, inputs and market access** | Non-engineering constraints that bind in practice |
| **DRAINAGE capacity** | **Intensive irrigation without drainage causes waterlogging** |

> **The DRY SEASON water availability is the constraint that shapes Nepali and North Indian irrigation, and it connects back to the hydrology:**

> **Monsoon flows are abundant — kharif intensity is limited by land and by rainfall rather than by canal supply.**

> **Dry-season flows are a small fraction of the monsoon — so rabi intensity is limited by the river's low flow, and a run-of-river diversion may be able to command only a third of its CCA in rabi.**

> **Which is exactly why STORAGE projects are valued so highly: a reservoir raises the RABI intensity, and rabi is where the water is scarce and the crop most valuable.**

> **So the two intensities are limited by entirely different things, and a project's improvement strategy differs accordingly.**

**The related design quantity — the CAPACITY FACTOR and the canal's design discharge:**

> **A canal's design discharge follows from the CCA, the intensity, the crop water requirement and the efficiency:**

> **Q = (Area irrigated × delta) / (base period × efficiency)**, in consistent units

> **Or through the DUTY:  Q = area irrigated / duty**

> **For a rabi area of 2000 ha with a duty of 1800 ha/cumec:  Q = 2000/1800 = 1.11 m³/s at the field.**

> **Divided by a conveyance efficiency of 0.7, the canal must carry 1.59 m³/s at its head.**

> **Note again that the duty must be stated with its LOCATION — at the field or at the head — since the two differ by exactly that efficiency**, and confusing them undersizes the canal by 30 per cent.

**The KHARIF and RABI seasons, since the terms are specific:**

| Season | Months (approximate) | Rainfall | Typical crops |
|---|---|---|---|
| **KHARIF (monsoon)** | **June to October** | **ABUNDANT — the monsoon** | **Rice, maize, millet, cotton, jute** |
| **RABI (winter)** | **November to March** | **Little** | **Wheat, barley, gram, mustard, potato** |
| **ZAID (hot weather)** | **March to June** | **Almost none** | Melons, vegetables, fodder |

> **The critical asymmetry: KHARIF crops are grown WITH the monsoon and need irrigation only to supplement it, while RABI crops depend on irrigation almost entirely.**

> **So the same nominal intensity means very different things in the two seasons: 60 per cent kharif intensity may require only a few supplementary waterings, while 40 per cent rabi intensity requires the crop's whole water requirement to be delivered.**

> **The WATER demanded per hectare in rabi is therefore far greater than the intensity figures suggest**, and a canal system's dry-season capacity, not its monsoon capacity, is what determines what it can actually achieve.

examTip.trap: **Total intensity CAN EXCEED 100 per cent** — it is a sum over SEASONS, not a fraction of land, and the same field may be irrigated twice. Options (a) and (b) are the single seasons.
examTip.mnemonic: **GCA ⊃ CCA ⊃ irrigable ⊃ net irrigated**, and benefits are computed on the CCA, never the GCA. And KHARIF intensity is limited by land, RABI by dry-season water — which is why storage projects are valued for rabi.

questions.stem: Using Lacey's regime theory, the wetted perimeter of a channel designed to carry 25 m³/s is:
questions.solution:
**23.75 m.**

**Lacey's wetted perimeter equation:**

> **P = 4.75 √Q**

> **= 4.75 × √25 = 4.75 × 5 = 23.75 m** ✓

> **Note that option (d) 4.75 m is the coefficient alone (the √Q omitted), option (b) 11.88 m is half the answer, and option (c) 118.75 m is 4.75 × Q with the square root omitted.**

> **So each distractor is a specific mishandling of the same formula, and the √Q is what discriminates.**

**Lacey's three equations, which is what makes his theory complete:**

| Relation | Equation |
|---|---|
| **VELOCITY** | **V = 0.4382 (f² Q)^{1/6}**, or V² = (2/5) f R |
| **WETTED PERIMETER (or area)** | **P = 4.75 √Q**, and A = 1.26 (Q^{5/6})/(f^{1/3}) ← |
| **SLOPE** | **S = f^{5/3} / (3340 Q^{1/6})** |

> **And the SILT FACTOR that appears throughout:**

> **f = 1.76 √(m_r)**, with m_r the mean particle size in millimetres.

| Material | Mean size (mm) | Silt factor f |
|---|---|---|
| **Very fine silt** | **0.05** | **0.4** |
| **Fine silt** | **0.08 - 0.12** | **0.5 - 0.6** |
| **Medium silt** | **0.16** | **0.7** |
| **Standard silt** | **0.32** | **1.00** ← the reference |
| **Coarse sand** | **0.5** | **1.25** |
| **Fine gravel** | **2.0 - 8.0** | **2.5 - 5.0** |

> **Note that f = 1.0 corresponds to "standard silt" of 0.32 mm mean size** — the same kind of calibration datum as Kennedy's m = 1.

**Why THREE equations matter — the decisive advantage over Kennedy:**

| | **KENNEDY (1895)** | **LACEY (1930)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Equations provided** | **ONE (V₀ = 0.55 m y^{0.64})** | **THREE** |
| **Unknowns for a given Q** | **Two (B and y)** | Two |
| **Design determinate?** | **NO — the B/y ratio must be ASSUMED** | **YES — a UNIQUE section results** ← |
| **Slope** | **Must be brought in from Kutter or Manning** | **Given by the theory itself** |
| **Silt held in suspension by** | **The BED only (eddies rising from it)** | **The WHOLE PERIMETER** |
| **Section shape** | Assumed trapezoidal | **SEMI-ELLIPTICAL regime section** |
| **Initial vs final regime** | **Not distinguished** | **DISTINGUISHED** |

> **The determinacy in the third row is the practical difference: with Lacey's three equations and a known Q and f, the velocity, the area, the perimeter and the slope all follow uniquely.**

> **With Kennedy, two competent engineers designing the same canal from the same data can arrive at two different sections, because each assumes a different B/y ratio.**

> **That is not a small matter for a design standard — reproducibility is part of what makes a method usable in practice.**

**Working the full design for this canal, to show the theory in use:**

> **Take f = 1.0 (standard silt), Q = 25 m³/s.**

| Quantity | Computation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter** | **4.75 √25** | **23.75 m** ✓ |
| **Velocity** | **0.4382 (1² × 25)^{1/6} = 0.4382 × 25^{0.1667} = 0.4382 × 1.7100** | **0.749 m/s** |
| **Area** | **Q/V = 25/0.749** | **33.4 m²** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **A/P = 33.4/23.75** | **1.406 m** |
| **Slope** | **1/(3340 × 25^{1/6}) = 1/(3340 × 1.710)** | **1 in 5711** |

> **Check on the hydraulic radius by Lacey's own relation: R = (5/2)(V²/f) = 2.5 × 0.749²/1.0 = 2.5 × 0.561 = 1.403 m** ✓ — agreeing with A/P, which verifies the whole set.

> **That internal consistency check is worth making, because it confirms that the three equations have been applied correctly.**

> **And note the resulting velocity of 0.75 m/s and slope of 1 in 5711 — both entirely typical of a large alluvial canal**, which is a check that the answer describes something real.

**Lacey's INITIAL and FINAL regime, since the distinction is his own refinement:**

| Regime | Condition |
|---|---|
| **INITIAL regime** | **A newly cut canal: the SIDES have adjusted but the BED has not; the slope is still the artificial one it was excavated to** |
| **FINAL (true) regime** | **After years of operation: the bed and sides have BOTH adjusted, and the slope has changed to its regime value** ← |

> **The practical importance is real: a canal designed for its initial condition will CHANGE SHAPE over its first years, silting or scouring until it reaches its own regime.**

> **Lacey's equations describe the FINAL regime, which is what a designer should aim at — because that is the section the canal will settle into whatever it is built as.**

> **So designing for the regime section means the canal is built in the shape it wants to be, and remains stable from the outset instead of eroding into it.**

**The honest limitation of the whole regime approach:**

> **Both theories are EMPIRICAL, derived from observations on the canals of Punjab and Sindh in a particular kind of alluvium.**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Applies only to ALLUVIAL channels carrying silt in suspension** | **Not to lined canals, rocky channels or boulder streams** ← |
| **Assumes a steady discharge and a steady silt charge** | Real canals run intermittently |
| **The silt factor f is difficult to determine reliably** | The single largest uncertainty |
| **Derived from a specific region's soils** | Transfer to other alluvium is uncertain |
| **Says nothing about bank stability or seepage** | Separate considerations |

> **So for a LINED canal neither theory applies at all: a lining cannot scour or silt its boundary, so the section is designed by Manning's equation for the required discharge, with the MOST ECONOMICAL SECTION as the shape objective and the lining material's velocity limits as the constraint.**

> **Which is worth stating plainly, because it is a common error to apply regime theory to a lined canal** — the theory answers a question the lined canal does not pose.

examTip.trap: **Every distractor mishandles the √Q** — 4.75 alone, half the answer, or 4.75 × Q without the root. The square root is the discriminating step.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lacey gives THREE equations (velocity, area/perimeter, slope), so the section is DETERMINATE; Kennedy gives one, so B/y must be assumed.** And neither applies to a LINED canal — there the most economical section and Manning govern.

questions.stem: The principal function of UNDER-SLUICES in a diversion headworks is:
options: To dissipate the energy of the flood water passing over the weir
To keep the pocket in front of the canal head regulator clear of silt and to dispose of the river's low flow
To provide a roadway across the river
To measure the discharge entering the offtaking canal
questions.solution:
**To keep the pocket in front of the canal head regulator clear of silt, and to pass the river's low flow.**

**What the under-sluices are:**

> **Under-sluices are a section of the weir or barrage, adjacent to the CANAL HEAD REGULATOR, whose crest is set at a LOWER LEVEL than the rest of the weir and which is provided with gates.**

> **The enclosed area of river in front of the head regulator, bounded by a divide wall, is called the POCKET or the still pond.**

**The functions, in order of importance:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **SCOUR the silt deposited in the pocket** | **Opening the gates draws a strong current through the pocket, flushing the deposits downstream** ← the primary purpose |
| **Pass the river's LOW FLOW** | **In the dry season the whole river passes through the under-sluices, keeping the main weir dry** |
| **Pass a part of the flood** | Increasing the works' total capacity |
| **Maintain a well-defined river channel toward the head regulator** | Ensures the canal can always draw |
| **Lower the flood level upstream** | The deeper section conveys more |

> **The SILT problem they solve is a serious one and worth understanding, because it explains the whole layout of a headworks.**

**Why silt collects in front of the head regulator at all:**

> **A weir raises the water level, so the river slows down upstream of it.**

> **A slower river cannot carry its sediment, so it DEPOSITS — and the deposition is heaviest in the still water of the pocket, exactly where the canal draws its supply.**

> **If nothing is done, the pocket silts up, the canal's intake is buried, and the canal itself begins drawing silt-laden water and silting up in turn.**

> **So a diversion headworks CREATES the silt problem by the very act of raising the water level, and the under-sluices are the device that manages what the weir causes.**

> **Recognising that a structure's principal problem is one it creates itself is a useful habit of thought in engineering.**

**The silt exclusion arrangement in full, since the under-sluices are one part of a system:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **UNDER-SLUICES with a low crest** | **Scour the pocket and pass low flow** ← |
| **DIVIDE WALL** | **Separates the under-sluice pocket from the main weir, so that a still pond can be maintained and the scouring current concentrated** |
| **SILT EXCLUDER (in front of the regulator, in the pocket)** | **Tunnels along the bed that carry the BOTTOM, silt-laden layer through to the under-sluices, letting the canal draw the CLEANER TOP water** |
| **SILT EJECTOR (in the canal, downstream of the regulator)** | **Removes silt that HAS entered the canal, ejecting it back to the river** |
| **Fish ladder** | Passage for fish past the obstruction |
| **Canal head regulator with gates** | Controls the canal's supply |

> **The EXCLUDER and EJECTOR distinction is worth being clear about, since the names are similar and the locations are not:**

> **A silt EXCLUDER keeps silt OUT of the canal — it is upstream of the head regulator, in the river.**

> **A silt EJECTOR removes silt that HAS ENTERED — it is downstream of the head regulator, in the canal.**

> **Exclusion is better than ejection, because silt in the canal has already caused abrasion and has to be lifted out; but exclusion is never complete, so both are commonly provided on a large system.**

**The STILL POND versus OPEN FLOW operation, since the under-sluice gates offer a choice:**

| Method | Operation | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **STILL POND** | **Under-sluice gates CLOSED while the canal draws; the pocket is a quiet pond so silt settles in it. The gates are then opened periodically to FLUSH it** | **Better silt exclusion; requires periodic flushing and loses water** ← |
| **OPEN FLOW (semi-open)** | **Under-sluice gates kept partly OPEN continuously, so a current runs through the pocket carrying silt past the regulator** | **Continuous; wastes water continuously; less complete exclusion** |

> **The STILL POND method is generally preferred where water can be spared for flushing, because settling the silt in a quiet pool and then flushing it is more effective than trying to sweep it past continuously.**

> **The choice therefore depends on the river's dry-season flow: where water is abundant, open flow is simpler; where every cubic metre is needed for irrigation, still pond operation with occasional flushing wastes less.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each names a real element of a headworks:**

| Option | The element that actually does it |
|---|---|
| **(a) Dissipate flood energy** | **The STILLING BASIN / cistern below the weir, with baffle blocks and an end sill** |
| **(c) Provide a roadway** | **A ROAD BRIDGE, commonly built over a barrage — a real and valuable secondary benefit, but not the under-sluices' purpose** |
| **(d) Measure the canal discharge** | **A METER FLUME or a modular outlet in the canal** |

> **Option (c) is a genuine and important side benefit of a barrage and deserves the note: a barrage across a large river provides a road or rail crossing at a small marginal cost, and that benefit has often justified projects on its own.**

> **But it is not what the under-sluices are for, and a question about FUNCTION is asking about purpose rather than about incidental advantage.**

**A final note on the layout, since it follows from all of the above:**

> **The head regulator is always placed at RIGHT ANGLES, or nearly so, to the weir axis — commonly at 90° to 110° to the direction of the river flow.**

> **The reason is silt again: an offtake taking water at a sharp angle from the main flow draws the SURFACE layers, which are cleaner, while the bottom silt-laden layers continue downstream past it.**

> **An offtake aligned with the flow would draw the bed load straight into the canal.**

> **So even the geometry of the headworks is determined by sediment**, and the whole layout — the pocket, the divide wall, the low-crested sluices, the angled regulator, the excluder tunnels — is one integrated answer to a single problem.

examTip.trick: **Under-sluices have a LOWER crest and gates: they scour the POCKET in front of the head regulator and pass the dry-season flow.**
examTip.trap: **Each distractor names a real element of a headworks doing a different job** — the stilling basin dissipates flood energy, a road bridge carries traffic, a meter flume measures the canal flow.
examTip.mnemonic: **A weir CREATES its own silt problem by slowing the river, and the whole layout answers it**: low-crested sluices, divide wall, silt EXCLUDER (upstream, keeps silt out) and silt EJECTOR (in the canal, removes what got in), plus a regulator angled to draw the cleaner surface water.

questions.stem: A groyne (spur) constructed with its axis inclined UPSTREAM, against the direction of flow, is called:
questions.solution:
**A REPELLING groyne.**

**The classification by ORIENTATION:**

| Groyne | Inclination | Effect on the current |
|---|---|---|
| **REPELLING** | **Pointing UPSTREAM (against the flow), typically at 60-75° to the bank** | **REPELS the current AWAY from the bank it protects** ← |
| **ATTRACTING** | **Pointing DOWNSTREAM (with the flow)** | **ATTRACTS the current TOWARD the bank — used to hold a channel in position** |
| **DEFLECTING** | **PERPENDICULAR to the bank (90°)** | **Deflects the current locally, changing its direction without moving it far** |

> **The naming is by EFFECT ON THE CURRENT, not by appearance — which is what makes it easy to get backwards.**

> **A groyne angled UPSTREAM presents an inclined face to the oncoming flow, and the water is turned away from the bank, much as a plough turns soil.**

> **A groyne angled DOWNSTREAM lets the current run into the pocket behind it and thereby draws the channel toward the bank.**

**Why an ATTRACTING groyne would ever be wanted — the point that puzzles people:**

> **It seems perverse to attract a river toward the bank one is trying to protect. The purpose is different:**

| Use of an attracting groyne | Note |
|---|---|
| **To hold the DEEP CHANNEL against a particular bank** | **So that an intake, a pump house or a navigation channel always has water** ← |
| **To guide the flow toward a bridge or barrage opening** | Keeping the approach channel where it is wanted |
| **To prevent the channel wandering away from a structure** | A river that abandons an intake is as much a problem as one that attacks a bank |

> **So attracting groynes are used where the objective is to FIX the channel's position rather than to push it away** — and the bank at that location is then given hard protection to survive the attack it is deliberately inviting.

> **That is a genuine engineering choice: accept erosion at a controlled, protected location in order to prevent it elsewhere, and in order to keep the river where the works need it.**

**The other classifications, since papers ask by any of them:**

| Basis | Types |
|---|---|
| **ORIENTATION** | **Repelling (upstream), attracting (downstream), deflecting (perpendicular)** ← |
| **HEIGHT relative to the water level** | **SUBMERGED (sloping, permeable — retards flow and induces silting) and NON-SUBMERGED (impermeable — deflects flow)** |
| **PERMEABILITY** | **PERMEABLE (pile screens, timber, bamboo — slows the current and encourages deposition) and IMPERMEABLE (solid earth or stone — deflects)** |
| **SHAPE in plan** | **Straight, T-headed (Denehy), hockey-stick, L-headed, inverted-hockey** |
| **Construction** | Earth core with stone armour; stone; concrete blocks; gabion |

> **The PERMEABLE / IMPERMEABLE distinction is functionally the most important after orientation:**

> **An IMPERMEABLE groyne DEFLECTS the flow, which creates a strong scour hole at its nose and a vortex that must be protected against.**

> **A PERMEABLE groyne lets water through slowly, which REDUCES the velocity behind it and encourages SILTING — building new land rather than pushing water away.**

> **So a permeable groyne works WITH the river's sediment to rebuild the bank, while an impermeable one works AGAINST the river's flow to push it aside.**

> **Permeable groynes are therefore preferred in heavily silt-laden rivers, where deposition can be recruited to do the work** — which describes most Nepali and North Indian rivers, and is why bamboo and timber pile screens remain in use alongside modern stone work.

**The T-HEADED (Denehy) groyne, since option (d) names it:**

> **A T-headed groyne has a shank normal or inclined to the bank and a HEAD running PARALLEL to the flow at its outer end.**

> **The head acts as a short length of guide bank, so the groyne both projects into the river and guides the flow past it — combining the effects of a spur and a guide bund.**

> **Its advantage is that the parallel head reduces the local scour and the flow disturbance that a plain nose produces.**

> **Note that it is classified by its SHAPE and could be built in either orientation** — so it is not an alternative to "repelling" but a different axis of description, which is why option (d) is a category error rather than merely a wrong answer.

**The critical detail in groyne design — the NOSE:**

> **The most heavily attacked point of any groyne is its NOSE, the tip projecting into the river.**

| Feature at the nose | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Heaviest armour, largest stone** | **The highest velocity and greatest turbulence occur there** ← |
| **A LAUNCHING APRON of loose stone at the bed** | **When the bed scours, the apron stone falls ("launches") into the hole and armours it automatically** |
| **A generous slope and rounded plan** | Reduces the vortex strength |
| **Scour depth estimated by Lacey's formula** | **d = 0.473 (Q/f)^{1/3}, with a multiplier of 2 to 2.75 at a nose** |

> **The LAUNCHING APRON is the most elegant idea in river training and deserves the emphasis: rather than trying to prevent scour, it provides a stockpile of loose stone at bed level which the scour itself pulls down into the hole.**

> **The structure thus repairs itself as it is attacked, and the quantity of stone in the apron is calculated to be just sufficient to cover the anticipated scour slope when it has all launched.**

> **That is designing WITH a destructive process rather than against it, and it is the reason river training works survive at all in a river that can scour twenty metres below its bed.**

> **The corollary is that an apron with too little stone launches, is exhausted, and the structure then fails from below** — so the apron quantity is not a detail but the design's central calculation.

**The SPACING of groynes, since they are built in series:**

> **Typically 2 to 2.5 times the groyne's length for repelling groynes on a straight reach, closer on a curve.**

> **Too WIDE a spacing lets the current re-attack the bank between them; too CLOSE wastes money.**

> **And the FIRST groyne of a series takes the heaviest attack, so it is made the strongest — and is often supplemented by a shorter guide groyne upstream of it to take the initial impact.**

examTip.trick: **Pointing UPSTREAM = REPELLING (pushes the current away); pointing DOWNSTREAM = ATTRACTING (draws it toward the bank); perpendicular = DEFLECTING.** The naming is by EFFECT, not appearance.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) T-headed is a SHAPE classification, not an orientation** — a category error rather than a wrong orientation. Groynes are classified by orientation, permeability, submergence and shape, all independently.
examTip.mnemonic: **The LAUNCHING APRON is the key idea: loose stone at bed level that the scour itself pulls down into the hole, so the structure armours itself as it is attacked.** Too little stone and it launches, is exhausted, and the groyne fails from below.

questions.stem: The function of a CROSS REGULATOR in a canal system is:
options: To measure the discharge of the offtaking channel
To control the supply entering the offtaking channel
To scour the silt deposited in the parent channel
To head up the water level in the parent channel
questions.solution:
**To HEAD UP the water level in the PARENT channel, so that the offtaking channel can draw its full supply.**

**The two regulators and where each sits:**

| Structure | Location | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **CROSS regulator** | **ACROSS the PARENT channel, just DOWNSTREAM of the offtake** | **Raises the water level in the parent channel upstream of itself** ← |
| **HEAD regulator (distributary head regulator)** | **At the HEAD of the OFFTAKING channel** | **Controls the discharge entering the offtake** ← option (b) |

> **So the two work as a PAIR at every offtake point, and confusing them is the trap this question sets.**

> **Option (b) describes the HEAD regulator — a correct function attributed to the wrong structure.**

**Why the cross regulator is needed — the situation it addresses:**

> **A distributary offtakes from a main canal at a fixed sill level, and it needs a certain water level in the main canal to draw its design discharge.**

> **When the main canal is running at FULL SUPPLY LEVEL, that level is available and all is well.**

> **But canals frequently run BELOW full supply — in the early years of a scheme, at the end of a season, during a rotation, or when the upstream supply is short.**

> **At a reduced level the offtake cannot command its share, and the distributaries at the TAIL of the system suffer worst of all.**

> **A CROSS REGULATOR solves it: partially closing its gates PONDS the water upstream, raising the level at the offtake back to what it needs.**

> **So the parent canal's level is manipulated to serve the offtake, and the water that is not needed downstream at that moment is used to provide the head.**

**The functions of a cross regulator in full:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **HEAD UP the water level for the offtake** | **The primary purpose** ← |
| **Enable ROTATIONAL running of the system** | **Feed the upper distributaries for a period, then close and feed the lower ones** |
| **Regulate the supply passing downstream** | Control of the parent channel itself |
| **Assist in silt control** | By adjusting velocities in the reach |
| **Provide a ROAD crossing over the canal** | A common secondary benefit |
| **Allow a reach to be closed for maintenance** | Isolating a length for repair |

> **The ROTATIONAL RUNNING function deserves explanation, because it is how a canal system copes with insufficient water — and it is a policy as much as an engineering matter.**

> **When supply is less than the total demand, there are two options:**

| Option | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Supply EVERYONE at a reduced rate** | **Every farmer gets water, and nobody gets enough to grow a crop. All the water is wasted** |
| **ROTATION (warabandi): supply a GROUP at FULL rate for a period, then close and supply the next** | **Each farmer gets an adequate irrigation, less often. Crops survive** ← |

> **Rotation is decisively better, and the reason is agronomic rather than hydraulic: a crop needs a sufficient DEPTH of water at each watering to wet its root zone, and a trickle that only dampens the surface does the crop almost no good.**

> **So dividing scarce water thinly among everyone loses the whole crop, while rotating it gives each field a real irrigation.**

> **Cross regulators are what make rotation physically possible: closing one raises the level and diverts the whole supply into the distributaries above it.**

> **And that in turn explains why the equitable distribution of irrigation water is an OPERATIONAL question, decided at the gates, as much as a design question** — and why the maintenance and honest operation of regulators matters so much to a scheme's actual performance.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | The structure that does it |
|---|---|
| **(a) Measure the offtake discharge** | **A METER FLUME, a standing wave flume, or a modular OUTLET** |
| **(b) Control the offtake supply** | **The HEAD REGULATOR of the distributary** |
| **(c) Scour silt in the parent channel** | **A SILT EJECTOR, or an escape; a cross regulator can assist but that is not its function** |

> **Option (a) is worth a note because MEASUREMENT and CONTROL are genuinely different jobs, and the same structure need not do both.**

> **A MODULE (an outlet designed to pass a fixed discharge regardless of the parent channel's level — an Adjustable Proportional Module or a Gibb's module) does both at once, which is why modules are used at the smallest outlets: no gate is needed and no operator is required.**

> **That matters practically: an outlet with a gate can be tampered with, and a farmer at the head of a watercourse who opens his gate wider deprives everyone below.**

> **A rigid module cannot be adjusted, so it enforces the allocation mechanically** — which is a genuine instance of engineering design substituting for enforcement, and the reason modules are preferred over gated outlets on small distributaries.

**The related structures in a canal system, for context:**

| Structure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **CROSS regulator** | **Head up the parent channel** ← |
| **HEAD regulator** | Control the offtake |
| **CANAL FALL (drop)** | **Lower the canal bed where the ground slope exceeds the canal slope, dissipating the surplus energy** |
| **CANAL ESCAPE** | **Dispose of surplus water — a safety valve against a closed gate downstream or a sudden fall in demand** |
| **OUTLET / module** | Deliver a farmer's share |
| **METER flume** | Measure discharge |
| **Cross-drainage works** | Take natural drainage across the canal |

> **The CANAL ESCAPE is the one most often overlooked and the most important for safety: if a canal is running full and a gate downstream is closed suddenly — by an operator, a landslide or a breach — the water has nowhere to go and the canal overtops and breaches its own banks.**

> **An escape gives it a controlled outlet back to a natural drain, and a canal without escapes at suitable intervals is a hazard to itself.**

> **A breach in a canal embankment on a hillside is not merely a loss of water — it is a landslide waiting to be triggered**, which is why escapes matter especially in hill irrigation.

examTip.trick: **CROSS regulator: across the PARENT channel, downstream of the offtake, to RAISE its level. HEAD regulator: at the head of the OFFTAKE, to control its discharge.** They work as a pair.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the HEAD regulator's function** — a correct job attributed to the wrong structure. That swap is the standard trap in this pair.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cross regulators make ROTATION possible**, and rotation beats thin universal supply because a crop needs a sufficient DEPTH per watering — a trickle to everyone loses every crop. Also note the CANAL ESCAPE: without one, a closed gate downstream makes the canal breach itself.

questions.stem: A drainage system is designed for a coefficient of 6 mm per day over an area of 500 hectares. The required capacity of the drain is approximately:
questions.solution:
**0.35 m³/s.**

**Step 1 — the daily volume to be removed:**

> **Area = 500 ha = 500 × 10⁴ m² = 5 × 10⁶ m²**

> **Depth = 6 mm/day = 0.006 m/day**

> **Volume = 5 × 10⁶ × 0.006 = 30,000 m³/day**

**Step 2 — convert to a flow rate:**

> **Q = 30,000 / 86,400 = 0.347 m³/s ≈ 0.35 m³/s** ✓

**The useful shortcut, worth carrying:**

> **1 mm/day over 1 hectare = 10 m³/day = 0.1157 litres/s**

> **So Q (l/s) = 0.1157 × (mm/day) × (hectares) = 0.1157 × 6 × 500 = 347 l/s = 0.347 m³/s** ✓

> **Or more memorably: 1 mm/day over 1 km² = 1000 m³/day = 11.57 l/s.**

> **Those identities turn every drainage-coefficient problem into a single multiplication, and they eliminate the powers-of-ten errors that the options are built to catch.**

> **Note that option (b) 3.5 m³/s and option (c) 0.035 m³/s are factors of ten either side of the answer** — precisely the kind of slip that arises from converting hectares and millimetres separately.

> **And option (d) 1.16 m³/s is the answer for 20 mm/day, or equivalently the 0.1157 coefficient misapplied by a factor.**

**What the DRAINAGE COEFFICIENT is:**

> **It is the DEPTH OF WATER, per unit area, that the drainage system must remove per day.**

> **Expressing it as a depth per day rather than as a flow rate is convenient because it is directly comparable with rainfall and with irrigation depths.**

| Situation | Typical drainage coefficient |
|---|---|
| **Irrigated land, subsurface drainage of excess irrigation and seepage** | **2 - 6 mm/day** ← |
| **Humid area, removing excess rainfall** | **6 - 12 mm/day** |
| **Paddy land requiring rapid drainage before harvest** | **Higher, for a short period** |
| **Urban storm drainage** | **Not expressed this way — the rational method with an hourly intensity is used instead** |

> **The distinction in the last row is worth making: agricultural drainage removes a steady excess over DAYS, so a depth-per-day coefficient suits it.**
