> **Urban storm drainage must handle an intense burst over MINUTES, so it is designed on a rainfall INTENSITY (mm/hour) with the rational method.**

> **A 6 mm/day coefficient is 0.25 mm/hour — utterly inadequate for a storm drain, which might be designed for 50 mm/hour.**

> **So the two kinds of drainage differ by a factor of about two hundred in design rate, and applying an agricultural coefficient to an urban drain is a serious error of category.**

**Why agricultural drainage needs so much less capacity:**

> **Because agricultural land TOLERATES temporary inundation, and urban land does not.**

| | **Agricultural drainage** | **Urban storm drainage** |
|---|---|---|
| **What is being prevented** | **Waterlogging of the ROOT ZONE over days** | **Flooding of streets and property within minutes** |
| **Acceptable temporary storage** | **Ponding on fields is tolerable for a day or two** ← | Essentially none |
| **Design rate** | **mm per DAY** | **mm per HOUR** |
| **Consequence of exceedance** | Reduced yield | Property damage, danger to life |

> **So the vast difference in design capacity reflects a difference in TOLERANCE, not in the rainfall.** A field can hold the water while the drain catches up; a street cannot.

> **That is why agricultural drainage systems are designed for a modest steady rate and accept that an extreme storm will inundate the land briefly** — an entirely rational choice, since sizing farm drains for a cloudburst would cost more than the crops are worth.

**Subsurface against surface drainage, since both remove the same water:**

| | **SURFACE drainage** | **SUBSURFACE (tile) drainage** |
|---|---|---|
| **Removes** | **PONDED water from the surface** | **Water from within the SOIL PROFILE; LOWERS THE WATER TABLE** ← |
| **Suits** | Flat land with poor infiltration; heavy clay | **Permeable soil with a high water table** |
| **Addresses waterlogging?** | **Only partly — the water table remains high** | **YES — it is the definitive answer** |
| **Addresses SALINITY?** | **NO** | **YES — it permits leaching to carry salts away** |
| **Cost** | Lower | **Much higher** |
| **Interference with farming** | **Open ditches occupy land and obstruct machinery** | **None once installed — buried** |

> **The SALINITY row is the decisive one and connects drainage to the whole waterlogging problem:**

> **Salts can only be removed from a root zone by LEACHING — passing water down through it and carrying the salts away.**

> **But leaching water must have somewhere to GO. If the water table is already at the root zone, applied leaching water simply cannot drain, and the salts remain.**

> **So SUBSURFACE DRAINAGE IS A PRECONDITION FOR LEACHING, and therefore for reclaiming or protecting saline land.**

> **Which means the two great problems of irrigated agriculture — waterlogging and salinity — have a single engineering answer, and it is the expensive one.**

> **That is the honest position: surface drains and better water management help, and only subsurface drainage or vertical drainage by tube wells actually lowers a water table** — and irrigation projects that omitted drainage from their original scope have had to retrofit it at far greater cost, or lose the land.

> **It is worth stating as a general lesson in project scoping: drainage is the component most often deferred and the one whose absence most reliably destroys the benefit of the rest.**

examTip.trick: **1 mm/day over 1 ha = 0.1157 l/s.** So Q = 0.1157 × 6 × 500 = 347 l/s = **0.35 m³/s** — one multiplication, no unit conversions.
examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (c) are factors of TEN either side** — exactly the slip that arises from converting hectares and millimetres separately. Use the identity instead.
examTip.mnemonic: **Agricultural drainage is designed in mm/DAY, urban storm drainage in mm/HOUR — a factor of about 200** — because a field tolerates a day's ponding and a street does not. And SUBSURFACE drainage is a PRECONDITION for leaching, hence for controlling salinity.

questions.stem: The principal benefit of LINING an irrigation canal is that:
options: It increases the available bed slope of the canal
It reduces seepage losses, prevents waterlogging, and permits a higher velocity in a smaller section
It eliminates the need for cross-drainage works along the canal
It increases the silt-carrying capacity so that desilting becomes unnecessary
questions.solution:
**It reduces seepage losses, prevents waterlogging, and permits a higher velocity in a smaller section.**

**The benefits of lining, in order of importance:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **REDUCES SEEPAGE loss** | **The primary benefit — seepage from unlined canals commonly amounts to 25-50 per cent of the water diverted** ← |
| **PREVENTS WATERLOGGING and salinity in the command** | **The direct consequence of stopping the seepage that raises the water table** |
| **Permits a HIGHER VELOCITY** | **A lined surface cannot scour, so the non-scouring limit no longer applies** |
| **Hence a SMALLER section for the same discharge** | Less excavation, less land acquired |
| **Prevents WEED growth** | Weeds increase roughness and consume water |
| **Reduces MAINTENANCE** | No annual desilting or bank repair to the same extent |
| **Prevents BREACHES and bank erosion** | A lined bank is far more stable |
| **Prevents the canal SILTING or SCOURING out of shape** | Regime considerations no longer apply |

> **The first two are the same benefit seen from two sides — the water saved, and the harm the lost water would have done.**

> **That double benefit is what makes lining economically attractive: it both delivers more water to the crop AND avoids the cost of the waterlogging that the seepage would have caused.**

**Why the HIGHER VELOCITY matters more than it appears:**

> **An unlined alluvial canal must run within a narrow velocity band: fast enough to avoid silting, slow enough to avoid scouring its own bed.**

> **A LINED canal has no such upper limit — the lining cannot be scoured — so it can run at 2 m/s or more where an earth channel is limited to perhaps 0.8 m/s.**

> **The consequence follows from continuity: a canal carrying the same discharge at two and a half times the velocity needs only 40 per cent of the cross-sectional area.**

| | **Unlined** | **Lined** |
|---|---|---|
| **Permissible velocity** | **~0.8 m/s** | **~2.0 m/s** |
| **Area for 10 m³/s** | **12.5 m²** | **5.0 m²** ← |
| **Manning's n** | **0.025** | **0.014** |
| **Excavation** | Large | **Much less** |
| **Land acquired** | Large | Much less |

> **So a lined canal is a much smaller structure, and the saving in excavation and land partly offsets the cost of the lining itself.**

> **The lower roughness compounds the advantage: with n falling from 0.025 to 0.014, the same section and slope carry about 80 per cent more water.**

> **Which means the choice is not simply "the same canal with a lining added" but a fundamentally different and smaller design** — and comparing a lined canal's cost against an unlined one of the same dimensions understates its economy considerably.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **(a) Increases the available bed slope** | **The slope is fixed by the TOPOGRAPHY and the need to command the land — lining does not change the ground. Lining lets a canal work at a given slope more efficiently; it does not create slope** |
| **(c) Eliminates cross-drainage works** | **FALSE. Natural drainage still has to cross the canal, lined or not. Cross-drainage works are determined by the alignment and the drainage pattern, not by the lining** ← |
| **(d) Increases silt-carrying capacity so desilting is unnecessary** | **Partly true and misleadingly stated: the higher velocity does carry more silt through, but a lined canal still needs desilting where silt enters, and it does not remove the need for silt exclusion at the headworks** |

> **Option (c) is the one worth being firm about, because it confuses two independent things.**

> **A canal crossing a country's natural drainage lines must take that drainage over, under or through it, and an impervious lining is irrelevant to that requirement.**

> **If anything a lined canal makes the crossing MORE necessary, since an unlined canal can absorb a small drain's flow into its own supply while a lined one cannot.**

**The lining materials and their trade-offs:**

| Lining | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cast in-situ CONCRETE** | **Most durable; most expensive; needs joints for movement** |
| **Precast concrete slabs / tiles** | Quicker; joints are the weakness |
| **BRICK lining, single or double** | **Common in South Asia; cheap where bricks are local; higher roughness** |
| **Stone masonry / dry stone with mortar pointing** | Suits hill canals where stone is at hand |
| **Boulder lining, gabion** | For steep hill sections |
| **COMPACTED EARTH / clay lining** | **Cheapest; reduces seepage substantially without eliminating it; can be eroded** |
| **Shotcrete** | Repairs and thin sections |
| **Plastic / geomembrane, buried under earth cover** | **Excellent impermeability; must be protected from puncture and sunlight** |

> **The choice is usually governed by LOCAL MATERIAL AVAILABILITY and LABOUR rather than by technical performance** — which is why brick lining predominates in the plains and stone in the hills.

**The critical failure mode of a lining, since it explains the details:**

> **A canal lining's most dangerous condition is when the canal is EMPTY and the surrounding water table is HIGH.**

> **The lining is then subject to UPLIFT from behind, with no water inside to hold it down — and a concrete or brick lining has almost no weight or strength to resist it.**

> **The lining can be lifted, cracked and floated off its bed, and a canal that has been lined for years can be destroyed in one closure period.**

> **The remedies are specific and worth knowing:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **PRESSURE RELIEF VALVES or weep holes through the lining** | **Let the groundwater in rather than resisting it** ← |
| **A drainage layer and longitudinal drains behind the lining** | Relieve the pressure before it builds |
| **Controlled, SLOW dewatering when the canal is closed** | Never empty a canal rapidly |
| **A thicker, heavier lining in high-water-table reaches** | Weight to resist uplift |

> **The relief valve is the elegant answer, and it embodies a general principle worth extracting: it is usually cheaper and safer to RELIEVE a water pressure than to RESIST it.**

> **The same principle appears in retaining wall drainage, basement drainage, dam gallery drains and the weep holes in a bridge abutment** — in each case a small deliberate leak removes a load that would otherwise require a much heavier structure.

examTip.trick: **Lining reduces SEEPAGE (25-50 % of diverted water), prevents WATERLOGGING, and removes the non-scouring velocity limit — hence a smaller, smoother section.**
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is false: natural drainage must still cross the canal, so CROSS-DRAINAGE WORKS are unaffected by lining.** If anything a lined canal makes them more necessary, since it cannot absorb a small drain's flow.
examTip.mnemonic: **A lined canal is a DIFFERENT, SMALLER canal** — 2.0 m/s against 0.8, n = 0.014 against 0.025, so about 40 % of the area for the same flow. And its worst condition is EMPTY with a HIGH water table: relieve the uplift with weep holes rather than resisting it.

questions.stem: The essential distinction between a WEIR and a BARRAGE is that:
options: A weir has gates whereas a barrage has none
A weir is founded on a permeable bed whereas a barrage is founded on rock
In a barrage the water level is controlled mainly by gates over a low crest, whereas in a weir it is raised mainly by a solid raised crest
A barrage is used only for hydropower and a weir only for irrigation
questions.solution:
**In a BARRAGE the level is controlled mainly by GATES over a LOW crest; in a WEIR it is raised mainly by a solid RAISED CREST.**

**The comparison in full:**

| | **WEIR** | **BARRAGE** |
|---|---|---|
| **How the level is raised** | **A solid RAISED CREST; gates, if any, are a small proportion of the height** | **Mainly by GATES over a LOW crest** ← |
| **Crest level** | **HIGH** | **LOW, at or near the river bed** |
| **Gates** | **Few or none (shutters at most)** | **Full-width gates, the principal control** |
| **Control over the upstream level** | **POOR — the level is fixed by the crest** | **EXCELLENT — the level can be set at will** |
| **Afflux (rise in flood level upstream)** | **HIGH** | **LOW — gates are opened and the flood passes freely** |
| **Silt disposal** | **Poor — silt accumulates upstream** | **Good — gates can be opened to sluice silt through** |
| **Cost** | **LOWER** | **HIGHER** |
| **Operation and maintenance** | **Minimal — nothing to operate** | **Continuous — gates must be worked, and skilled staff kept** |
| **Road/rail crossing** | Not usually | **Commonly incorporated on the gate piers** |
| **Suits** | **Small schemes; sites where afflux is unimportant; where staff are unavailable** | **Large schemes; where upstream land must be protected from afflux** |

> **Note that option (a) INVERTS the answer — it is the BARRAGE that has the gates.**

> **And option (b) is simply false: both weirs and barrages are commonly founded on PERMEABLE alluvial beds, which is precisely why seepage, uplift and exit gradient analysis (Bligh, Lane, Khosla) exists at all.** A structure on rock poses none of those problems.

> **Option (d) is false in both halves: barrages serve irrigation (the great majority of them do) and weirs serve hydropower diversion routinely.**

**Why the AFFLUX difference is the decisive practical advantage of a barrage:**

> **AFFLUX is the rise in the upstream flood level caused by the obstruction.**

> **A WEIR, with its high solid crest, obstructs the flood permanently — so the flood level upstream is raised by a metre or more, and that raised level extends for kilometres upstream.**

> **The consequences are substantial and expensive:**

| Consequence of afflux | Note |
|---|---|
| **Land upstream is FLOODED or waterlogged** | Compensation, or loss of cultivation |
| **MARGINAL BUNDS must be built for kilometres upstream** | **Often a large part of the project cost** ← |
| **Bridges, roads and buildings upstream may need raising** | |
| **The river's silting regime upstream is altered** | Aggradation extends upstream over years |

> **A BARRAGE, with its low crest, obstructs the flood hardly at all once its gates are raised: the flood passes through at nearly the natural level, and the afflux is small.**

> **So the barrage's higher capital cost buys the avoidance of marginal bunds, land acquisition and upstream flooding — and on a large river in a populated plain that saving frequently exceeds the extra cost of the gates.**

> **Which is why nearly all modern large diversion works in the Indo-Gangetic plain are barrages rather than weirs**, and why weirs survive for small schemes and in gorges where there is nothing upstream to flood.

**The operational cost that runs the other way — and it is a genuine consideration:**

> **A barrage must be OPERATED. Its gates have to be raised as a flood arrives and lowered as it passes, and that requires staff, power, hoists, communications and flood forecasting.**

> **A gate that fails to open in time converts the barrage into a weir at the worst possible moment — obstructing the flood with its full structure, and producing exactly the afflux it was built to avoid.**

> **And a gate that fails to close leaves the canal without supply.**

> **So a barrage transfers risk from DESIGN to OPERATION**, and that trade is only sound where the operating organisation is capable and adequately funded.

> **In a remote location with no reliable staff, a WEIR that needs no operation may be the better engineering answer despite its afflux** — which is a real judgement and not merely a cost comparison.

> **It is the same trade that appears between a surge tank (no moving parts) and a pressure relief valve (a moving part that must work when needed), and the same conclusion applies: prefer the passive solution where the consequences of non-operation are severe.**

**The components common to both, since they share most of their anatomy:**

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Weir or barrage proper** | Raises and controls the level |
| **UNDER-SLUICES** | **Scour the pocket; pass low flow** |
| **DIVIDE WALL** | Separates the under-sluice pocket from the main structure |
| **CANAL HEAD REGULATOR** | Controls the canal's supply |
| **SILT EXCLUDER** | Keeps bed load out of the canal |
| **FISH LADDER** | Passage for migratory fish |
| **Impervious floor, cut-offs, launching aprons** | **Control seepage, uplift and scour** |
| **Guide banks and marginal bunds** | Confine and guide the river |
| **Stilling basin / cistern** | Dissipate the energy of the falling water |

> **The IMPERVIOUS FLOOR and CUT-OFFS are the part of the design that occupies most of the analysis, and for a reason: a structure founded on deep alluvium is at risk from seepage beneath it in two distinct ways.**

| Failure mode | Mechanism | Design check |
|---|---|---|
| **PIPING (undermining)** | **Seepage at the downstream exit lifts the soil, progressively eroding a channel back beneath the floor until the structure collapses** | **EXIT GRADIENT ≤ i_c/F, with F = 4 to 5** |
| **UPLIFT (floor rupture)** | **Seepage pressure beneath the floor exceeds its weight, and the floor cracks upward** | **Floor thickness ≥ (residual head)/(G−1)** |

> **Both are computed from the same seepage analysis — Khosla's method in modern practice — and both are why the FLOOR of a weir is so much thicker than its structural loading would require.**

> **A weir floor 1.5 m thick is not carrying a load of that magnitude; it is holding itself down against the water pressure underneath.** That is worth understanding, because it explains a thickness that otherwise looks arbitrary.

examTip.trick: **BARRAGE: LOW crest, GATES do the work, LOW afflux, higher cost. WEIR: HIGH solid crest, few or no gates, HIGH afflux, cheaper.**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) INVERTS it — the barrage has the gates.** And option (b) is false: both are commonly founded on permeable alluvium, which is exactly why seepage, uplift and exit-gradient analysis exists.
examTip.mnemonic: **A barrage's real advantage is low AFFLUX** — it avoids marginal bunds and upstream flooding, often worth more than the gates cost. But it transfers risk from DESIGN to OPERATION: a gate that fails to open makes it a weir at the worst moment.

questions.stem: Subsurface (tile) drains for irrigated agricultural land are generally laid at a depth of:
questions.solution:
**1.5 to 2.5 m below the ground surface.**

**Why that depth and not shallower:**

> **The purpose of a subsurface drain is to hold the WATER TABLE below the crop's root zone — and the water table between drains is not flat.**

> **It rises in a curve between adjacent drains, reaching its highest point midway between them.**

> **So the drain must be deep enough that even the MIDPOINT of that curve stays below the root zone.**

| Requirement | Depth needed |
|---|---|
| **Root zone depth for most field crops** | **0.6 - 1.0 m** |
| **Plus the height the water table rises MIDWAY between drains** | **0.3 - 0.8 m** |
| **Plus a margin for capillary rise above the water table** | **0.3 - 0.5 m** ← in fine soils this is substantial |
| **TOTAL drain depth** | **1.5 - 2.5 m** ✓ |

> **Options (a) and (b) are too shallow to hold the water table clear of the root zone at the midpoint, and option (c) is deeper than either necessary or economic to excavate.**

**The trade-off between DEPTH and SPACING — the central design relation:**

> **A given drainage duty can be achieved by DEEP drains widely spaced, or SHALLOW drains closely spaced.**

| | **Deep, wide spacing** | **Shallow, close spacing** |
|---|---|---|
| **Excavation per metre of drain** | **High** | Low |
| **Total LENGTH of drain per hectare** | **LOW** | **HIGH** |
| **Total cost** | **Usually LOWER** ← | Usually higher |
| **Constraint** | **Trench depth limited by machinery, stability and the depth to an impermeable layer** | — |

> **DEEPER AND WIDER IS ALMOST ALWAYS CHEAPER, because the cost of a drainage system is dominated by the LENGTH of pipe and trench rather than by the depth of each metre.**

> **So the design practice is to go as DEEP as the site allows and then compute the spacing that follows.**

> **The limits on depth are practical: the reach of the trenching machine, the stability of the trench in the soil, the depth to a barrier layer, and the outfall level available.**

> **The OUTFALL is frequently the binding constraint and is worth naming: a drain can be no deeper than its outfall permits, since it must discharge by gravity into a collector, a ditch or a river.**

> **On flat land near a river whose bed is high, that may limit the whole system to less depth than the agronomy wants — in which case pumped drainage becomes necessary, at a permanent operating cost.**

**The spacing formulae, since depth and spacing are computed together:**

> **HOOGHOUDT'S equation, for steady-state drainage:**

> **S² = (8 K d h + 4 K h²) / q**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **S** | **Drain SPACING** |
| **K** | **Hydraulic conductivity of the soil** |
| **d** | **Equivalent depth from the drain to the impermeable layer** |
| **h** | **Height of the water table MIDWAY between drains, above the drain level** ← |
| **q** | **Drainage coefficient (the flux to be removed)** |

> **Note that S appears SQUARED, so the spacing depends on the SQUARE ROOT of the permeability:**

| Soil | K (m/day) | Typical spacing |
|---|---|---|
| **Clay** | **0.02 - 0.1** | **10 - 20 m** |
| **Clay loam** | **0.1 - 0.5** | **20 - 35 m** |
| **Loam** | **0.5 - 2.0** | **35 - 60 m** |
| **Sandy loam** | **2 - 5** | **60 - 100 m** |
| **Sand** | **5 - 20** | **100 m and more** |

> **So a clay soil needs drains four to ten times closer than a sandy one, and the cost of drainage per hectare varies accordingly by nearly an order of magnitude.**

> **Which explains a hard practical fact: the soils that MOST need drainage — heavy clays with a high water table — are the MOST EXPENSIVE to drain, because their low permeability demands the closest spacing.**

> **The economics therefore work against the places that need it most, and that is a real reason why drainage is under-provided rather than merely an oversight.**

**The components of a subsurface drainage system:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **FIELD (lateral) drains** | **Perforated pipe, 80-150 mm, at the computed spacing** |
| **ENVELOPE / filter material around the pipe** | **Gravel or synthetic — prevents fine soil entering and clogging the perforations** ← essential in fine soils |
| **COLLECTOR drains** | Larger pipes gathering the laterals |
| **Main drain / outfall** | To a ditch, river or pump sump |
| **Manholes and inspection chambers** | For cleaning and monitoring |
| **Outfall structure with a flap valve** | **Prevents backflow from the receiving water** |

> **The ENVELOPE deserves emphasis because its omission is the commonest cause of subsurface drainage failure:**

> **Water entering a perforated pipe carries fine soil with it. Without a filter, that soil enters the pipe, settles, and progressively blocks it.**

> **The system then fails invisibly — buried, with no external sign — and the land waterlogs again while the drains are assumed to be working.**

> **So the envelope is not an accessory but part of the drain, and specifying its grading correctly against the soil's grading is the same problem as designing a filter behind a dam or a retaining wall.**

> **The filter criteria are the familiar ones: the filter must be coarse enough to drain freely and fine enough to retain the soil it protects** — typically D₁₅(filter) ≤ 4 to 5 × D₈₅(soil) for retention, and D₁₅(filter) ≥ 4 × D₁₅(soil) for permeability.

> **Which is a satisfying instance of one piece of soil mechanics serving three quite different structures**, and worth recognising as such: a tile drain envelope, a dam's chimney filter and a retaining wall's drainage layer are the same design problem.

**The alternative — VERTICAL drainage — since it competes directly:**

> **Instead of horizontal pipes, TUBE WELLS can pump the groundwater down.**

| | **Horizontal (tile) drainage** | **VERTICAL (tube well) drainage** |
|---|---|---|
| **Capital cost** | **High — the whole area must be piped** | **Lower — a few wells serve a large area** |
| **Operating cost** | **NIL — gravity** ← | **Continuous PUMPING energy** |
| **Suits** | Any soil; shallow aquifers | **A permeable aquifer of good yield** |
| **The water pumped** | Discharged away | **CAN BE USED FOR IRRIGATION if fresh** ← |
| **Reliability** | Passive, permanent | Depends on power and maintenance |

> **The fourth row is what makes vertical drainage attractive where it is feasible: the water pumped to lower the table is itself a resource, so the same pumping both drains the land and irrigates it.**

> **That is CONJUNCTIVE USE, and it turns the drainage problem into part of the water supply** — the most elegant available answer where the groundwater is fresh and the aquifer will yield.

> **Where the groundwater is SALINE, however, the pumped water cannot be used and must be disposed of — which is a serious problem in itself, since a saline drainage effluent cannot simply be discharged to a river.** In that situation horizontal drainage with a proper outfall, or evaporation ponds, becomes unavoidable.

examTip.trick: **1.5 to 2.5 m** — deep enough that the water table, which arches UPWARD midway between drains, still clears the root zone with a margin for capillary rise.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (b) are too shallow for the MIDPOINT of the water table curve**, and (c) is uneconomic. The depth must cover root zone + midpoint rise + capillary margin.
examTip.mnemonic: **DEEPER AND WIDER is almost always CHEAPER**, since cost follows the LENGTH of trench, not its depth — so go as deep as the OUTFALL allows and compute the spacing. And never omit the ENVELOPE filter: without it the drain silts up invisibly.

questions.stem: The ECONOMICALLY FEASIBLE hydropower potential of Nepal is generally quoted as:
questions.solution:
**About 42,000 MW.**

**The three figures that must be distinguished:**

| Potential | Magnitude | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **THEORETICAL (gross)** | **~83,000 MW** | **The total energy in the falling water of all rivers, ignoring all practical constraints** ← option (b) |
| **TECHNICALLY feasible** | **~45,000 - 46,000 MW** | What can be developed with available technology |
| **ECONOMICALLY feasible** | **~42,000 - 43,000 MW** | **Technically feasible AND economically viable** ← ✓ |
| **Currently developed** | **A few thousand MW** | The actual installed capacity |

> **So option (b) 83,000 MW is the THEORETICAL figure** — the most widely quoted and the most widely misquoted, since it is frequently reported as though it were the developable potential.

> **The distinction matters because the theoretical figure counts every river's every metre of fall, including reaches in inaccessible gorges, inside protected areas, and at flows too small or too variable to be worth developing.**

> **Being precise about which figure is meant is part of professional competence in this field, and confusing them overstates the country's realisable resource by a factor of two.**

**Why Nepal's potential is so large — the two multiplied factors:**

> **Power is proportional to Q × H, and Nepal has an unusual abundance of BOTH.**

| Factor | Nepal's position |
|---|---|
| **HEAD (H)** | **The greatest altitude range on earth over a short horizontal distance — from about 60 m to 8,848 m within 200 km** ← |
| **DISCHARGE (Q)** | **High monsoon rainfall plus SNOW AND GLACIER MELT, giving perennial flow in the major rivers** |
| **River gradient** | Extremely steep, so head is gained over short conveyance lengths |
| **Number of rivers** | Some 6,000 rivers and streams, with four major systems |

> **The SNOW AND GLACIER contribution deserves a note because it is what makes the major rivers perennial: the Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali systems draw from snowfields that release water in the dry season, when rainfall has ceased.**

> **A river fed only by rainfall would run dry in spring; a snow-fed river carries its minimum flow precisely when the demand for power is highest.**

> **That is why the trans-Himalayan rivers are far more valuable per unit of catchment than the purely rain-fed southern rivers, and why the four major systems dominate the country's potential.**

**The structural problem, stated honestly — the reason the potential is not simply an asset:**

| Constraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **SEASONALITY** | **Monsoon flows are 5-10 times dry-season flows, so a run-of-river plant's dry-season output is a fraction of its capacity** ← |
| **SEDIMENT** | **Himalayan sediment loads are among the world's highest, abrading turbines and filling reservoirs** |
| **SEISMICITY** | Major structures in a highly active zone |
| **GLACIAL LAKE OUTBURST FLOODS (GLOFs)** | A design flood that is not hydrological in origin |
| **Access and transmission** | The best sites are the least accessible |
| **Market** | **The domestic market is small relative to the resource, so large development depends on export** |

> **The SEASONALITY constraint is the one that shapes everything, and it explains why the installed-capacity figure understates and overstates the country's position at once:**

> **Nepal has a monsoon SURPLUS that must be exported or spilled, and a dry-season DEFICIT that must be imported — from the same installed capacity.**

> **Only STORAGE projects can move water across seasons, and they are the hardest to build: large reservoirs, inundation of valleys, resettlement, and payback periods measured in decades.**

> **So the difference between the 42,000 MW figure and what is actually developed is not primarily a matter of engineering capability. It is a matter of storage, capital, transmission and market.**

> **A candidate who can state that clearly understands the sector better than one who can recite the number.**

**The four major river systems, since questions ask by basin:**

| System | Note |
|---|---|
| **KOSHI (Sapta Koshi)** | **The largest catchment; seven major tributaries; the highest potential** |
| **GANDAKI (Narayani)** | Seven tributaries; central Nepal |
| **KARNALI** | **Western Nepal; the Karnali multipurpose project is among the largest storage prospects** |
| **MAHAKALI** | Westernmost; forms the border |
| **Southern (Churia/Terai) rivers** | **Rain-fed only, so seasonal and unsuitable for firm power** |

> **The distinction between the four snow-fed major systems and the rain-fed southern rivers is the practically useful one: the first are perennial and support firm power, the second are seasonal and support little.**

**The capacity classification used in Nepal, since it governs licensing:**

| Class | Capacity |
|---|---|
| **MICRO** | **Below 100 kW** |
| **MINI** | **100 kW to 1 MW** |
| **SMALL** | **1 to 25 MW** |
| **MEDIUM** | **25 to 100 MW** |
| **LARGE** | **Above 100 MW** |

> **The bands matter administratively as well as technically: the survey and generation license requirements, the royalty regime and the environmental assessment tier all step at these boundaries.**

> **A scheme below 1 MW faces a materially lighter approval process than one above it** — which is a genuine incentive shaping the size at which small schemes are proposed, and worth being aware of as a matter of professional practice rather than only of examination.

examTip.trick: **~83,000 MW theoretical, ~45,000 MW technically feasible, ~42,000 MW ECONOMICALLY feasible.** The stem asks for the third.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 83,000 MW is the THEORETICAL figure** — the most quoted and most misquoted, since it counts inaccessible gorges and protected areas. Confusing them overstates the realisable resource twofold.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepal has both H (the world's greatest altitude range over 200 km) and Q (monsoon plus SNOWMELT, which keeps the major rivers perennial).** The constraint is SEASONALITY: a monsoon surplus and a dry-season deficit from the same capacity, fixable only by STORAGE.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant operates under a net head of 90 m with a design discharge of 12 m³/s. Taking the overall efficiency as 85 per cent, the power output is:
questions.solution:
**9.0 MW.**

**The power equation:**

> **P = ρ g Q H η**

> **= 1000 × 9.81 × 12 × 90 × 0.85 watts**

**Working it in stages:**

> **9.81 × 12 = 117.72**

> **117.72 × 90 = 10,594.8**

> **So ρgQH = 10,594.8 kW = 10.59 MW — the THEORETICAL (water) power.**

> **× 0.85 = 9005.6 kW ≈ 9.0 MW** ✓

> **Note that option (a) 10.6 MW is exactly the theoretical power with the EFFICIENCY OMITTED** — the intended trap, and a useful intermediate to recognise.

**The shortcut worth memorising:**

> **P (kW) ≈ 9.81 × Q × H × η**, with Q in m³/s and H in metres.

> **And for a quick estimate, **P (kW) ≈ 8 Q H** at a typical 82 per cent efficiency, or **P ≈ 7 Q H** for a small scheme at 70 per cent.**

> **Check: 8 × 12 × 90 = 8640 kW — within 4 per cent of the exact answer.**

> **That approximation is genuinely useful in the field, and it lets a scheme's order of magnitude be settled before any calculation.**

**What the OVERALL efficiency comprises — the chain of losses:**

| Component | Typical efficiency |
|---|---|
| **TURBINE** | **88 - 93 per cent (a large modern machine)** |
| **GENERATOR** | **95 - 98 per cent** |
| **Speed increaser / gearbox, if fitted** | **96 - 98 per cent** |
| **Transformer** | **98 - 99 per cent** |
| **OVERALL (product)** | **80 - 90 per cent** ← 0.85 here |

> **The efficiencies MULTIPLY, so 0.90 × 0.96 × 0.98 = 0.847 ≈ 0.85** — consistent with the stem.

> **Note that the TURBINE is the least efficient link and therefore the one where improvement is worth most.** A generator is already near its theoretical limit; a turbine's efficiency depends strongly on how close it runs to its design point.

**The distinction between GROSS and NET head, which the stem settles explicitly:**

| Head | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS head** | **The difference in elevation between the intake water level and the tailwater level** |
| **NET (effective) head** | **Gross head MINUS all the hydraulic losses in the conveyance system** ← used in the power equation |

> **The losses deducted:**

| Loss | Note |
|---|---|
| **Trash rack loss** | Small but real, and grows as the rack blocks |
| **Intake and entry loss** | |
| **Headrace channel or tunnel friction** | **Often the largest single loss in a long conveyance** ← |
| **Settling basin losses** | |
| **Penstock friction and bend losses** | |
| **Valve losses** | |

> **The NET head is what generates power, and it is worth stating why: the water arriving at the turbine has already spent part of its potential energy on friction, and that part is unrecoverable.**

> **Typical practice is to design the conveyance so that total losses do not exceed about 5 to 10 per cent of the gross head.**

> **The choice is an economic optimum: a LARGER conveyance costs more capital and loses less head; a smaller one is cheaper and generates less for the whole life of the plant.**

> **Since a plant runs for fifty years or more, quite a large capital premium is justified to recover a few per cent of head** — which is why penstocks and headrace tunnels are usually larger than a first estimate suggests.

**The ANNUAL ENERGY, which is what the plant is actually paid for:**

> **Power is the instantaneous rate; ENERGY is what is sold.**

> **E = P × 8760 × (plant factor)**

> **For this 9 MW plant at a plant factor of 0.55 — typical for a run-of-river scheme in Nepal:**

> **E = 9 × 8760 × 0.55 = 43,362 MWh = 43.4 GWh per year**

> **The distinction between CAPACITY and ENERGY is fundamental to the sector and worth stating plainly: a plant is BUILT for its capacity and PAID for its energy, and the two are related only through the plant factor, which depends on the hydrology.**

> **Two 9 MW plants on different rivers may generate 43 GWh and 65 GWh respectively, and the second is a much better investment for the same nameplate.**

> **Which is why the FLOW DURATION CURVE, not the design discharge, determines a scheme's value.**

**A note on the DESIGN DISCHARGE, since the stem gives it:**

> **Choosing the design discharge for a run-of-river plant is the central economic decision in its planning, and it is a genuine optimisation:**

| Design discharge chosen | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **A HIGH flow (say Q₂₀ — exceeded 20 % of the time)** | **Large capacity, but the plant runs at part load most of the year; low plant factor; much spillage of capacity** |
| **A LOW flow (say Q₈₀)** | **Small capacity, running at full output nearly all year; high plant factor; much monsoon water spilled unused** |
| **Typically Q₃₀ to Q₄₅** | **The usual optimum for a Nepali run-of-river scheme** ← |

> **The optimum maximises the NET PRESENT VALUE, not the energy: beyond a point, additional capacity earns too little additional energy to pay for itself.**

> **So the design discharge is chosen by computing the energy and the cost for a range of candidate flows and selecting the best return** — which is why a feasibility study contains a table of alternatives rather than a single calculation.

examTip.trap: **Option (a) 10.6 MW is the THEORETICAL power with the efficiency omitted** — a useful intermediate to recognise, and the intended error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use the NET head — gross minus all conveyance losses, designed to about 5-10 %.** And a plant is BUILT for capacity but PAID for energy: E = P × 8760 × plant factor, so the FLOW DURATION CURVE, not the design discharge, decides a scheme's value.

questions.stem: The crest profile of an OGEE spillway is shaped so that:
options: The discharge coefficient is minimised to limit the flood outflow
The flow springs clear of the crest, forming an air pocket beneath the nappe
It follows the lower nappe of a freely falling jet, so the pressure on the crest is nearly atmospheric
The velocity of flow over the crest is constant along its whole length
questions.solution:
**It follows the LOWER NAPPE of a freely falling jet, so that the pressure on the crest is nearly ATMOSPHERIC.**

**The idea, which is elegant and worth understanding fully:**

> **Consider water discharging over a SHARP-CRESTED weir. The jet leaves the crest and falls freely, and its underside — the LOWER NAPPE — traces a particular curve.**

> **Along that curve the water is in free fall: it touches nothing, so the pressure on its underside is ATMOSPHERIC everywhere.**

> **Now build a solid concrete surface exactly along that curve.**

> **The water follows the same path it would have followed anyway, so it exerts NO pressure on the surface beyond atmospheric — and the surface exerts none on it.**

> **The result is a crest over which the water flows as though the concrete were not there.**

**Why atmospheric pressure on the crest is the objective:**

| Pressure condition | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **NEGATIVE (sub-atmospheric)** | **CAVITATION — the water can boil at ambient temperature, and the collapsing vapour cavities PIT AND ERODE the concrete** ← the danger |
| **Positive** | **The crest is pushed on, and the discharge coefficient falls — the spillway passes less water for the same head** |
| **ATMOSPHERIC** | **Neither: no cavitation risk, and the MAXIMUM discharge coefficient** ✓ |

> **So the ogee profile achieves two things at once, and that is why it is universal:**

> **It gives the HIGHEST possible discharge coefficient — a spillway passes more flood for a given crest length and head than any other shape.**

> **And it avoids the NEGATIVE pressures that would destroy the concrete.**

> **Which is a rare instance in engineering of the efficient shape and the safe shape being the same shape** — and the reason no better spillway profile has been found in a century.

**Why option (a) is exactly backwards:**

> **The ogee profile MAXIMISES the discharge coefficient, it does not minimise it.**

> **Typical values: C ≈ 2.2 (SI) for an ogee crest, against about 1.7 for a broad-crested weir and 1.5-1.6 for a flat-topped one.**

> **A spillway's whole purpose is to pass the design flood safely, so a high coefficient is the objective: it means a SHORTER, CHEAPER spillway, or a LOWER flood level upstream, or both.**

> **Limiting the outflow is never the aim — a dam that cannot pass its flood overtops and, if it is an embankment dam, fails.**

**Why option (b) is a real phenomenon and the wrong answer:**

> **The AIR POCKET beneath a nappe is what occurs at a SHARP-CRESTED weir, and it is genuinely important — for a MEASURING weir, the nappe must be VENTILATED so that the air pocket stays at atmospheric pressure.**

> **If it is not ventilated, the falling water entrains the air, the pocket's pressure DROPS, the nappe is drawn inward, and the discharge INCREASES above the calibrated value.**

> **So a measuring weir gives a wrong reading if its nappe is not aerated — a real and common source of error.**

> **But an OGEE crest is designed for the water to CLING to it, not to spring clear of it.** The whole point is that the concrete occupies the space where the air pocket would be.

**The DESIGN HEAD and what happens away from it — an important qualification:**

> **The ogee profile is derived for ONE particular head, the DESIGN HEAD H_d.**

| Operating head | Pressure on the crest |
|---|---|
| **Equal to H_d** | **ATMOSPHERIC — the design condition** ✓ |
| **LESS than H_d** | **POSITIVE — the nappe is pressed onto the crest; safe, but a lower coefficient** |
| **GREATER than H_d** | **NEGATIVE — the nappe tends to spring away, sub-atmospheric pressure develops, and CAVITATION becomes possible** ← |

> **So a spillway operating ABOVE its design head is at risk, and that governs how the design head is chosen.**

> **Common practice is to set the design head at about 75 to 80 per cent of the maximum head, deliberately accepting slight negative pressures at the extreme flood** — a rare event of short duration — in exchange for a better coefficient through the whole normal range.

> **That is a considered trade, not an oversight: cavitation damage requires sustained exposure, and a few hours at the probable maximum flood does far less harm than years of reduced discharge capacity would cost.**

**The standard profile equation, since it is quoted:**

> **The downstream face follows:  x^{1.85} = 2 H_d^{0.85} y**

> **(the US Bureau of Reclamation / WES form, with the origin at the crest apex, x horizontal and y downward)**

> **And the upstream quadrant is made up of compound circular arcs.**

> **The exponent 1.85 rather than a simple parabola's 2 is what distinguishes the real nappe shape from an approximation** — and it is an empirically fitted value rather than a derived one.

**The other spillway types, for context:**

| Spillway | Note |
|---|---|
| **OGEE (overflow)** | **The standard for concrete dams; highest coefficient** ← |
| **CHUTE (trough)** | **An open channel down the flank — common for EMBANKMENT dams, which cannot be overtopped** |
| **SIDE CHANNEL** | Crest parallel to a channel that carries the flow away; suits narrow gorges |
| **SHAFT (morning glory)** | **A circular crest around a vertical shaft; capacity is limited once it drowns** |
| **SIPHON** | **Self-priming, automatic; small capacity; can be dangerous if it fails to prime** |
| **Emergency / fuse plug** | **A deliberately erodible section that washes out in an extreme flood** |

> **The SHAFT spillway's limitation is worth knowing because it is a genuine hazard: once the shaft drowns, the discharge is controlled by the SHAFT rather than the crest, and further rise in reservoir level produces almost no additional outflow.**

> **So a shaft spillway has a capacity that effectively CEILINGS**, and a flood beyond that point raises the reservoir with no relief — which is why they are provided with an auxiliary spillway or generous freeboard.

> **A spillway whose discharge stops increasing with head is the most dangerous kind, and recognising which types behave that way is a practical judgement worth having.**

examTip.trick: **The ogee follows the LOWER NAPPE of a free jet, so the water flows as though the concrete were not there — pressure ATMOSPHERIC, hence no cavitation AND the maximum discharge coefficient (C ≈ 2.2).**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is exactly backwards — the profile MAXIMISES the coefficient.** And option (b) describes a SHARP-CRESTED weir's ventilated nappe, a real phenomenon at the wrong structure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Above the DESIGN head the pressure goes NEGATIVE**, so the design head is set at 75-80 % of the maximum — accepting brief cavitation risk at the extreme flood for a better coefficient all year. And beware SHAFT spillways: their capacity ceilings once the shaft drowns.

questions.stem: In a run-of-river hydropower scheme, the structure provided to remove suspended sediment from the diverted water before it enters the headrace is the:
questions.solution:
**The SETTLING (desilting) BASIN.**

**How it works:**

> **A settling basin is a WIDENED, DEEPENED section of the conveyance in which the velocity is reduced so that suspended particles settle out.**

> **The design is exactly the sedimentation tank problem: the basin's SURFACE AREA determines the size of the smallest particle removed.**

> **Length required L = (V × D)/v_s**, where V is the through-velocity, D the depth and v_s the settling velocity of the target particle.

| Design parameter | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Through-velocity** | **0.2 - 0.4 m/s — low enough for settling, high enough to avoid depositing everywhere** |
| **Target particle size removed** | **0.2 - 0.3 mm for a Francis or Pelton machine; finer for high heads** ← |
| **Removal efficiency aimed at** | **80 - 95 per cent of particles above the target size** |
| **Flushing** | **Continuous or periodic, through a low-level flushing gate back to the river** |

**Why the sediment MUST be removed — the reason this structure exists:**

> **Himalayan rivers carry among the world's highest suspended sediment loads, and a large part of it is QUARTZ — hard, angular and highly abrasive.**

> **Water carrying quartz sand through a turbine at high velocity acts as a sandblaster.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **ABRASION of the runner buckets, needles and nozzles** | **The efficiency falls, and the machine must be repaired or replaced** ← |
| **Damage to the guide vanes and labyrinth seals** | Increasing leakage losses |
| **Combined abrasion and CAVITATION** | The two reinforce each other: pitting gives cavitation nuclei |
| **Deposition in the headrace and forebay** | Reducing capacity |
| **Wear of gates and valves** | |

> **The economics are severe and worth stating: a Pelton runner in a sediment-laden Himalayan river may lose several per cent of its efficiency in a single monsoon and require refurbishment every few years, where the same machine on a clear river would run for decades.**

> **The velocity dependence makes it worse: erosion rate goes roughly as the CUBE of the particle velocity, so a HIGH-HEAD plant — where the jet velocity is greatest — suffers far more from the same sediment concentration.**

> **For a 400 m head the jet velocity is 88 m/s, and at that speed even fine sand is destructive.**

> **Which is why high-head plants specify FINER particle removal than low-head plants: the target size falls as the head rises**, and a 500 m Pelton scheme may aim to remove particles down to 0.15 mm where a 40 m Francis tolerates 0.3 mm.

**Why each of the other structures is wrong — and each is real:**

| Structure | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| **FOREBAY** | **A small pond at the END of the headrace, immediately before the penstock. It provides a stable water surface, absorbs short-term flow fluctuations, allows final trash and sediment removal, and prevents air entering the penstock** ← |
| **SURGE TANK** | **Relieves WATER HAMMER and supplies water on load acceptance — a hydraulic transient device, not a sediment device** |
| **TRASH RACK** | **Screens FLOATING and coarse debris — leaves, branches, plastic — not suspended sediment** |

> **The TRASH RACK is the most tempting distractor because it does remove solid matter. The distinction is SIZE and STATE:**

> **A trash rack has bar spacings of tens of millimetres and stops FLOATING or LARGE debris.**

> **A settling basin removes SUSPENDED PARTICLES measured in fractions of a millimetre.**

> **They are three orders of magnitude apart and address entirely different threats: the rack protects against blockage and impact, the basin against abrasion.**

> **The FOREBAY is worth understanding properly because its functions are easily confused with the settling basin's — and one of them genuinely overlaps:**

| Forebay function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provide a stable water level at the penstock intake** | |
| **Absorb short-term flow variation between the headrace and the turbine demand** | **A very small pondage** |
| **PREVENT AIR ENTERING the penstock** | **The submergence of the penstock intake is the governing dimension** ← |
| **Final removal of any remaining trash and coarse sediment** | The overlap |
| **House the spillway that disposes of surplus headrace flow** | |

> **The AIR ENTRY function is the critical one and the reason the forebay's depth matters: if the water level falls too low, a VORTEX forms at the penstock mouth and draws air in.**

> **Air in a penstock is dangerous — it collects at high points, reduces the effective flow area, and can be released suddenly into the turbine, causing severe transients and damage.**

> **So a minimum SUBMERGENCE of the penstock intake is specified, and the forebay's operating level is never allowed below it.**

**The full conveyance chain of a run-of-river scheme, in order:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **INTAKE (side, trench weir or Tyrolean)** | **Divert water; exclude BOULDERS and bed load** |
| **Gravel trap** | **Remove coarse gravel that got past the intake** |
| **TRASH RACK** | Screen floating debris |
| **SETTLING BASIN** | **Remove SUSPENDED sediment** ← |
| **HEADRACE (canal or tunnel)** | Convey water at a low gradient to gain head |
| **FOREBAY** | Stabilise the level; final protection; prevent air entry |
| **SURGE TANK (where the conveyance is long)** | Relieve water hammer |
| **PENSTOCK** | Carry water under pressure to the machines |
| **POWERHOUSE** | Turbines, generators, controls |
| **TAILRACE** | Return water to the river |

> **Note that sediment is removed in THREE STAGES of decreasing particle size — boulders at the intake, gravel in the trap, suspended sand in the basin.**

> **That staging is deliberate and necessary: no single structure can handle a metre-diameter boulder and a 0.2 mm sand grain, so each stage removes what the next cannot cope with.**

> **It is the same principle as a water treatment train, and the same principle as screening before grit removal before sedimentation in a sewage works** — a sequence of processes each sized for the material the previous one passed.

examTip.trick: **The SETTLING (desilting) BASIN removes SUSPENDED sediment** — a widened, deepened reach where the velocity falls to 0.2-0.4 m/s so particles above 0.2-0.3 mm settle out.
examTip.trap: **The TRASH RACK is the tempting distractor** — it stops FLOATING debris at tens of millimetres, three orders of magnitude coarser. The rack protects against blockage; the basin against ABRASION.
examTip.mnemonic: **Erosion rate goes roughly as the CUBE of particle velocity**, so high-head plants must remove FINER sediment — a 400 m head gives an 88 m/s jet. And sediment is removed in THREE stages: boulders at the intake, gravel in the trap, sand in the basin.

questions.stem: Water flows in a penstock at 3 m/s. If the pressure wave velocity is 1000 m/s, the head rise due to INSTANTANEOUS closure of the valve is approximately:
questions.solution:
**306 m.**

**The Joukowsky (water hammer) equation for instantaneous closure:**

> **Δp = ρ c V**, and as a head: **Δh = c V / g**

**The computation:**

> **Δh = (1000 × 3)/9.81 = 3000/9.81 = 305.8 m ≈ 306 m** ✓

> **Or as a pressure: Δp = 1000 × 1000 × 3 = 3 × 10⁶ Pa = 3.0 MPa = 30 atmospheres.**

**The magnitude is the point of the question — and it is startling:**

> **A velocity of only 3 m/s, stopped suddenly, produces a pressure rise equivalent to 306 METRES of head.**

> **For a plant operating on a net head of, say, 90 m, that is more than THREE TIMES the static pressure — arriving in a fraction of a second.**

> **The velocity head of the flowing water is only V²/2g = 9/19.62 = 0.46 m.**

> **So the pressure rise is SIX HUNDRED AND SIXTY TIMES the velocity head.**

> **That ratio is worth dwelling on, because it demolishes the intuition that stopping slow-moving water cannot do much harm.**

> **The reason for the enormous factor is that the pressure rise depends on the WAVE speed (1000 m/s), not on the flow speed — the water's momentum is destroyed over the wave's travel, not over the flow's.**

> **And it is exactly why penstocks burst, why valves must never be closed quickly, and why surge protection is not optional.**

**The distractors, each a specific slip:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **153 m** | **Half the answer — a factor of 2 introduced, or c taken as 500 m/s** |
| **306 m** | ✓ |
| **612 m** | **Twice the answer** |
| **30.6 m** | **A factor of ten — g taken as 98.1, or the pressure/head conversion mishandled** |

> **The safeguard against all three is the sanity check: the head rise for instantaneous closure should be of the order of 100 c V / 981, that is roughly 0.1 c V — here 0.1 × 1000 × 3 = 300 m.** That estimate lands within 2 per cent.

**When closure counts as INSTANTANEOUS — the critical time:**

> **Closure is "instantaneous" (or rapid) if it is completed BEFORE the pressure wave can travel to the reservoir and return:**

> **T_critical = 2 L / c**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **L** | **Length of the penstock from the valve to the free surface (reservoir or surge tank)** |
| **c** | **Pressure wave velocity** |
| **2L/c** | **The time for the wave to travel up and back — the round trip** |

> **For a 500 m penstock with c = 1000 m/s: T_critical = 2 × 500/1000 = 1.0 second.**

> **So any closure faster than one second is "instantaneous" for that penstock and produces the full Joukowsky rise.**

> **A SLOWER closure produces a smaller rise, because the returning negative wave from the reservoir arrives and partly relieves the pressure while the valve is still closing.**

> **For slow closure the Allievi or Michaud approximation applies:  Δh ≈ 2 L V/(g T), with T the closure time.**

> **Check the consistency: setting T = 2L/c in that expression gives Δh = 2LV/(g × 2L/c) = cV/g** ✓ — the Joukowsky value, as it must.

> **That consistency is worth verifying once, because it confirms the two formulae are one relation with a boundary rather than two unrelated results.**

**Where the wave velocity comes from, and why 1000 m/s rather than 1450:**

> **In a perfectly RIGID pipe:  c = √(K/ρ) = √(2.1 × 10⁹/1000) = 1449 m/s**

> **In a REAL, elastic pipe the wall stretches too, and the effective wave speed is reduced:**

> **c = √(K/ρ) / √[1 + (K D)/(E t)]**

| Pipe | Typical wave speed |
|---|---|
| **Perfectly rigid (theoretical)** | **1449 m/s** |
| **Steel penstock** | **900 - 1300 m/s** ← 1000 here |
| **Cast iron** | 1000 - 1200 m/s |
| **Concrete** | 1000 - 1200 m/s |
| **PVC** | **300 - 500 m/s** |
| **HDPE** | **200 - 350 m/s** |

> **The PLASTIC pipes' low wave speed is a genuine practical advantage: a flexible pipe suffers a far smaller water hammer pressure for the same velocity change, because its walls absorb the shock by stretching.**

> **For HDPE at c = 300 m/s the head rise here would be 300 × 3/9.81 = 92 m rather than 306 m — a third as much.**

> **Which is why surge is much less of a design problem in plastic pipe systems, and why a rigid steel system needs surge protection that a plastic one may not.**

**The protection measures, since the calculation shows why they are needed:**

| Measure | How it works |
|---|---|
| **SURGE TANK** | **Reflects the wave, confining water hammer to the penstock and shortening L** ← the primary measure |
| **SLOW valve closure** | **Increasing T reduces Δh in proportion — a governor closing time of 3-6 seconds is typical** |
| **PRESSURE RELIEF valve** | Dumps water when the pressure exceeds a set value |
| **Air vessel / accumulator** | An air cushion absorbs the surge |
| **FLYWHEEL on the machine** | Increases the rotating inertia, so the speed rises more slowly and the governor has more time |
| **DEFLECTOR on a Pelton jet** | **Deflects the jet away from the runner instantly, so the flow need not be stopped quickly at all** ← elegant |

> **The PELTON DEFLECTOR is the most satisfying of these and worth knowing: on a load rejection, the machine must stop producing power immediately, but the water column must NOT be stopped quickly.**

> **A deflector plate swings into the jet and throws it past the buckets in a fraction of a second — removing the power instantly — while the needle valve then closes slowly over many seconds to stop the flow.**

> **So the two conflicting requirements are separated: the ELECTRICAL demand for instant unloading and the HYDRAULIC demand for slow closure are met by two different devices.**

> **That is a genuinely instructive piece of design, and it is the reason impulse turbines handle load rejection more gracefully than reaction turbines, which have no equivalent trick available.**

examTip.trick: **Δh = cV/g = 1000 × 3/9.81 = 306 m.** A quick check: Δh ≈ 0.1 cV.
examTip.trap: **The magnitude is the lesson: 3 m/s stopped suddenly gives 306 m of head — 660 times the velocity head of 0.46 m.** The rise depends on the WAVE speed, not the flow speed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Closure is "instantaneous" if faster than T = 2L/c** (the wave's round trip); slower closure gives Δh ≈ 2LV/(gT), which reduces to cV/g at T = 2L/c. And a PELTON DEFLECTOR separates instant unloading from slow closure — two devices for two conflicting needs.

questions.stem: The DRAFT TUBE of a reaction turbine serves to:
options: Increase the velocity of water entering the runner
Regulate the discharge according to the load on the machine
Screen debris from the water before it reaches the runner
Recover part of the kinetic energy leaving the runner and permit the turbine to be set above the tailwater level
questions.solution:
**To recover part of the kinetic energy leaving the runner, and to permit the turbine to be set ABOVE the tailwater level.**

**The two functions, and both matter:**

> **FIRST — ENERGY RECOVERY.**

> **Water leaves a reaction runner still moving, carrying kinetic energy that would otherwise be lost.**

> **The draft tube is a GRADUALLY EXPANDING passage: as the area increases, the velocity falls, and by Bernoulli's equation the pressure rises.**

> **So kinetic energy is converted back into pressure energy, and that pressure recovery is felt at the runner exit as a REDUCED back-pressure — which means a greater pressure drop across the runner and more work extracted.**

> **A well-designed draft tube can recover a substantial part of the exit kinetic energy, adding several per cent to the machine's efficiency.**

> **SECOND — IT PERMITS THE TURBINE TO BE SET ABOVE THE TAILWATER.**

> **Because the draft tube is full of water and airtight, and its lower end is SUBMERGED in the tailrace, the water column in it hangs below the runner and creates a partial vacuum — a NEGATIVE pressure at the runner exit.**

> **That suction effectively extends the machine's available head down to the tailwater level, even though the runner itself is above it.**

> **Without a draft tube, a reaction turbine would have to be placed AT or BELOW the tailwater level to use the full head — which would flood the powerhouse.**

> **So the draft tube is what makes a dry, accessible powerhouse possible above the river.**

**Why each distractor is wrong — and each names a real component:**

| Option | The component that does it |
|---|---|
| **(a) Increase the velocity entering the runner** | **The NOZZLE (impulse turbine) or the SPIRAL CASING and GUIDE VANES (reaction turbine)** |
| **(b) Regulate the discharge with load** | **The GOVERNOR, acting on the WICKET (guide) VANES, or on the SPEAR/needle valve in a Pelton** ← |
| **(c) Screen debris** | **The TRASH RACK, at the intake or forebay** |

> **Option (a) is the opposite of the truth and worth naming as such: the draft tube DECREASES the velocity. It is a diffuser, not a nozzle.**

**The critical constraint — CAVITATION and the turbine setting:**

> **The draft tube's suction is its virtue and also its danger: if the pressure at the runner exit falls to the water's VAPOUR PRESSURE, the water boils and CAVITATION occurs.**

> **Vapour cavities formed at the runner exit are carried into higher pressure and COLLAPSE violently, pitting the runner blades and the draft tube.**

> **The guard against it is the THOMA CAVITATION FACTOR:**

> **σ = (H_atm − H_vapour − H_s) / H**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **H_atm** | **Atmospheric pressure head (10.3 m at sea level)** |
| **H_vapour** | Vapour pressure head (about 0.24 m at 20 °C) |
| **H_s** | **The turbine SETTING — height of the runner above the tailwater** ← the design variable |
| **H** | Net head |

> **The computed σ must EXCEED a critical value σ_c that depends on the specific speed:**

| Turbine | Approximate σ_c |
|---|---|
| **Francis, low specific speed** | **0.10 - 0.20** |
| **Francis, high specific speed** | **0.20 - 0.40** |
| **KAPLAN** | **0.40 - 1.50** ← much higher |

> **The consequence is decisive and worth extracting: a KAPLAN turbine's high critical sigma means H_s must be SMALL or even NEGATIVE — the runner must be set AT or BELOW the tailwater level.**

> **Which is exactly what one observes in practice: a Kaplan powerhouse has its machines low, sometimes below the river, with the generator floor above.**

> **A low-specific-speed Francis, by contrast, can be set several metres above the tailwater.**

> **And note the ALTITUDE term: H_atm falls with elevation — about 8.7 m at 1500 m and 8.0 m at 2200 m.**

> **So a turbine installed high in the Himalaya has LESS atmospheric pressure available and must be set LOWER relative to its tailwater than the identical machine at sea level.**

> **That is a real and easily overlooked correction in Nepali powerhouse design, and getting it wrong produces a machine that cavitates from the day it is commissioned.**

**The draft tube types, since the shape is a design choice:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Straight conical (divergent)** | **Highest efficiency (85-90 % recovery); needs great DEPTH below the machine** |
| **Simple ELBOW** | Low efficiency (~60 %); minimum excavation |
| **ELBOW with a rectangular outlet** | **The standard for Kaplan and large Francis machines — a compromise** ← |
| **Moody spreading (hydracone)** | Reduces whirl; used where the exit swirl is strong |
| **Bell-mouthed** | |

> **The choice is a straight trade between EFFICIENCY and EXCAVATION: a straight conical tube recovers the most energy and requires the deepest and most expensive hole beneath the powerhouse.**

> **The elbow type turns the flow horizontally and so needs far less depth, at the cost of losses in the bend.**

> **For a large low-head plant the excavation is enormous and the elbow wins; for a small high-head Francis the depth is trivial and a conical tube is used.**

> **The divergence angle is the detail that governs performance: it must be kept below about 8 degrees included, because a steeper expansion causes the flow to SEPARATE from the walls, which destroys the pressure recovery entirely.**

> **A draft tube that expands too rapidly is worse than a shorter one that expands gently** — the same principle as a diffuser in any hydraulic or aerodynamic system, and a reliable place for an inexperienced design to go wrong.

**Why an IMPULSE turbine has no draft tube — the contrast that makes the point:**

> **A Pelton wheel runs in AIR at atmospheric pressure, and its water leaves the buckets at low velocity and simply falls to the tailrace.**

> **There is no pressure to recover and no continuous water column, so a draft tube would serve no purpose.**

> **The cost is that the Pelton runner must be set ABOVE the maximum tailwater level, and any head between the runner and the tailwater is LOST.**

> **On a 400 m head, losing two metres is half a per cent and irrelevant. On a 20 m head it would be 10 per cent, which is why impulse turbines are unsuitable for low heads** — and that, rather than any efficiency limit, is the fundamental reason for the head-based division between impulse and reaction machines.

examTip.trick: **Two functions: RECOVER exit kinetic energy (it is a diffuser — velocity falls, pressure rises) and let the runner sit ABOVE the tailwater** via the suction of its submerged water column.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) inverts it — a draft tube DECREASES velocity.** And option (b) is the GOVERNOR acting on the guide vanes, a different component entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Thoma's σ = (H_atm − H_vap − H_s)/H must exceed σ_c**, which is much higher for KAPLAN — so Kaplan runners sit at or BELOW tailwater. And H_atm falls with ALTITUDE (8.0 m at 2200 m), so a Himalayan machine must be set lower than the same one at sea level.

questions.stem: The power that is available from a hydropower plant for 100 per cent of the time throughout the year is called:
questions.solution:
**FIRM (primary) power.**

**The definitions:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **FIRM (primary) power** | **The power available for 100 per cent of the time — that is, at the MINIMUM flow of the record** ← |
| **SECONDARY power** | **The power available only PART of the time, above the firm level — surplus power when flows exceed the minimum** |
| **INSTALLED CAPACITY** | **The nameplate rating of the machines** |
| **PEAK power** | The maximum demand a system must meet at any instant |
| **DUMP power** | Secondary power for which there is no market at all |

> **So the FIRM power is set by the DRIEST condition in the record, and the secondary power is everything the river provides above that.**

**Why firm power is worth so much more than secondary power:**

> **A power system must meet its demand AT ALL TIMES. It therefore needs generation it can COUNT ON.**

> **FIRM power can be counted on, so it displaces the need to build other capacity — and it is priced accordingly.**

> **SECONDARY power arrives when the river is high, which in Nepal means the monsoon, when every other hydropower plant in the country is also generating abundantly.**

> **So secondary power is available exactly when it is least needed, and unavailable exactly when it is most needed.**

| | **FIRM power** | **SECONDARY power** |
|---|---|---|
| **Availability** | **Always** | **Seasonal, coinciding with everyone else's surplus** |
| **Displaces other capacity?** | **YES** | **NO — the capacity must exist anyway for the dry season** |
| **Value** | **HIGH** | **LOW; sometimes zero (dump power)** |
| **Contractual treatment** | **Capacity payment plus energy payment** | **Energy payment only, at a lower rate, if saleable** |

> **That asymmetry is the economic core of Nepali hydropower, and it explains a great deal that the raw capacity figures do not.**

**How the two are read off the FLOW DURATION CURVE:**

> **A FLOW DURATION CURVE plots discharge against the percentage of time it is EQUALLED OR EXCEEDED.**

| Point on the curve | What it gives |
|---|---|
| **Q₁₀₀ — the flow equalled or exceeded 100 % of the time** | **The FIRM power flow** ← |
| **Q₉₅ or Q₉₀** | **Often used instead, since a true 100 % flow may be unreasonably small** |
| **Q₃₀ to Q₄₅** | **The usual DESIGN discharge for a run-of-river plant** |
| **The area under the curve** | Total annual volume, hence annual energy |

> **The practical qualification in the second row is important and honest: the absolute minimum flow of a long record may be so small that designing for it gives a derisory firm power.**

> **So firm power is commonly quoted at Q₉₅ (exceeded 95 per cent of the time) rather than at the true minimum, and the definition used must always be stated.**

> **A firm power figure without its exceedance percentage is an incomplete statement**, and comparisons between projects quoted on different bases are meaningless.

**How STORAGE transforms firm power — the central argument for reservoirs:**

> **A RUN-OF-RIVER plant's firm power is fixed by the river's minimum flow, and there is nothing to be done about it.**

> **A STORAGE plant can hold monsoon water and release it in the dry season, so its firm power is limited by the RESERVOIR'S CAPACITY rather than by the river's minimum flow.**

| Scheme | Firm power |
|---|---|
| **Run-of-river, no pondage** | **Low — set by the driest week of the year** |
| **Peaking run-of-river (daily pondage)** | **Slightly better within the day; unchanged across seasons** |
| **STORAGE (seasonal)** | **MUCH higher — the reservoir carries water into the dry season** ← |

> **That is why a storage project's value is out of proportion to its installed capacity: it converts SECONDARY power (abundant, cheap, monsoon) into FIRM power (scarce, valuable, dry-season).**

> **The reservoir does not create energy — it MOVES it in time, from when it is worthless to when it is valuable.**

> **Which is the clearest way to state what a storage reservoir is for, and it applies equally to pumped storage, to a battery and to a service reservoir in a water supply: all four are devices for moving a commodity from a time of surplus to a time of scarcity.**

**The LOAD DURATION CURVE, its counterpart on the demand side:**

> **The flow duration curve describes what the river can supply; the LOAD DURATION curve describes what the system demands, arranged in descending order of magnitude against time.**

| Feature of the load duration curve | Use |
|---|---|
| **The BASE — demand present all the time** | **Met by base-load plant: storage hydro, thermal, run-of-river** |
| **The PEAK — demand present for a few hours** | **Met by peaking plant: PROR hydro, storage hydro, gas turbines** ← |
| **The AREA under the curve** | Total energy demanded |
| **Average ÷ maximum ordinate** | **The LOAD FACTOR of the system** |

> **Matching the two curves — supply against demand — is the essence of power system planning, and hydropower's peculiar advantage lies in the peak:**

> **A hydro machine can go from standstill to full load in a minute or two, where a thermal plant needs hours.**

> **So hydropower is uniquely suited to PEAKING and to spinning reserve, and that capability is worth paying for separately from the energy it produces** — which is why a storage or PROR plant earns a capacity payment as well as an energy payment.

> **And it is the reason a modest reservoir with good regulation can be more valuable to a system than a larger run-of-river plant generating more units: the system is buying the ability to respond, not only the energy.**

examTip.trick: **FIRM (primary) power is available 100 per cent of the time — read at Q₁₀₀ on the flow duration curve.** Everything above it is SECONDARY power.
examTip.trap: **A firm power figure is incomplete without its EXCEEDANCE basis** — in practice Q₉₅ is often used, since the true minimum of a long record gives a derisory value. Projects quoted on different bases cannot be compared.
examTip.mnemonic: **Secondary power arrives when it is least needed** — monsoon, when every other plant is also full — so it is worth little. A STORAGE reservoir does not create energy; it MOVES it from a time of surplus to a time of scarcity, converting secondary into firm.

questions.stem: A generator with 12 poles is connected to a 50 Hz system. Its synchronous speed is:
questions.solution:
**500 rpm.**

**The synchronous speed relation:**

> **N = 120 f / p**, where f is the frequency in hertz and p the NUMBER OF POLES.

> **N = 120 × 50 / 12 = 6000/12 = 500 rpm** ✓

> **Equivalently, with PAIRS of poles: N = 60 f / (pole pairs) = 60 × 50/6 = 500 rpm** ✓

> **The commonest error is confusing POLES with POLE PAIRS, which gives a factor of two — hence option (d) 1000 rpm, the answer for 6 poles.**

**Why the relation is exact and not approximate:**

> **A synchronous generator's rotor field must rotate in step with the stator's rotating field, and the stator field's speed is fixed by the supply frequency and the winding's pole arrangement.**

> **So the speed is not a design choice but a CONSEQUENCE of the frequency and the pole number — and since the pole number must be an even integer, only certain speeds are possible.**

**The permissible speeds at 50 Hz — worth knowing as a table:**

| Poles | Synchronous speed (rpm) |
|---|---|
| **2** | **3000** |
| **4** | **1500** |
| **6** | **1000** |
| **8** | **750** |
| **10** | **600** ← option (b) |
| **12** | **500** ✓ |
| **16** | **375** |
| **20** | **300** |
| **24** | **250** ← option (c) |
| **40** | 150 |
| **60** | 100 |

> **Note that every distractor is a legitimate synchronous speed for a DIFFERENT pole number** — 600 for 10 poles, 250 for 24, 1000 for 6.

> **So the option set is drawn from this table and the pole count is what discriminates.**

> **And observe that the speeds are NOT freely available: between 500 and 600 rpm there is nothing, because 11 poles is impossible.**

> **That discreteness has a real consequence in turbine design, examined below.**

**Why the discrete speeds constrain the TURBINE — the practically important point:**

> **The turbine's ideal speed follows from its SPECIFIC SPEED:**

> **N_s = N √P / H^{5/4}**

> **A designer computes the specific speed appropriate to the head, and hence the ideal rotational speed N.**

> **But the generator can only run at one of the speeds in the table above.**

> **So the turbine must be designed for the NEAREST AVAILABLE synchronous speed, not for its own optimum** — and the mismatch is absorbed by adjusting the runner geometry, accepting a slightly sub-optimal specific speed.

> **The alternatives, where the mismatch is large:**

| Solution | Note |
|---|---|
| **Accept the nearest synchronous speed** | **The usual answer; a small efficiency cost** ← |
| **Fit a SPEED INCREASER (gearbox or belt drive)** | **Lets a slow turbine drive a fast, cheaper generator — common in small hydro** |
| **Use more poles** | A slower, larger, more expensive generator |
| **Variable-speed operation with a power converter** | Modern, costly, and increasingly used in pumped storage |

> **The SPEED INCREASER deserves the note because it is a real economic device in small hydropower: a generator's cost and size fall sharply with speed, so a 1500 rpm machine with a gearbox can be cheaper than a direct-coupled 250 rpm one.**

> **The cost is another component to maintain and a further 2 to 4 per cent efficiency loss — which is worth it for a small scheme and not for a large one, where the generator's cost is a smaller fraction and reliability matters more.**

> **So large plants are direct-coupled and small ones frequently geared**, and that is a consistent pattern worth recognising.

**RUNAWAY SPEED, since it is the related design case:**

> **If a generator's electrical load is suddenly lost and the governor fails to close the flow, the turbine ACCELERATES until the hydraulic torque balances the windage and friction.**

> **That is the RUNAWAY (or no-load) speed, and it is far above synchronous:**

| Turbine | Runaway speed as a multiple of rated |
|---|---|
| **PELTON** | **1.8 - 1.9** |
| **FRANCIS** | **1.8 - 2.2** |
| **KAPLAN** | **2.0 - 3.2** ← the highest |

> **The generator's rotor, the shaft and the bearings must all be designed to SURVIVE the runaway speed without disintegrating, even though they will never operate there.**

> **Since centrifugal stress goes as the SQUARE of the speed, a runaway at twice the rated speed produces FOUR TIMES the centrifugal stress** — which is a governing design case for the rotor.

> **The KAPLAN's high runaway multiple is a consequence of its adjustable blades: at no load and full gate the blades present a favourable angle and the machine accelerates further than a fixed-geometry runner would.**

> **Which is why a Kaplan installation's mechanical design is dominated by a condition it should never reach**, and a good illustration of designing for the accident rather than the operation.

**FREQUENCY control, since the speed and the frequency are locked together:**

> **Because N = 120f/p, a change in machine speed IS a change in system frequency.**

> **So if the load exceeds the generation, the machines SLOW DOWN and the frequency FALLS; if generation exceeds load, the frequency RISES.**

> **The system frequency is therefore a direct, instantaneous measure of the balance between supply and demand across the entire grid — which is why it is the primary control signal in power system operation.**

> **A governor responds to a falling frequency by admitting more water, and to a rising one by admitting less, and every machine on the system does so simultaneously.**

> **That is why the grid holds together at all: the frequency is a shared signal that requires no communication, and every generator responds to it automatically.**

> **And it is why hydropower is so valuable for frequency regulation: a hydro governor can change output in seconds, where a thermal plant takes minutes** — so a system with substantial hydro capacity holds its frequency far more steadily than one without.

examTip.trick: **N = 120 f / p = 120 × 50/12 = 500 rpm.** With pole PAIRS instead: N = 60f/(pairs).
examTip.trap: **Confusing POLES with POLE PAIRS gives a factor of two — option (d) 1000 rpm is the 6-pole answer.** Every distractor is a valid synchronous speed for a different pole count.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only discrete speeds exist (3000, 1500, 1000, 750, 600, 500, 375, 300...)**, so the TURBINE must be designed for the nearest one rather than its own optimum — or fitted with a speed increaser, which is why small plants are often geared and large ones direct-coupled.

questions.stem: For the ELEMENTARY PROFILE of a gravity dam 60 m high, built of material of specific gravity 2.4 and NEGLECTING uplift, the base width required is:
questions.solution:
**38.7 m.**

**The elementary profile base width, neglecting uplift:**

> **B = H / √S**, where S is the specific gravity of the dam material.

> **B = 60/√2.4 = 60/1.5492 = 38.73 m** ✓

**And WITH uplift considered:**

> **B = H / √(S − 1) = 60/√1.4 = 60/1.1832 = 50.71 m** — which is option (d).

> **So the two forms differ by 31 per cent, and option (d) is the answer to the same question WITH uplift.**

> **Reading the stem's "neglecting uplift" is therefore the discriminating step, and both formulae must be known.**

**Where the formula comes from — the two criteria it satisfies simultaneously:**
