> **The elementary profile is a TRIANGLE with its apex at the water surface and its base at the foundation. Its width is fixed by two independent requirements, which happen to give the same answer:**

| Criterion | Requirement | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **NO TENSION at the heel** | **The resultant must pass within the MIDDLE THIRD of the base** | **B = H/√S** |
| **NO SLIDING** | **The friction at the base must resist the water thrust** | **B = H/(μ S)** |

> **The base width adopted is the GREATER of the two, and for typical values (S ≈ 2.4, μ ≈ 0.7) the no-tension criterion governs:**

> **No tension: 60/1.549 = 38.7 m**

> **No sliding: 60/(0.7 × 2.4) = 60/1.68 = 35.7 m**

> **So 38.7 m governs** ✓ — and it is worth computing both, because with a lower friction coefficient the sliding criterion can take over.

**Why NO TENSION is required — the reason behind the criterion:**

> **Mass concrete and masonry have very little tensile strength, and a crack at the heel would be catastrophic in a specific way:**

> **If tension develops at the heel (the upstream face), a crack opens there.**

> **WATER ENTERS THE CRACK, and the full reservoir pressure now acts INSIDE the dam.**

> **That pressure both drives the crack deeper and adds to the uplift on the reduced base area.**

> **So the process is SELF-PROPAGATING: a crack that opens tends to extend, and the dam's stability deteriorates as it does.**

> **That is why the no-tension rule is absolute rather than a matter of margin: it is not that a small tension would slightly overstress the concrete, but that ANY tension initiates a mechanism that feeds on itself.**

> **And it explains why the middle-third rule is stated in terms of the RESULTANT'S POSITION rather than a stress limit — the geometry is what guarantees compression everywhere.**

**UPLIFT, and why it costs so much width:**

> **Water seeps into the foundation and into the dam's own pores, and it exerts an UPWARD pressure on the base.**

> **That pressure REDUCES the effective weight of the dam — which is the dam's only means of resisting the water thrust.**

> **In the formula, the specific gravity S is replaced by (S − 1), because the uplift is equivalent to buoying the dam in water:**

| | **Neglecting uplift** | **With full uplift** |
|---|---|---|
| **Effective specific gravity** | **S = 2.4** | **S − 1 = 1.4** |
| **Base width** | **38.7 m** | **50.7 m** |
| **Increase** | — | **+31 per cent** ← |

> **A 31 per cent increase in base width, and hence roughly in concrete volume, is an enormous cost — which is why controlling uplift is one of the central concerns of gravity dam design.**

> **The measures used:**

| Measure | How it works |
|---|---|
| **GROUT CURTAIN near the heel** | **A line of grouted holes reduces the foundation's permeability, cutting the seepage and the pressure entering beneath the dam** ← |
| **DRAINAGE GALLERY with relief drains** | **Holes drilled from a gallery into the foundation INTERCEPT the seepage and release its pressure to the gallery, where it is pumped away** |
| **Drainage holes within the concrete** | Relieve pore pressure in the body |
| **Upstream impervious blanket** | Lengthens the seepage path |

> **The DRAINAGE GALLERY is the most effective, and its logic is the same one that appears throughout hydraulic engineering: RELIEVE the pressure rather than RESIST it.**

> **A drain that lets the water out costs a trivial amount of concrete; resisting the same pressure by weight costs 31 per cent of the dam.**

> **With an effective grout curtain and drainage, the uplift is commonly reduced to about a third of the full value, so the design width lies between the two figures computed above** — and modern practice computes the uplift diagram explicitly rather than using either extreme.

> **That is the same principle as the canal lining's relief valves, the retaining wall's weep holes and the tile drain's outfall: four different structures, one idea.**

**The full set of forces and checks on a gravity dam, for completeness:**

| Force | Note |
|---|---|
| **SELF WEIGHT** | **The stabilising force — everything depends on it** |
| **WATER PRESSURE (horizontal)** | ½ γ H², acting at H/3 above the base |
| **UPLIFT** | ← discussed above |
| **SILT pressure** | Acts like a submerged soil; often significant in Himalayan reservoirs |
| **EARTHQUAKE — inertia of the dam** | Horizontal and vertical components |
| **EARTHQUAKE — HYDRODYNAMIC pressure** | **Von Karman or Zangar; the water's inertia adds to the thrust** |
| **Wave pressure** | Near the crest |
| **Ice pressure** | Cold climates |

| Stability check | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **No TENSION** | Resultant within the middle third |
| **No SLIDING** | **Factor of safety against sliding ≥ 1.5; shear friction factor ≥ 4-5** |
| **No OVERTURNING** | Factor of safety ≥ 1.5 (usually automatic if no tension) |
| **Compressive stress within limits** | At the toe, under the full reservoir |

> **The SILT PRESSURE row deserves a note for the Himalayan context: as a reservoir fills with sediment, the silt exerts a lateral pressure considerably greater than water's — because a submerged silt deposit has a submerged unit weight of perhaps 10 kN/m³ and an active pressure coefficient of around 0.4 to 0.5, giving a horizontal pressure comparable to water's own.**

> **So a dam on a heavily silt-laden river faces an INCREASING lateral load over its life, and the load case that governs may be one that does not exist when the dam is built.** Designing for the silted condition is therefore not conservatism but a recognition of the structure's actual future.

examTip.trap: **Option (d) 50.7 m is the same question WITH uplift** — a 31 per cent wider dam. The stem's "neglecting uplift" is the discriminating phrase.
examTip.mnemonic: **No tension is ABSOLUTE, not a margin**: a crack at the heel admits reservoir pressure INSIDE the dam, which drives the crack deeper — a self-propagating mechanism. And RELIEVE uplift with a drainage gallery rather than resisting it by weight: a drain costs nothing, weight costs 31 % of the dam.

questions.stem: In the planning of a run-of-river hydropower project, the single most important hydrological input is:
options: The peak flood discharge of the river
The gross storage capacity available at the site
The average annual rainfall over the catchment
The long-term daily flow record, from which the flow duration curve is derived
questions.solution:
**The long-term DAILY FLOW RECORD, from which the FLOW DURATION CURVE is derived.**

**Why the flow duration curve is the governing input:**

> **Almost every decision in a run-of-river scheme's planning is read off it:**

| Decision | Read from the FDC |
|---|---|
| **DESIGN DISCHARGE, and hence the installed capacity** | **The chosen exceedance flow, typically Q₃₀ to Q₄₅** ← |
| **FIRM POWER** | **Q₁₀₀ (or Q₉₅ in practice)** |
| **ANNUAL ENERGY** | **The area under the curve, up to the design discharge** |
| **Plant factor** | The ratio of energy to capacity × 8760 |
| **Number and size of units** | How the flow range is best covered by machines |
| **Economic optimum** | Energy against cost, across candidate design flows |

> **So the flow duration curve is not one input among several — it is the object from which the scheme's capacity, output, revenue and viability all follow.**

> **Note that it must be built from DAILY flows, not monthly means: monthly averaging conceals the variation within the month and OVERSTATES the energy a plant can capture**, because a plant limited by its design discharge cannot use the high days to compensate for the low ones.

> **That is a real and consequential error in feasibility work, and it flatters the project.**

**Why each distractor is important and not the answer:**

| Option | Its actual role |
|---|---|
| **(a) Peak flood discharge** | **Essential — but it sizes the SPILLWAY, the intake's flood protection, the powerhouse platform level and the diversion works during construction. It determines SAFETY, not OUTPUT** ← |
| **(b) Gross storage capacity** | **Not applicable to a RUN-OF-RIVER scheme, which by definition has little or no storage** |
| **(c) Average annual rainfall** | **Far too crude: it gives no information about seasonal distribution, and the relation between rainfall and runoff depends on the catchment's geology, land use, snow cover and evaporation** |

> **Option (a) deserves the emphasis it gets: the design flood is indispensable, and it answers a different question.**

> **The FDC tells you what the plant will EARN; the design flood tells you whether it will SURVIVE.**

> **Both are required, and confusing their roles leads to a scheme that is either uneconomic or unsafe.**

> **Option (c) is worth a note because rainfall-runoff relations ARE used — where no flow record exists, which in Nepal is common.**

**What to do when there is NO adequate flow record — the practical situation:**

> **Most Nepali project sites are ungauged, and a 20-year daily record at the site is a luxury. The methods used instead:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **CATCHMENT AREA RATIO transfer from a gauged site** | **Q_site = Q_gauged × (A_site/A_gauged)^n, with n typically 0.7-1.0. Valid only for hydrologically similar catchments** ← |
| **Regional regression (the Medium Hydrology Project method in Nepal)** | Flow related to area, elevation and rainfall by regional equations |
| **Rainfall-runoff modelling** | Where rainfall records are longer than flow records |
| **SHORT-TERM gauging at the site, correlated with a long-term nearby station** | **The best practical approach — extend a short local record using a long regional one** |
| **Snow and glacier melt components estimated separately** | Essential for high catchments |

> **The fourth row is the professionally sound answer and worth stating as a recommendation: install a gauge at the site as early as possible, measure for a year or two, and CORRELATE that record with a long-term station to synthesise a long series.**

> **A two-year local record correlated with a forty-year regional one is far more reliable than either a two-year record alone or a pure area-ratio transfer.**

> **The critical caution: the ELEVATION and the PROPORTION OF SNOW-FED CATCHMENT must match between the two sites.**

> **Transferring flows from a rain-fed southern catchment to a snow-fed Himalayan one by area ratio will get the annual total roughly right and the SEASONAL DISTRIBUTION badly wrong — understating the dry-season flow, which is exactly the figure that determines the firm power and the project's value.**

> **So an area-ratio transfer between dissimilar catchments can produce an annual energy estimate that looks reasonable and a firm power estimate that is wrong by a factor of two.**

**The length of record required — a matter of judgement:**

| Record length | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **Under 5 years** | **Inadequate — cannot capture a dry sequence** |
| **10 years** | **A minimum for a preliminary study** |
| **20 - 25 years** | **Reasonable for a run-of-river feasibility study** ← |
| **40 years or more** | **Necessary for a STORAGE project, whose reservoir must be sized against a multi-year drought sequence** |

> **The last row is worth understanding: a run-of-river plant responds to the flow of the moment, so a record long enough to characterise the year's distribution suffices.**

> **A STORAGE project must be sized against the worst DROUGHT SEQUENCE — perhaps several dry years in succession — and identifying such a sequence requires a much longer record.**

> **So the hydrological data requirement scales with the project's storage, and a reservoir designed on a 15-year record may be sized against a drought that the record never contained.**

**The other hydrological and related inputs a planning study needs, for completeness:**

| Input | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Daily flow series / FDC** | **Capacity, energy, firm power** ← |
| **Design flood (various return periods)** | Spillway, intake, diversion, platform levels |
| **Low flow and RESIDUAL (environmental) flow requirement** | **A statutory minimum must be left in the river — typically 10 per cent of the minimum monthly flow in Nepal** |
| **SEDIMENT load and its grading** | Settling basin, turbine material, reservoir life |
| **Sediment rating curve** | Annual sediment yield |
| **Water quality** | Corrosion, and downstream effects |
| **GLOF risk assessment** | **A design flood not of hydrological origin** |
| **Water rights and upstream/downstream abstractions** | The flow actually available |

> **The RESIDUAL FLOW requirement is easy to overlook and directly reduces the project's output: the water left in the river for the ecosystem and downstream users is water that cannot be generated with.**

> **In a dry-season month when the whole river is barely enough for the plant, giving up 10 per cent of it is a 10 per cent reduction in the firm power** — precisely where the project's value is most concentrated.

> **So the environmental flow is not a marginal deduction but a first-order design input, and a feasibility study that computes energy from the gross flow overstates the project.**

examTip.trick: **The FLOW DURATION CURVE from a long DAILY record gives the design discharge, firm power, annual energy and plant factor — everything the scheme earns.**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) the design flood is indispensable but answers a different question: the FDC tells you what the plant EARNS, the flood whether it SURVIVES.** And monthly means overstate energy — daily flows are required.
examTip.mnemonic: **For an ungauged site, gauge locally for a year or two and CORRELATE with a long regional record.** But match the ELEVATION and SNOW-FED proportion: an area-ratio transfer between dissimilar catchments gets the annual total right and the dry-season flow — the valuable part — badly wrong.

questions.stem: In Nepal's road classification, the class of road whose function is to connect district headquarters and other important centres to the strategic (national highway) network is:
questions.solution:
**A FEEDER road.**

**Nepal's road classification, as administered by the Department of Roads:**

| Class | Function | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| **NATIONAL HIGHWAY (NH)** | **The main arterial routes running the length and breadth of the country, connecting regions and international border points** | **Department of Roads** |
| **FEEDER ROAD (F)** | **Connects DISTRICT HEADQUARTERS and important economic centres TO the national highway network** | **Department of Roads** ← |
| **DISTRICT ROAD (D)** | **Roads within a district, serving village and rural centres** | **Local government (district)** |
| **URBAN (municipal) ROAD** | **Roads within municipal areas** | **Municipality** |

> **The NATIONAL HIGHWAYS and FEEDER ROADS together form the STRATEGIC ROAD NETWORK (SRN), which is the Department of Roads' responsibility.**

> **The DISTRICT and URBAN roads form the LOCAL ROAD NETWORK (LRN), the responsibility of local government.**

> **That split of responsibility is the practically important consequence of the classification, and it is why the classification exists: it determines WHO plans, builds, funds and maintains a road.**

**The logic of the hierarchy, which is worth stating because it is a general principle:**

> **A road network is organised as a HIERARCHY, in which each level collects traffic from the level below and delivers it to the level above.**

| Level | Predominant function |
|---|---|
| **National highway** | **MOBILITY — moving traffic long distances at speed** |
| **Feeder road** | **A balance of mobility and access** |
| **District road** | **ACCESS to villages and land** |
| **Urban street / village track** | **ACCESS almost exclusively** |

> **The fundamental tension in road design is between MOBILITY and ACCESS, and they are in direct conflict:**

> **MOBILITY requires few interruptions — limited access, no frontage development, wide spacing of junctions, high speed.**

> **ACCESS requires many connections — frequent junctions, direct entry to properties, low speed.**

> **A road that tries to do both does neither well: a national highway with shops and houses along it and unrestricted access becomes slow, dangerous and congested, while a purely mobility-focused road serves nobody along its length.**

> **So the hierarchy exists precisely to SEPARATE the two functions onto different classes of road**, and the commonest failure of road planning in practice is allowing ribbon development along a high-mobility route, which converts it into an access road while it is still being used as a highway.

> **That is why ACCESS CONTROL is a legal and planning matter as much as an engineering one, and why a bypass built to relieve a town is worthless within a decade if development is permitted to line it.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Its actual function |
|---|---|
| **(a) National highway** | **The arterial routes THEMSELVES, which the feeder roads connect TO** |
| **(c) District road** | **Roads WITHIN a district serving villages — one level below** |
| **(d) Urban road** | Municipal streets |

> **Option (a) is the near miss: national highways and feeder roads are BOTH part of the strategic network and both are the Department of Roads' responsibility, so they are frequently conflated.**

> **The distinction is one of ROLE: a national highway is a through route in its own right, while a feeder road exists to CONNECT something to that route.**

> **The name itself carries the meaning — it FEEDS traffic into the network.**

**The Indian classification, for comparison, since papers sometimes use it:**

| Class | Note |
|---|---|
| **National Highways (NH)** | Central government |
| **State Highways (SH)** | State arterials |
| **Major District Roads (MDR)** | Between district roads and state highways |
| **Other District Roads (ODR)** | Serving rural areas |
| **Village Roads (VR)** | Connecting villages to higher classes |

> **The five-tier Indian system (from the Nagpur Plan) and Nepal's four-tier system serve the same purpose with different names**, and the mapping is approximate: Nepal's feeder roads occupy roughly the position of India's state highways and major district roads together.

**Terrain classification, since it governs the design standards applied:**

> **Nepal's topography makes terrain classification unusually consequential, and it is defined by the CROSS SLOPE of the ground:**

| Terrain | Cross slope |
|---|---|
| **PLAIN** | **0 - 10 per cent** |
| **ROLLING** | **10 - 25 per cent** |
| **MOUNTAINOUS** | **25 - 60 per cent** |
| **STEEP** | **Above 60 per cent** ← |

> **Nearly every geometric standard — design speed, minimum radius, maximum gradient, sight distance, carriageway width — is tabulated against the terrain class.**

> **A national highway in plain terrain may have a design speed of 100 km/h; the same class of road in steep terrain may be designed for 30 km/h.**

> **So the CLASS of road and the TERRAIN together determine the standard, and neither alone is sufficient** — which is the practical reason both classifications must be known.

> **And it means that a "national highway" in Nepal is not a uniform object: the same route may be a 100 km/h dual carriageway in the Terai and a 30 km/h single lane with hairpin bends within a hundred kilometres.** Design standards that vary along a route are themselves a safety problem, which is why consistency of standard within a reach, and clear signing where it changes, matter so much.

examTip.trick: **FEEDER roads connect district headquarters TO the national highway network** — the name carries the meaning. NH + feeder = the STRATEGIC network (DoR); district + urban = the LOCAL network (local government).
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the near miss** — both NH and feeder roads are in the strategic network under DoR. The distinction is ROLE: a highway is a through route, a feeder connects something to it.
examTip.mnemonic: **The hierarchy exists to SEPARATE MOBILITY from ACCESS**, which are in direct conflict. Ribbon development along a highway converts it into an access road while it is still used as a highway — the commonest failure of road planning. And terrain class (plain/rolling/mountainous/steep by cross slope) sets the geometric standard.

questions.stem: The stopping sight distance for a design speed of 50 km/h, taking the reaction time as 2.5 seconds and the longitudinal friction coefficient as 0.37, is:
questions.solution:
**61.35 m.**

**The stopping sight distance is the sum of two components:**

> **SSD = (lag distance) + (braking distance)**

> **SSD = 0.278 V t + V²/(254 f)**

**Component 1 — the LAG (reaction) distance:**

> **The distance travelled while the driver perceives the hazard and applies the brakes — during which the vehicle does not slow at all.**

> **d₁ = 0.278 V t = 0.278 × 50 × 2.5 = 34.75 m** ← option (a)

**Component 2 — the BRAKING distance:**

> **d₂ = V²/(254 f) = 50²/(254 × 0.37) = 2500/93.98 = 26.60 m** ← option (b)

**The total:**

> **SSD = 34.75 + 26.60 = 61.35 m** ✓

> **So options (a) and (b) are the two COMPONENTS taken alone, and option (d) 122.70 m is TWICE the SSD — which is the INTERMEDIATE SIGHT DISTANCE.**

> **Every distractor is therefore a meaningful quantity in the wrong role, which is a well-formed option set.**

**Where the constants come from — worth deriving so they need not be trusted:**

> **The 0.278 converts km/h to m/s: 1 km/h = 1000/3600 = 0.2778 m/s.** ✓

> **The 254 comes from the braking distance formula v²/(2gf) with v in m/s:**

> **v = V/3.6, so v² = V²/12.96**

> **d₂ = V²/(12.96 × 2 × 9.81 × f) = V²/(254.3 f)** ✓

> **So both constants are pure unit conversions, and reconstructing them takes ten seconds if either is misremembered.**

**The striking feature of the result — which component dominates:**

> **At 50 km/h, the REACTION distance (34.75 m) EXCEEDS the braking distance (26.60 m).**

> **More than half the stopping distance is covered before the brakes even begin to act.**

> **The reason is that the reaction distance grows LINEARLY with speed while the braking distance grows as the SQUARE:**

| Speed (km/h) | Reaction distance | Braking distance | Total SSD | Braking as a share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **30** | **20.85** | **9.6** | **30.4** | **32 %** |
| **50** | **34.75** | **26.6** | **61.4** | **43 %** ← |
| **80** | **55.6** | **68.1** | **123.7** | **55 %** |
| **100** | **69.5** | **106.4** | **175.9** | **60 %** |

> **So at low speeds the driver's REACTION dominates and at high speeds the BRAKING dominates, with the crossover around 60 to 65 km/h.**

> **That has a real practical implication: at urban speeds, the greatest single contributor to stopping distance is the 2.5 seconds of human reaction — which is why measures that IMPROVE VISIBILITY and give earlier warning are so effective in towns, and why braking technology improvements matter more on high-speed roads.**

> **And note the total: SSD roughly TRIPLES between 30 and 80 km/h, and increases nearly SIXFOLD between 30 and 100.**

> **Since sight distance governs the vertical curve length and the setback at horizontal curves, that non-linearity is why high design speeds are so expensive in difficult terrain.**

**The PIEV reaction time of 2.5 seconds, since it is a large number:**

> **PIEV stands for PERCEPTION, INTELLECTION, EMOTION and VOLITION — the four stages of the driver's response:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **PERCEPTION** | The hazard registers on the senses |
| **INTELLECTION** | **It is understood and identified** |
| **EMOTION** | **The decision is made — and any fear or hesitation occurs** |
| **VOLITION** | **The action is executed — the foot moves to the brake** |

> **IRC adopts 2.5 seconds for SSD calculations, which is generous compared with a laboratory reaction time of 0.5 to 1.0 second.**

> **The generosity is deliberate and correct: the design value must accommodate an ordinary driver — tired, distracted, elderly, unfamiliar with the road — and not an alert test subject expecting a signal.**

> **A design based on a 1-second reaction would be adequate for most drivers and fatal for the rest, and a road must be safe for the population that uses it rather than for its most capable users.**

> **That principle — design for the ordinary user, not the expert — runs through all safety-related engineering.**

**The sight distances in the family, since SSD is only the first:**

| Sight distance | Definition | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **STOPPING (SSD)** | **Distance to stop safely** | **= 0.278Vt + V²/254f** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE (ISD)** | **Twice the SSD** | **122.7 m here** — option (d) |
| **OVERTAKING (OSD)** | **Distance needed to overtake safely: d₁ + d₂ + d₃** | Much larger |
| **Head light sight distance** | Equal to the SSD, for night design | |
| **Safe sight distance at an uncontrolled intersection** | Based on the time to cross | |

> **INTERMEDIATE SIGHT DISTANCE is provided where full overtaking sight distance cannot be economically achieved, and its logic is worth knowing: it gives enough distance for two vehicles approaching from opposite directions to each stop within half of it.**

> **So ISD = 2 × SSD is the minimum for a two-way single-lane situation, and it is the practical standard on hill roads where OSD is impossible.**

> **And the OVERTAKING sight distance is far larger — for 50 km/h it is around 235 m for a two-way road — which is why designated overtaking zones are provided at intervals rather than continuously in difficult terrain.**

> **A road on which overtaking sight distance is nowhere available becomes dangerous not because overtaking is impossible but because drivers attempt it anyway**, which is why marking and signing the prohibition matters as much as providing the geometry where it can be provided.

examTip.trick: **SSD = 0.278Vt + V²/(254f) = 34.75 + 26.60 = 61.35 m.** The constants are pure unit conversions: 0.278 = 1000/3600 and 254 = 12.96 × 2 × 9.81.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (b) are the two COMPONENTS alone, and (d) is twice the SSD — the INTERMEDIATE sight distance.** Each is a real quantity in the wrong role.
examTip.mnemonic: **At 50 km/h the REACTION distance EXCEEDS the braking distance** — reaction grows linearly with speed, braking as the square, crossing over around 60-65 km/h. So visibility measures help most in towns and braking improvements most on fast roads.

questions.stem: Using the IRC formula, the superelevation required for a design speed of 50 km/h on a curve of 250 m radius is:
questions.solution:
**4.4 per cent.**

**The IRC design formula:**

> **e = V² / (225 R)**, with V in km/h and R in metres.

> **= 50²/(225 × 250) = 2500/56,250 = 0.0444 = 4.4 %** ✓

**Where the 225 comes from — and it is not arbitrary:**

> **The full equilibrium relation for a vehicle on a banked curve is:**

> **e + f = V²/(127 R)**, with V in km/h

> **IRC's design practice is to provide superelevation for only SEVENTY-FIVE PER CENT of the design speed, ignoring friction, so that the curve is comfortable for slow-moving vehicles too:**

> **e = (0.75V)²/(127 R) = 0.5625 V²/(127 R) = V²/(225.8 R) ≈ V²/(225 R)** ✓

> **So the 225 encodes a deliberate policy decision: DESIGN THE BANKING FOR THREE-QUARTERS OF THE DESIGN SPEED.**

> **Knowing that means the formula is a consequence rather than a fact to memorise, and it also explains why it exists alongside the 127 relation.**

**Why superelevation is deliberately provided for LESS than the design speed:**

> **This is the substance of the question and a genuinely interesting piece of design reasoning.**

> **If a curve were banked for its full design speed, a vehicle travelling SLOWER than that speed would slide DOWN the slope — the banking would be excessive for it.**

> **On a mixed-traffic road that is a real problem: a bullock cart, a loaded truck climbing a gradient, or a vehicle stopped in a queue on the curve.**

| Vehicle speed relative to the banking | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Faster than the equilibrium speed** | **Tends to slide OUTWARD; friction acts inward** |
| **At the equilibrium speed** | **No lateral friction required at all** |
| **SLOWER than the equilibrium speed** | **Tends to slide INWARD/downward; friction must act outward** ← |

> **A steeply banked curve is uncomfortable and, in wet or icy conditions, actually hazardous for slow vehicles — and a stationary vehicle on a heavily banked wet curve can simply slide.**

> **So the design compromises: bank for 75 per cent of the design speed, and let FRICTION make up the difference for vehicles travelling at the full design speed.**

> **The friction available (f ≈ 0.15 for lateral comfort) is ample for that remainder, so the fast vehicle is safe and the slow vehicle is comfortable.**

> **That is a good example of a design standard mediating between conflicting users rather than optimising for one.**

**The LIMITS on superelevation, which frequently override the formula:**

| Situation | Maximum e |
|---|---|
| **Plain and rolling terrain** | **7.0 per cent** ← option (b) |
| **Hilly terrain (snow-free)** | **10.0 per cent** |
| **Hill roads liable to snow** | **7.0 per cent** |
| **URBAN roads with frequent intersections** | **4.0 per cent** |
| **MINIMUM (for drainage)** | **Equal to the camber, so water drains off the carriageway** ← |

> **Option (b) 7.0 per cent is the MAXIMUM permitted in plain terrain**, offered as though it were the computed value — a correct number in the wrong role.

> **The computed 4.4 per cent is below the maximum, so it is adopted as it stands.**

> **The MINIMUM in the last row is easy to overlook and matters: a curve so gentle that its computed superelevation is less than the camber would leave part of the carriageway draining inward or not at all, so the superelevation is set at least equal to the camber (typically 2 to 2.5 per cent for a bituminous surface).**

**The design procedure in full, since the formula is only step one:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute e = V²/(225R), assuming no friction and 75 % of design speed** |
| **2** | **If e ≤ e_max, ADOPT it — done** ← this case |
| **3** | **If e > e_max, set e = e_max and CHECK the friction: f = V²/(127R) − e_max. If f ≤ 0.15, the curve is safe at the design speed** |
| **4** | **If f > 0.15, restrict the speed: V_safe = √(127R(e_max + 0.15))** |
| **5** | **Or increase the radius — the preferred solution where the alignment allows** |

> **Step 5 is worth stating as the professional preference: RESTRICTING THE SPEED is an admission that the geometry is inadequate, and it relies on drivers obeying a sign.**

> **Increasing the radius solves the problem physically and permanently.**

> **A curve whose safe speed is below the road's design speed is an INCONSISTENCY in the alignment, and inconsistency is the single most reliable predictor of accidents on a rural road** — because drivers form expectations from the preceding kilometres and a curve sharper than the rest of the road violates them.

> **Which is why a single substandard curve on an otherwise good road is more dangerous than a road that is uniformly substandard.** Drivers adapt to a consistently difficult road; they crash on the one bad curve.

**Attaining the superelevation — the practical detail:**

| Element | Practice |
|---|---|
| **Attained over the TRANSITION curve** | **Progressively, so the curvature and the banking develop together** ← |
| **Rate of change of superelevation** | **Not steeper than 1 in 150 (plain/rolling), 1 in 60 (hilly)** |
| **Method of rotation** | About the CENTRE LINE (common), the inner edge, or the outer edge |
| **Extra widening** | Attained over the same transition length |

> **Rotating about the CENTRE LINE is usual because it minimises the change in the road's vertical profile at the edges, and hence the earthwork.**

> **Rotating about the INNER EDGE is used where drainage requires the inner edge to be held at grade — in a hill cutting, for instance, where lowering the inner edge would drown the side drain.**

> **So the choice of rotation axis is usually settled by DRAINAGE rather than by geometry**, which is a recurring theme in road design: the drainage requirement quietly determines a great many decisions that appear geometric.

examTip.trick: **e = V²/(225R) = 2500/56,250 = 4.4 %.** The 225 comes from banking for only 75 % of the design speed: (0.75V)²/127 = V²/225.8.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 7.0 % is the MAXIMUM permitted in plain terrain**, offered as though computed. Since 4.4 % is below it, the computed value is adopted as it stands.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bank for 75 % of design speed so SLOW vehicles do not slide inward** — friction covers the fast ones. And prefer INCREASING THE RADIUS to restricting the speed: a single substandard curve on a good road is more dangerous than a uniformly poor road, because it violates driver expectation.

questions.stem: The test in which a steel ball is placed on a bitumen sample held in a brass ring, and the temperature at which the bitumen softens enough to let the ball fall a specified distance is recorded, is:
options: The ring and ball (softening point) test
questions.solution:
**The RING AND BALL test, which determines the SOFTENING POINT.**

**The test as specified:**

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Sample** | **Bitumen cast in a brass RING** |
| **Load** | **A STEEL BALL, 9.5 mm diameter, 3.5 g, placed on the sample** |
| **Bath** | **Water (for softening points below 80 °C) or glycerine (above)** |
| **Heating rate** | **5 °C per minute** |
| **Measured** | **The temperature at which the softened bitumen, with the ball, touches a plate 25 mm below** ← |

> **The result is the SOFTENING POINT in degrees Celsius.**

**What the softening point actually means — an important conceptual point:**

> **Bitumen is not a crystalline solid and has NO SHARP MELTING POINT. It softens gradually over a wide temperature range.**

> **So the "softening point" is not a physical transition temperature but the temperature at which the material reaches an ARBITRARY but REPRODUCIBLE consistency, defined by the test procedure itself.**

> **That is why the test conditions are specified so precisely — the ball's mass and diameter, the 25 mm fall, the 5 °C/min heating rate.**

> **Change any of them and the answer changes, because the answer IS a property of the test as much as of the bitumen.**

> **Recognising that a material property can be DEFINED BY ITS TEST is a genuinely useful habit: the same is true of the penetration value, the CBR, the fineness modulus and the Los Angeles abrasion value, none of which measures a fundamental physical constant.**

**Why the softening point matters practically:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Indicates resistance to FLOWING at high service temperature** | **A low softening point means the pavement will soften, rut and bleed in hot weather** ← |
| **Guides the choice of grade for the climate** | **Hot climates need a HIGHER softening point** |
| **Together with penetration, indicates TEMPERATURE SUSCEPTIBILITY** | How sharply the consistency changes with temperature |
| **Informs mixing and compaction temperatures** | |

> **Typical values: 35 to 70 °C, with the paving grades commonly 45 to 60 °C.**

> **The climate argument is direct: a pavement surface in the Terai can reach 60 °C or more on a summer afternoon, so a bitumen softening at 45 °C will rut under wheel loads.**

> **And the converse: a very hard, high-softening-point bitumen suits a hot climate and CRACKS in a cold one, because it is too brittle at low temperature.**

> **So bitumen selection is a compromise between the two ends of the annual temperature range**, which is precisely what modern PERFORMANCE GRADED (PG) specifications express directly — a PG 64-10 binder being one that performs at 64 °C at the top and −10 °C at the bottom.

**The full suite of bitumen tests, since this is one of a family:**

| Test | What it measures | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| **PENETRATION** | **The depth a standard needle (100 g, 5 s, 25 °C) sinks, in 1/10 mm** | **CONSISTENCY at service temperature; defines the GRADE (80/100, 60/70, 30/40)** ← |
| **SOFTENING POINT (ring and ball)** | **Temperature of a defined consistency** | **High-temperature behaviour** ← this question |
| **DUCTILITY** | **The distance a briquette stretches before breaking (27 °C, 50 mm/min), in cm** | **Ability to deform without cracking; minimum 50 cm for paving grades** |
| **VISCOSITY** | Resistance to flow, in poise or centistokes | **Mixing and spraying temperatures; the basis of VG grading** |
| **FLASH and FIRE POINT** | Temperature at which vapours ignite | **SAFETY during heating; minimum 175 °C** |
| **SPECIFIC GRAVITY** | ~1.0 for bitumen | Volume-mass conversions |
| **LOSS ON HEATING / thin film oven** | Volatile loss and hardening | **AGEING during mixing and in service** |
| **SOLUBILITY in trichloroethylene** | Purity — the proportion of true bitumen | Minimum 99 per cent |
| **Water content** | Moisture present | Foaming during heating |

> **The PENETRATION test deserves the emphasis because it defines the GRADE, which is how bitumen is ordered and specified:**

| Grade | Penetration (1/10 mm) | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **30/40** | **30-40 — HARD** | **Hot climates; heavy traffic** |
| **60/70** | 60-70 | **The general-purpose paving grade** |
| **80/100** | **80-100 — SOFTER** | **Colder climates; surface dressing; hill roads** ← |
| **180/200** | Very soft | Cold regions |

> **Note the INVERSE relation between penetration and softening point: a HARDER bitumen has a LOWER penetration and a HIGHER softening point.**

> **So 30/40 grade is hard, penetrates little and softens at a high temperature; 80/100 is soft, penetrates more and softens lower.**

> **That inverse relation is a reliable cross-check: any answer that pairs a high penetration with a high softening point is wrong.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each is a real test with a distinct apparatus:**

| Option | Apparatus and measurement |
|---|---|
| **(a) Penetration** | **A NEEDLE under a 100 g load for 5 s at 25 °C; measures depth in 1/10 mm** |
| **(b) Ductility** | **A BRIQUETTE pulled apart at 50 mm/min in a water bath at 27 °C; measures elongation in cm** |
| **(c) Absolute viscosity** | **A capillary VISCOMETER under vacuum at 60 °C; measures poise** |

> **The distinguishing feature named in the stem is the STEEL BALL and the BRASS RING, which belong only to the softening point test** — so identifying the apparatus identifies the test, and that is the intended route.

> **It is worth learning these tests by their APPARATUS rather than by their names, since examination questions describe the procedure and ask for the test.** Needle, ball-and-ring, briquette, capillary: four objects, four tests.

examTip.trick: **Steel BALL in a brass RING = the SOFTENING POINT test.** Learn these tests by their apparatus: NEEDLE = penetration, BALL AND RING = softening point, BRIQUETTE = ductility, CAPILLARY = viscosity.
examTip.trap: **Bitumen has NO sharp melting point** — the softening point is the temperature at which it reaches an ARBITRARY consistency defined by the test itself. Change the ball's mass or the heating rate and the answer changes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Penetration and softening point are INVERSE**: 30/40 is HARD (low penetration, high softening point) for hot climates; 80/100 is SOFT for cold ones. Any answer pairing high penetration with a high softening point is wrong.

questions.stem: As per IRC, the recommended DESIGN SERVICE VOLUME for a two-lane undivided road with good access control in plain terrain is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 15,000 PCU per day.**

**The IRC design service volumes for rural roads (plain and rolling terrain, good access control):**

| Road type | Design service volume (PCU/day) |
|---|---|
| **SINGLE LANE (3.75 m)** | **2,000** ← option (d) |
| **INTERMEDIATE lane (5.5 m)** | **6,000** ← option (a) |
| **TWO LANE, undivided (7.0 m)** | **15,000** ✓ |
| **FOUR LANE, divided** | **35,000** ← option (c) |

> **So every distractor is the design service volume for a DIFFERENT road width**, and the option set is exactly this table.

> **The four figures — 2,000, 6,000, 15,000 and 35,000 — are worth memorising as a set, since they define the width at which each traffic volume requires an upgrade.**

> **Note the pattern: the values are NOT proportional to the number of lanes.**

> **Two lanes carry 15,000 against a single lane's 2,000 — SEVEN AND A HALF TIMES, not twice.**

> **The reason is that a single-lane road forces every meeting vehicle to slow and pull onto the shoulder, so its capacity is limited by the INTERACTION between opposing vehicles rather than by the lane's own throughput.**

> **Providing a second lane removes that interaction entirely, which is why the gain is so disproportionate.**

> **That has a direct planning consequence: widening a single-lane road to two lanes is one of the highest-return interventions available in road improvement, because a modest amount of construction removes a severe capacity constraint.**

**What a PCU is, and why traffic is counted in them:**

> **A PASSENGER CAR UNIT is a measure of the road space and interference a vehicle imposes, expressed relative to a car.**

| Vehicle | PCU (equivalency factor) |
|---|---|
| **Passenger car, taxi, van** | **1.0** |
| **Motorcycle, scooter** | **0.5** |
| **BICYCLE** | **0.5** |
| **Auto-rickshaw** | **1.2** |
| **Truck or bus** | **3.0** ← |
| **Tractor with trailer** | **4.5** |
| **CYCLE RICKSHAW** | **2.0** |
| **Hand cart** | **3.0** |
| **BULLOCK CART** | **6.0 to 8.0** ← the largest |

> **Traffic is counted in PCUs rather than vehicles because vehicles differ enormously in the road space and delay they impose.**

> **A stream of 1,000 buses is not equivalent to 1,000 cars — it is equivalent to about 3,000 cars, and the road must be designed accordingly.**

> **The BULLOCK CART figure of 6 to 8 PCU is worth noticing and is not a curiosity: a slow-moving cart on a two-lane road creates a moving queue behind it, and the delay it imposes on the traffic stream is far greater than its physical size suggests.**

> **So the PCU value reflects INTERFERENCE, not dimensions — which is why a cycle rickshaw at 2.0 exceeds a car at 1.0 despite being much smaller.**

> **That is the key to understanding the whole table: a PCU measures how much a vehicle DISRUPTS the stream, and slow vehicles disrupt it most.**

**Why it is a DESIGN SERVICE VOLUME rather than a CAPACITY — an important distinction:**

| | **CAPACITY** | **DESIGN SERVICE VOLUME** |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | **The MAXIMUM flow the road can physically carry** | **The flow at which an ACCEPTABLE LEVEL OF SERVICE is maintained** ← |
| **Conditions** | Congested, unstable flow | **Reasonable speed, comfort and safety** |
| **Used for** | Analysis of the limit | **DESIGN** |
| **Relation** | — | **DSV is a FRACTION of capacity, typically 0.6-0.8** |

> **Designing a road for its theoretical CAPACITY would produce a road that is permanently congested, because capacity is reached only under unstable, stop-start conditions.**

> **The design service volume is deliberately lower, so that the road operates at an acceptable speed and safety level for its design traffic.**

> **The concept behind it is the LEVEL OF SERVICE (LOS), graded A to F:**

| LOS | Condition |
|---|---|
| **A** | **Free flow; drivers unaffected by others** |
| **B** | Reasonably free flow |
| **C** | **Stable flow; manoeuvring restricted — usually the DESIGN target for a rural road** ← |
| **D** | Approaching unstable flow |
| **E** | **AT CAPACITY; unstable** |
| **F** | **Forced or breakdown flow; congestion** |

> **So a design service volume corresponds to LOS C or thereabouts, and the road reaches capacity only at LOS E.**

> **The gap between them is not waste but the margin that makes the road usable.**

**The TERRAIN and ACCESS CONTROL qualifications, since the stem states both:**

| Factor | Effect on the design service volume |
|---|---|
| **Terrain: plain → rolling → mountainous** | **REDUCES it — gradients and curves slow the stream and reduce overtaking** |
| **Access control: good → poor** | **REDUCES it substantially — every access point is a source of turning, stopping and conflict** ← |
| **Proportion of slow vehicles** | Reduces it (reflected in the PCU count) |
| **Carriageway and shoulder width** | Narrow shoulders reduce it |

> **The ACCESS CONTROL factor can reduce the service volume by 20 to 40 per cent, which is a very large effect for something that costs nothing to provide at the planning stage and is impossible to recover afterward.**

> **A two-lane road with ribbon development and unrestricted access may carry only 9,000 or 10,000 PCU/day at an acceptable service level, against 15,000 for the same pavement with access control.**

> **So permitting frontage access is equivalent to throwing away a third of the road's capacity — and it is a PLANNING decision, taken by a body other than the road authority, that determines whether the engineering investment is realised.**

> **That is worth stating plainly, because it is a case where the engineer's work is undone by decisions outside the engineer's control, and the professional response is to make the consequence explicit at the time rather than to observe it later.**

examTip.trick: **2,000 (single lane) / 6,000 (intermediate) / 15,000 (two lane) / 35,000 (four lane divided) PCU per day.** Every distractor is another width from the same table.
examTip.trap: **The values are NOT proportional to lanes** — two lanes carry 7.5 times a single lane's volume, because a single-lane road is limited by the INTERACTION of opposing vehicles, not by throughput. Hence widening to two lanes is a very high-return intervention.
examTip.mnemonic: **A PCU measures INTERFERENCE, not size** — which is why a cycle rickshaw (2.0) exceeds a car (1.0) and a bullock cart reaches 6-8. And a DESIGN SERVICE VOLUME is 60-80 % of capacity, corresponding to LOS C; designing to capacity gives a permanently congested road.

questions.stem: The total reaction time of a driver, comprising perception, intellection, emotion and volition, adopted by IRC for stopping sight distance calculations, is:
questions.solution:
**2.5 seconds.**

**The PIEV theory of driver reaction:**

> **The total reaction time is broken into four stages, and the acronym PIEV names them:**

| Stage | What occurs |
|---|---|
| **P — PERCEPTION** | **The stimulus registers on the driver's senses; the hazard is SEEN** |
| **I — INTELLECTION** | **The information is UNDERSTOOD — the object is identified as a hazard, and related to previous experience** |
| **E — EMOTION** | **The DECISION is taken; fear, anger, indecision or superstition may intervene** ← the human variable |
| **V — VOLITION** | **The action is EXECUTED — the muscles move, the foot reaches the brake** |

> **IRC adopts 2.5 seconds for stopping sight distance calculations.**

> **Note that a fifth element is sometimes added conceptually — the BRAKE LAG, the mechanical delay between the pedal moving and the brakes acting — though it is normally included within the 2.5 s allowance.**

**Why 2.5 seconds rather than a laboratory value — the important reasoning:**

> **In controlled experiments, an alert driver EXPECTING a signal reacts in 0.5 to 1.0 second.**

> **So the design value is two to five times the measured value, and that generosity is deliberate rather than careless.**

| Reason for the allowance | Note |
|---|---|
| **The driver is NOT EXPECTING the hazard** | **An unexpected event takes far longer to process than a expected signal** ← |
| **The population includes elderly, tired, inexperienced and distracted drivers** | **A road must be safe for the drivers who use it, not for the best of them** |
| **The hazard may be ambiguous — needing recognition, not just detection** | Intellection takes real time |
| **Night, rain, glare and fatigue all lengthen the response** | |
| **The consequence of the value being too small is DEATH** | The asymmetry justifies conservatism |

> **The second row states the governing principle and it is worth holding onto: SAFETY DESIGN MUST ACCOMMODATE THE ORDINARY USER, NOT THE CAPABLE ONE.**

> **A road designed for a 1-second reaction would be adequate for most drivers and lethal for a substantial minority — and the minority is not identifiable in advance.**

> **That principle is the same one behind the minimum eccentricity in a column, the load factors in a code, and the minimum weld size: the design value is set for the unfavourable case that will certainly occur somewhere.**

**How the value enters the calculation, and how much it matters:**

> **The LAG DISTANCE is 0.278 V t, so it is directly proportional to t:**

| Reaction time | Lag distance at 50 km/h | SSD at 50 km/h (f = 0.37) |
|---|---|---|
| **1.0 s** | **13.9 m** | **40.5 m** |
| **1.5 s** | **20.9 m** | **47.5 m** |
| **2.5 s** | **34.8 m** | **61.4 m** ← |
| **4.0 s** | **55.6 m** | **82.2 m** |

> **So adopting 2.5 s rather than 1.0 s increases the required sight distance by more than 50 per cent, which translates directly into longer vertical curves, greater setbacks at horizontal curves, and more earthwork.**

> **The reaction time allowance is therefore expensive — and it is where a substantial share of a road's geometric cost originates.**

> **Which is worth knowing, because it shows that the choice of a design parameter is not a technicality: 1.5 seconds against 2.5 would materially reduce construction cost, and the reason it is not adopted is that people would die.**

**The related reaction times used elsewhere, since 2.5 s is not universal:**

| Application | Reaction time |
|---|---|
| **STOPPING sight distance** | **2.5 s** ← |
| **OVERTAKING sight distance (the initial manoeuvre)** | **2 s** |
| **Intersection sight distance / gap acceptance** | **2 to 3 s** |
| **Traffic signal AMBER period** | **Based on about 1 s perception-reaction plus braking or clearing time** |
| **Design of a signal's ALL-RED clearance** | Time to clear the intersection |

> **The SIGNAL AMBER period is worth a note because it uses a shorter reaction time, and legitimately so: a driver approaching a signal is ALERT TO IT and expecting a change, which is precisely the condition under which reaction times are short.**

> **So the reaction time appropriate to a situation depends on whether the driver is EXPECTING the stimulus — which is exactly why 2.5 s is used for an unexpected hazard and 1 s for a signal.**

> **An amber period computed with 2.5 seconds would be so long that drivers would learn to treat amber as a continuation of green, which is a real and observed consequence of over-generous amber timing.**

> **That is an instructive case where MORE conservatism produces LESS safety, because it changes behaviour** — and it is a genuine limit on the principle of designing for the worst case.

**The other side of the equation, since SSD has two terms:**

> **The FRICTION coefficient f used in the braking term is also a design value, and IRC's values are deliberately low:**

| Speed (km/h) | Longitudinal friction coefficient f |
|---|---|
| **20 - 30** | **0.40** |
| **40** | **0.38** |
| **50** | **0.37** |
| **60** | **0.36** |
| **80** | **0.35** |
| **100** | **0.35** |

> **Note that f DECREASES with speed, which is physically correct: the tyre-road friction available falls as speed rises, partly because of reduced contact time and partly because of the water film that cannot be expelled at speed.**

> **And these values represent a WET road with a somewhat worn tyre — a dry road with good tyres gives 0.7 or more.**

> **So the SSD calculation combines a pessimistic reaction time with a pessimistic friction value, which is appropriate: the two adverse conditions are correlated, since a wet night is exactly when a driver's reaction is slowest and the road's friction lowest.**

> **Combining two pessimistic values would be over-conservative if the conditions were independent, and it is not over-conservative here because they occur together.** Recognising when adverse conditions are correlated is part of judging whether a design combination is reasonable.

examTip.trick: **PIEV = Perception, Intellection, Emotion, Volition; IRC adopts 2.5 s for stopping sight distance.**
examTip.trap: **A laboratory reaction time is 0.5-1.0 s, and the design value is deliberately two to five times it** — because the driver is NOT EXPECTING the hazard and the population includes tired, elderly and inexperienced drivers.
examTip.mnemonic: **A SIGNAL's amber period uses about 1 s, legitimately** — a driver approaching a signal IS expecting a change. Over-generous amber teaches drivers to treat it as green, so here MORE conservatism gives LESS safety. And note f FALLS with speed (0.40 at 30 km/h, 0.35 at 100).

questions.stem: The essential difference in the way a FLEXIBLE and a RIGID pavement carry wheel loads is that:
options: A flexible pavement carries the load in flexure while a rigid pavement carries it in compression only
A flexible pavement requires no subgrade preparation whereas a rigid pavement does
A flexible pavement transmits the load to the subgrade by grain-to-grain transfer through its layers, whereas a rigid pavement distributes it by slab (flexural) action over a wide area
A flexible pavement is designed for a single wheel load and a rigid pavement for an axle load
questions.solution:
**A flexible pavement transmits load by GRAIN-TO-GRAIN transfer through its layers; a rigid pavement distributes it by SLAB (flexural) action over a wide area.**

**The two mechanisms:**

> **FLEXIBLE pavement:**

> **The wheel load is transmitted downward from particle to particle through the granular layers, spreading out as it goes in a roughly conical distribution.**

> **Each layer distributes the load over a larger area of the layer beneath, so the pressure diminishes with depth.**

> **The pavement has NO significant flexural strength — it deforms with the subgrade beneath it, which is why it is called "flexible".**

> **The SUBGRADE therefore carries the load directly, and its strength (measured by CBR) governs the design.**

> **RIGID pavement:**

> **A concrete slab has high FLEXURAL strength, so it acts as a BEAM or PLATE spanning over the subgrade.**

> **The load is carried in BENDING by the slab and distributed over a wide area — several times the slab thickness in radius.**

> **The subgrade's role is to provide UNIFORM SUPPORT rather than strength, and it is characterised by the MODULUS OF SUBGRADE REACTION k, not by CBR.**

**The consequences of the two mechanisms — a systematic comparison:**

| | **FLEXIBLE** | **RIGID** |
|---|---|---|
| **Load transfer** | **Grain-to-grain, layer by layer** | **SLAB flexural action** ← |
| **Governing subgrade property** | **CBR** | **Modulus of subgrade reaction k** |
| **Design criterion** | **Limiting subgrade strain and fatigue cracking of the bituminous layer** | **Flexural stress in the slab (Westergaard)** |
| **Number of layers** | **Several (subgrade, sub-base, base, binder, surfacing)** | **Slab on a sub-base, often only two** |
| **Sensitivity to SUBGRADE weakness** | **HIGH — a soft spot shows through as a depression** | **LOW — the slab bridges over it** |
| **Sensitivity to NON-UNIFORM support** | Low | **HIGH — a void beneath the slab causes cracking** ← |
| **Design life** | **10 - 15 years** | **30 - 40 years** |
| **Initial cost** | **LOWER** | **HIGHER** |
| **Maintenance cost** | **HIGHER — periodic resurfacing** | **LOWER, but repairs are difficult and disruptive** |
| **Stage construction possible?** | **YES — layers can be added later** | **NO** |
| **Temperature stresses** | **Negligible** | **SIGNIFICANT — warping and expansion require JOINTS** |
| **Riding quality when new** | **Excellent** | Good; joints cause a rhythmic bump |
| **Repairability** | **Easy — patch and overlay** | **Difficult — a slab must be broken out** |
| **Suitability where the subgrade may settle** | **Better — it deforms and can be levelled up** | **Poor — the slab cracks** |

> **The rows about UNIFORMITY of support are worth pausing on because they seem paradoxical:**

> **A rigid pavement is INSENSITIVE to a weak subgrade (it bridges over it) but VERY SENSITIVE to a non-uniform one (a void causes the slab to crack in bending).**

> **So the failure of a rigid pavement is usually caused not by the subgrade being weak but by LOSS OF SUPPORT — pumping of fines from beneath the slab at joints, erosion by water, or settlement leaving a void.**

> **Which is why a rigid pavement's sub-base exists primarily to provide UNIFORM, NON-ERODIBLE, DRAINED support rather than to add strength**, and why drainage and joint sealing are the critical maintenance items for concrete roads.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **(a)** | **INVERTED — it is the RIGID pavement that carries load in flexure. A flexible pavement has essentially no flexural strength** ← |
| **(b)** | **False and dangerous: subgrade preparation and compaction are CRITICAL for a flexible pavement, because the subgrade carries the load directly** |
| **(d)** | **Both are designed for axle loads, expressed as standard axles (80 kN). Neither is designed for a single wheel load in isolation** |

> **Option (a) is the most instructive error because it exactly reverses the two mechanisms — and it is easy to make, since "flexible" sounds as though it should imply flexure.**

> **The name means the opposite: a flexible pavement FLEXES WITH the subgrade because it cannot resist bending, while a "rigid" pavement stays flat BECAUSE it resists bending.**

> **Getting that etymology right settles the question.**

**The intermediate types, since real pavements are not always one or the other:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **FLEXIBLE (bituminous)** | Granular layers with a bituminous surfacing |
| **RIGID (cement concrete)** | A concrete slab |
| **SEMI-RIGID** | **Layers with some cohesion — soil-cement, lean concrete base, cement-treated base — behaving between the two** ← |
| **COMPOSITE** | **A bituminous overlay on a concrete slab; combines the riding quality of one with the strength of the other** |
| **White topping** | A thin concrete overlay on a bituminous pavement |

> **The SEMI-RIGID category is increasingly the norm in modern heavy-duty flexible pavement design: a CEMENT-TREATED BASE gives much of a slab's load spreading with much of a flexible pavement's constructability.**

> **Its characteristic problem is REFLECTION CRACKING — the cemented layer cracks from shrinkage, and the crack propagates upward through the bituminous layers above.**

> **The remedy is a STRESS ABSORBING MEMBRANE INTERLAYER (SAMI) or a crack-relief layer between the two**, which absorbs the differential movement rather than transmitting it.

> **That is a good illustration of a general truth about pavement engineering: gaining stiffness in a layer introduces cracking, and each solution generates the next problem.** A pavement is a compromise between load spreading, which wants stiffness, and crack resistance, which wants flexibility.
tags: CBR and modulus of subgrade reaction

examTip.trick: **FLEXIBLE: grain-to-grain transfer, load spreads conically, subgrade carries it (CBR governs). RIGID: SLAB flexural action, load spread over a wide area (k governs).**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) exactly REVERSES the mechanisms** — and it is tempting because "flexible" sounds like flexure. It means the opposite: a flexible pavement flexes WITH the subgrade because it cannot resist bending.
examTip.mnemonic: **A rigid pavement is insensitive to a WEAK subgrade and very sensitive to a NON-UNIFORM one** — so its failures come from LOSS OF SUPPORT (pumping, erosion, voids), which is why drainage and joint sealing are its critical maintenance items.

questions.stem: The STANDARD AXLE LOAD used as the basis of flexible pavement design in India and Nepal is:
questions.solution:
**80 kN (8160 kg) — a single axle with dual wheels.**

**Why a STANDARD axle is needed at all:**

> **Real traffic contains axles of every weight, from a motorcycle's to an overloaded truck's.**

> **A pavement's damage, however, is not proportional to the load — it rises very steeply with it — so axles cannot simply be counted or their loads added.**

> **The solution is to convert every axle into an EQUIVALENT NUMBER OF STANDARD AXLES, using the FOURTH POWER LAW:**

> **VDF (equivalency factor) = (axle load / 80)⁴**

**The fourth power law and its consequences — the substance of this topic:**

| Axle load (kN) | Ratio to standard | **Equivalency factor (ratio⁴)** |
|---|---|---|
| **40** | **0.5** | **0.06** |
| **60** | **0.75** | **0.32** |
| **80** | **1.0** | **1.00** ← |
| **100** | **1.25** | **2.44** |
| **120** | **1.5** | **5.06** |
| **160** | **2.0** | **16.0** ← |
| **200** | **2.5** | **39.1** |

> **The consequences are startling and worth stating explicitly:**

> **DOUBLING an axle load multiplies the pavement damage SIXTEENFOLD.**

> **A single 160 kN axle does as much damage as SIXTEEN legal 80 kN axles.**

> **A 200 kN axle — a 150 per cent overload — does as much damage as THIRTY-NINE legal axles.**

> **So one grossly overloaded truck can do more damage in a single pass than forty properly loaded ones.**

**Why that fact matters more than almost anything else in pavement engineering:**

> **It means OVERLOADING is by far the most destructive influence on a road, and it dwarfs every other factor a designer controls.**

| Consideration | Effect |
|---|---|
| **A 20 per cent increase in traffic VOLUME** | **20 per cent more damage** |
| **A 20 per cent increase in axle LOADS** | **(1.2)⁴ = 107 per cent more damage — more than DOUBLE** ← |
| **Improving the pavement's design by one layer** | A modest gain |
| **Enforcing axle load limits** | **Potentially doubles or trebles the pavement's life** |

> **So AXLE LOAD ENFORCEMENT is the highest-return road maintenance intervention available, and it costs a fraction of resurfacing.**

> **That is worth stating as a professional judgement rather than an aside: a road authority spending its budget on overlays while permitting unrestricted overloading is resurfacing a pavement that will be destroyed again on the same schedule.**

> **Weighbridges and enforcement are pavement engineering, not merely policing.**

> **And it is why cars are essentially IRRELEVANT to pavement design: a 10 kN car axle has an equivalency factor of (10/80)⁴ = 0.00024, so about FOUR THOUSAND cars do the damage of one standard truck axle.**

> **A road carrying nothing but cars would last almost indefinitely; pavements are designed for trucks and buses alone.**

**How the design traffic is computed, since the standard axle is its unit:**

> **N = 365 × A × [(1+r)ⁿ − 1]/r × F × D**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **N** | **Cumulative standard axles (msa) over the design life** |
| **A** | **Initial number of commercial vehicles per day (in the year of completion)** |
| **r** | **Annual growth rate of traffic (minimum 5 per cent per IRC)** |
| **n** | **Design life in years (10-15 for flexible pavements)** |
| **F** | **VEHICLE DAMAGE FACTOR — average standard axles per commercial vehicle** ← |
| **D** | **Lane distribution factor** |

> **The VEHICLE DAMAGE FACTOR F is where the fourth power law enters, and it is where the design is most uncertain:**

| Condition | Typical VDF |
|---|---|
| **Terrain with low axle loads, under 1500 CV/day** | **1.5 - 2.5** |
| **Plain terrain, over 1500 CV/day** | **3.5 - 4.5** |
| **Where overloading is prevalent** | **6 or more** ← |

> **The VDF should be MEASURED by an axle load survey rather than assumed, and the reason is direct: an assumed VDF of 3.5 where the true value is 7 will halve the design traffic and produce a pavement that fails in half its intended life.**

> **Since the VDF depends on the fourth power of loads, it is extremely sensitive to the tail of the load distribution — the small number of heavily overloaded vehicles dominates it.**

> **So a survey must capture enough vehicles to characterise that tail, and a short survey that happens to miss the worst offenders will understate the VDF badly.**

**The distractors, for completeness:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **50 kN** | Not a standard; roughly a light truck's axle |
| **100 kN** | **Some countries' legal limit; equivalency 2.44** |
| **120 kN** | **A common legal TANDEM axle limit; equivalency 5.06 as a single axle** |
| **80 kN** | ✓ **The standard axle: 8160 kg, single axle, dual wheels** |

> **The value 80 kN corresponds to 8.16 tonnes, and it originates from the AASHO Road Test in the United States, where the equivalency relations were first established empirically.**

> **It has been adopted internationally as the reference, which is why pavement design traffic is quoted in "msa" — millions of standard axles — everywhere.**

> **Note also the DUAL WHEEL specification: the standard axle carries its 80 kN on four tyres, two at each end.**

> **A SINGLE-wheel axle at the same load would do more damage, because the contact pressure and the stress concentration are higher** — which is why tyre configuration, not just axle weight, appears in modern mechanistic design methods, and why single "super-single" tyres were treated with suspicion when introduced.

examTip.trick: **80 kN (8160 kg), single axle with DUAL wheels — the reference from which all traffic is converted to standard axles.**
examTip.trap: **The FOURTH POWER law: VDF = (load/80)⁴.** Doubling an axle load multiplies damage SIXTEENFOLD, and a 200 kN axle equals thirty-nine legal ones. Options (b) and (c) are other countries' legal limits.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 20 % increase in VOLUME gives 20 % more damage; a 20 % increase in LOAD gives 107 % more.** So axle-load ENFORCEMENT is the highest-return intervention in road maintenance — and cars are irrelevant, since 4,000 car axles equal one standard truck axle.

questions.stem: The correct sequence of operations in the construction of a Water Bound Macadam (WBM) course is:
options: Binding material, coarse aggregate, screenings, rolling
Coarse aggregate spread and dry rolled, screenings applied and rolled, binding material applied with water and rolled
Screenings, coarse aggregate, dry rolling, binding material
Coarse aggregate and binding material mixed together, spread, then rolled
questions.solution:
**Coarse aggregate spread and DRY rolled; then SCREENINGS applied and rolled; then BINDING MATERIAL applied with water and rolled.**

**The sequence, and the reason for each step:**

| Step | Operation | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Prepare the subgrade or the previous layer; provide lateral confinement (shoulders or kerbs)** | **A WBM layer has no cohesion and will spread sideways without confinement** ← |
| **2** | **Spread the COARSE AGGREGATE to the required loose thickness** | The structural skeleton |
| **3** | **DRY ROLL — from the edges toward the centre, with the roller** | **Interlock the coarse aggregate into a stable, keyed structure** |
| **4** | **Apply SCREENINGS (small chippings) in three or more thin layers, rolling and brooming between each** | **Fill the VOIDS between the coarse aggregate, wedging it tighter** |
| **5** | **Apply BINDING MATERIAL (fine soil, murum or stone dust) with WATER; roll and brush** | **Fill the remaining small voids and bind the surface** |
| **6** | **Continue rolling with water until a WAVE of grout appears ahead of the roller** | The completion test |
| **7** | **Allow to DRY (set) before opening to traffic** | The layer gains strength as it dries |

**Why the order cannot be changed — the point of the question:**

> **The whole strength of a WBM layer comes from the MECHANICAL INTERLOCK of the coarse aggregate.**

> **That interlock can only develop if the coarse aggregate is rolled while it is CLEAN — stone against stone, with nothing between the contact points.**

> **If the screenings or the binding material were applied FIRST, or mixed in beforehand, they would sit between the stones and PREVENT them touching.**

> **The layer would then be a weak mixture of stone in soil rather than a keyed stone skeleton, and it would have a fraction of the strength.**

> **So the sequence is not a convention: it is the whole mechanism.** Coarse aggregate first and dry, so it interlocks; the fines afterward, only to fill what remains.

> **Option (d) — mixing the aggregate and binding material together — is precisely the error that destroys the interlock, and it is a real and common malpractice on site because it is quicker.**

> **Options (a) and (c) place the fines before the coarse aggregate, with the same consequence.**

**The materials and their roles:**

| Material | Size | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **COARSE AGGREGATE** | **90-45 mm (Grading 1), 63-45 mm (Grading 2), 53-22.4 mm (Grading 3)** | **The load-bearing INTERLOCKING skeleton** |
| **SCREENINGS** | **13.2 mm or 11.2 mm down** | **Fill the voids and WEDGE the coarse aggregate** ← |
| **BINDING MATERIAL** | **Fine soil, murum, stone dust passing 425 micron** | **Fill the final small voids; provide cohesion and a running surface** |

> **Note the practice for HARD, ANGULAR aggregate: where the coarse aggregate is hard and well-shaped, the interlock is good and the screenings may be reduced or the binding material omitted.**

> **Where the aggregate is soft or rounded, more screenings and binding material are needed to make up for the poor interlock.**

> **So the quantities depend on the aggregate's quality — which is the practical reason the specification gives quantities as ranges rather than fixed figures.**

**Why the ROLLING is done from the EDGES toward the CENTRE:**

> **On a cambered or superelevated surface, the layer would be pushed downhill if rolled from the centre outward.**

> **Rolling from the LOW EDGE inward and upward confines the material and compacts it against the already-compacted edge.**

> **And the edges are the most vulnerable part of any granular layer — unconfined on one side — so compacting them first and thoroughly is what prevents edge failure.**

> **EDGE FAILURE is in fact the characteristic failure of a WBM road: the unsupported edge crumbles under a wheel that strays onto it, and the failure progresses inward.**

> **Which is why proper SHOULDER construction, built up simultaneously with the WBM layer to confine it, is not a finishing operation but a structural requirement.**

**Why WBM survives at all, and its limitations — stated honestly:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Uses LOCAL stone and unskilled labour** | **No plant, no bitumen, no cement** ← |
| **Very cheap** | |
| **Repairable with hand tools** | |
| **Adequate as a BASE course under a bituminous surfacing** | Its principal modern use |

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Requires WATER in quantity during construction** | Difficult in dry seasons and remote sites |
| **The binding material can be WASHED OUT by rain** | Loss of cohesion |
| **Dusty in dry weather, muddy in wet** | Unsuitable as a running surface for significant traffic |
| **Not suitable for heavy traffic without a bituminous surfacing** | Ravels and forms potholes |
| **Slow — several rolling and drying stages** | |

> **The comparison with WET MIX MACADAM (WMM) is the practically relevant one, since WMM has largely displaced WBM for base courses:**

| | **WBM** | **WMM** |
|---|---|---|
| **Aggregate** | **Single-sized coarse, with separate screenings and binder** | **A GRADED aggregate, 45 mm to fines, premixed** |
| **Mixing** | **On the road, in stages** | **In a PLANT (pugmill), with optimum water** |
| **Fines** | **Applied afterward as binding material** | **Included in the grading from the start** |
| **Strength mechanism** | **INTERLOCK of coarse stone** | **DENSE GRADED aggregate matrix** |
| **Speed and quality control** | Slow, variable | **Fast, uniform** ← |
| **Water needed on site** | **Large quantities** | Only what the plant adds |

> **So WMM abandons the interlock principle in favour of a DENSE GRADING — a continuous distribution of sizes that achieves low voids and high strength by packing rather than by keying.**

> **That is a genuinely different mechanism, and it is why WMM's fines are mixed IN from the start while WBM's must be kept OUT until the interlock has formed.**

> **Which resolves an apparent contradiction: the very practice that ruins a WBM layer is the correct practice for a WMM layer.** The two are not variants of one method but different answers to the same problem, and applying one method's rules to the other produces a poor road either way.

examTip.trick: **Coarse aggregate → DRY roll → screenings (in thin layers, rolled) → binding material with water → roll until a grout wave appears → dry before opening.**
examTip.trap: **Option (d) — premixing aggregate and binding material — is the real site malpractice that destroys the layer.** The fines must be kept OUT until the coarse stone has interlocked, stone against stone.
examTip.mnemonic: **WBM works by INTERLOCK, WMM by DENSE GRADING** — which is why WBM's fines are added last and WMM's are mixed in from the start. The practice that ruins one is correct for the other. And roll from the EDGES inward, or the layer is pushed downhill.

questions.stem: The system of road planning in which the optimum road length for an area is determined from the UTILITY derived per unit length of road is called:
questions.solution:
**The MAXIMUM UTILITY system, also called the SATURATION system.**

**How the method works:**

> **The area to be served is considered, and the road network is planned so as to SATURATE it with the optimum length of road — the length at which the utility obtained per unit length is maximised.**

> **Utility is assessed by assigning UTILITY UNITS to the features a road serves:**

| Basis of utility | Typical unit assignment |
|---|---|
| **POPULATION served** | **Units by population range — e.g. 0.5 units per 1000 people under 2000, rising for larger settlements** |
| **PRODUCTIVE (agricultural and industrial) area served** | **Units per unit area, weighted by productivity** |
| **Industrial and agricultural produce** | Units by tonnage or value |

> **Alternative alignments and networks are then compared by their TOTAL UTILITY UNITS, and the one giving the greatest utility for a given road length — or the required utility for the least length — is selected.**

**Why the method is useful — and its honest limitations:**

| Strength | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provides an OBJECTIVE, comparable basis for choosing between alignments** | **Replaces pure judgement with a computable index** ← |
| **Explicitly accounts for the population and production actually served** | Rather than merely connecting points on a map |
| **Simple enough to apply without extensive data** | Suits a country with limited traffic data |

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The utility units are ARBITRARY** | **Chosen by convention; a different weighting gives a different answer** ← |
| **Ignores construction COST and terrain difficulty** | **A serious omission in mountainous country** |
| **Ignores the road's function in the network hierarchy** | A short link with low local utility may be strategically essential |
| **Treats utility as static** | Roads GENERATE development, which the index cannot foresee |

> **The COST omission is the most serious in the Nepali context and worth stating plainly: two alignments serving the same villages may differ by a factor of five in construction cost if one follows a ridge and the other crosses a gorge.**

> **A utility comparison that ignores that difference is not a sufficient basis for a decision, and the method must be used alongside a cost estimate rather than instead of one.**

> **The last limitation is the most interesting and the least tractable: a road does not merely serve existing population and production — it CREATES them.**

> **A road to a valley with little agriculture may, within a decade, generate the market access that makes agriculture worthwhile there.**

> **So a utility index computed on today's population systematically UNDERVALUES roads into undeveloped areas — which are precisely the roads that development policy wants to build.**

> **That is an inherent circularity in transport planning and not a defect of this method alone: traffic forecasts based on present activity always understate the effect of new access.**

**The other options — each a real concept in road planning:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **(b) STAR AND GRID system** | **A NETWORK PATTERN — radial routes from a centre (star) combined with a rectangular grid. One of several geometric patterns (star and block, star and circular, hexagonal, minimum travel)** |
| **(c) NAGPUR road plan** | **The FIRST twenty-year road development plan for India (1943-1963), which established the five-class road hierarchy (NH, SH, MDR, ODR, VR) and used the STAR AND GRID pattern** ← |
| **(d) LUCKNOW road plan** | **The THIRD twenty-year plan (1981-2001), which introduced the MAXIMUM UTILITY / saturation approach and planned for expressways** |

> **The relationship between (a) and (d) is worth being clear about, since they are connected: the LUCKNOW plan is the plan that ADOPTED the maximum utility approach.**

> **So option (d) names the plan and option (a) names the method — and the question asks for the method.**

> **The three Indian twenty-year plans, since papers ask for them:**

| Plan | Period | Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| **NAGPUR** | **1943 - 1963** | **The five-class classification; star and grid pattern; road length by area formula** |
| **BOMBAY** | **1961 - 1981** | **Introduced the concept of road DENSITY related to area and population; the second plan** |
| **LUCKNOW** | **1981 - 2001** | **MAXIMUM UTILITY (saturation) system; expressways; primary/secondary/tertiary system** ← |

> **The progression across the three plans is itself instructive: from a purely GEOMETRIC criterion (road length per unit area) in the Nagpur plan, through a DENSITY criterion in the Bombay plan, to a UTILITY criterion in the Lucknow plan.**

> **Each step moved from a measure of how much road EXISTS toward a measure of how much good it DOES — which is the right direction, and the maximum utility system is the furthest development of it.**

**The network PATTERNS, since option (b) names one:**

| Pattern | Character |
|---|---|
| **RECTANGULAR or block** | Grid; simple; poor for diagonal movement |
| **RADIAL or STAR and BLOCK** | Radials from a centre with a grid between |
| **STAR AND CIRCULAR** | **Radials plus ring roads — good for bypassing the centre** |
| **STAR AND GRID** | **Radials plus a grid; the Nagpur plan's choice** ← |
| **HEXAGONAL** | Three roads at each junction; efficient but unfamiliar |
| **MINIMUM TRAVEL** | Optimised for total travel distance |

> **The STAR AND CIRCULAR pattern deserves the note because it addresses the characteristic failure of a purely radial network: all traffic is forced through the centre.**

> **Adding RING roads lets traffic pass between radials without entering the centre, which is why every large city eventually builds one** — and why the Kathmandu Ring Road exists.
